Name: Mohd Arif Mir ( Figar)
Theme: Wisdom lies in reconciliation of our indentity based contradictions
Title: When Monster Meets Noble Savage Again Figar Arif
Content:
There are meetings that happen in places, and there are meetings that happen beyond places.
 
The first kind is easy to understand.
 
Two people sit across a table, exchange greetings, speak about ordinary things, laugh at familiar jokes, discuss the weather, work, society, friends, politics, or perhaps some incident of the day, and eventually leave. Such meetings begin and end within the boundaries of time. We remember where they happened, when they happened, and sometimes even what was said.
 
But there is another kind of meeting.
 
It may begin in an ordinary place, at an ordinary hour, among ordinary people, and yet something extraordinary may happen within it. The place remains the same, but the people are no longer quite the same. Words cease to be merely words. Silence begins to speak. Ideas become bridges. Questions become doors.
 
And somewhere between one thought and another, two human beings discover that they are no longer sitting in a dhaba, a room, a garden, or anywhere upon the physical earth.
 
They have entered another geography.
The geography of consciousness.
Perhaps our meeting was one such meeting.
 
It began without any grand announcement. There was no expectation that the evening would become memorable. We met again in a large dhaba, a place designed for movement rather than contemplation. People were coming and going. Voices were rising and falling. Steel glasses moved from one table to another. Plates travelled between strangers. Tea boiled somewhere behind the counter. The air carried the familiar mixture of smoke, spices, dust and conversation.
 
Outside, vehicles passed occasionally, their headlights cutting through the evening darkness.
Inside, people were eating, laughing, arguing and living their small portions of life.
Nothing suggested that something unusual was about to happen.
 
We exchanged the usual greetings: A smile.
 
A few ordinary questions.
● How are you?
● How have you been?
● What are you doing these days?
 
The kind of questions people ask without expecting that the answers will become important. But human beings are strange creatures. Sometimes the deepest revolutions begin with the simplest greetings.
 
A question was raised.
Another question followed.
An idea encountered another idea.
And then, almost imperceptibly, conversation stopped being conversation.
 
It became a journey.
At first, it walked.
Then it ran.
Then, without warning, it began to fly.
 
We began from our respective intellectual territories. Each of us carried our own history, our own convictions, our own doubts, our own experiences, and perhaps our own prejudices. We moved from one subject to another, sometimes deliberately and sometimes without direction.
 
Ethics appeared before us.
Religion entered the conversation.
Politics followed.
Morality stood somewhere between them.
Philosophy opened another door.
Poetry entered through the window.
Human nature became a question.
Freedom became another.
We did not seem to be travelling from one subject to another.
We seemed to be travelling through ourselves.
And perhaps that is why, after a while, the physical surroundings disappeared.
 
The dhaba was still there, but we were no longer entirely there.
Our bodies remained at the table.
Our minds had travelled elsewhere.
We had taken an aerial journey.
 
For a while, our intellectual spheres moved parallel to each other. Each had its own orbit, its own direction, its own history. Yet gradually, almost imperceptibly, the distance between them began to disappear.
 
Somewhere above ordinary time and space, they touched.
And when two intellectual worlds touch without trying to conquer each other, something rare happens.
 
Dialogue begins.
Not debate.
Not competition.
Dialogue.
The difference is profound.
Debate often asks:
● Who is right?
Dialogue asks:
● What can we discover together?
 
That evening, neither of us seemed particularly interested in victory.
We were interested in discovery.
And somewhere in that discovery, I encountered an old inhabitant of my own soul.
 
The Monster
For a long time, I had imagined my intellectual existence as a movement between two opposite poles.
 
One I called the Monster.
The other I called the Noble Savage.
The names are deliberately contradictory.
Perhaps that contradiction is the whole story.
 
The Monster is the part of me that refuses to accept the world as it is.
 
He is suspicious of inherited morality.
He questions authority.
He challenges conventions.
He is restless before injustice.
He does not easily bow before established truths.
 
He is sometimes arrogant, sometimes angry, sometimes excessively rational, and occasionally destructive in his insistence upon freedom.
 
The Noble Savage is different.
He is the innocent part of me.
He believes in love before argument, compassion before ideology, human dignity before political identity.
 
He does not possess an elaborate philosophy because perhaps he does not need one.
He knows some things instinctively.
He knows that a wounded person needs compassion.
He knows that beauty can exist without explanation.
He knows that nature does not need a theory in order to be beautiful.
He knows that silence can be meaningful.
 
For years, I imagined that these two personalities were fighting each other.
The Monster considered the Noble Savage.
The Noble Savage considered the Monster unnecessarily violent.
The Monster believed that the Noble Savage needed enlightenment.
The Noble Savage perhaps believed that the Monster needed healing.
 
And I, somewhere between them, kept calling myself Figar and Arif, as though two names could contain two different worlds.
 
But perhaps I was mistaken.
Perhaps the Monster and the Noble Savage were never enemies.
Perhaps they were two incomplete attempts to describe the same human being.
The Birth of the Monster
My Monster did not appear suddenly.
He was born slowly.
He was created by questions.
 
Every time I encountered an injustice that had been normalized, he became stronger.
Every time I saw hypocrisy disguised as morality, he became louder.
Every time authority demanded obedience without explanation, he asked why.
Every time society asked me to accept something merely because it had always been accepted, he became restless.
 
He was not satisfied with inherited answers.
He wanted to know.
● Why?
● Why should a person obey?
● Why should one truth be considered sacred while another is condemned?
● Why should morality belong exclusively to institutions?
● Why should religion become a boundary between human beings rather than a bridge between them?
● Why should politics consume compassion?
● Why should knowledge make us arrogant rather than humble?
● Why should civilization call itself civilized while repeatedly producing violence?
 
The Monster asked too many questions.
And society rarely likes people who ask too many questions.
 
So he was named difficult.
Then rebellious.
Then impractical.
Then dangerous.
 
Eventually, I began calling him Monster.
Perhaps the name was partly an accusation and partly an affection.
Because there was something beautiful about him too.
He refused to surrender his mind.
 
He protected a certain freedom within me.
He reminded me that intellectual slavery can be more dangerous than physical imprisonment.
He made me suspicious of certainty.
He taught me that every system deserves examination.
But there was also a price.
 
The Monster sometimes forgot that truth without compassion can become cruelty.
He sometimes believed that destroying an illusion was enough.
 
He sometimes thought that exposing hypocrisy was equivalent to creating justice.
 
He sometimes confused intellectual superiority with wisdom.
 
And perhaps that is where the Noble Savage became necessary.
 
### **The Innocence of the Noble Savage**
 
The Noble Savage was never interested in winning arguments.
 
He was interested in remaining human.
 
He did not have a library of philosophical references. He did not need Nietzsche, Rousseau, Gandhi, Iqbal, Marx, Foucault or anyone else to tell him that suffering mattered.
 
He simply felt it.
 
When someone was hurt, he wanted to help.
 
When someone cried, he wanted to listen.
 
When someone was lonely, he wanted to sit beside them.
 
He possessed something that the Monster frequently lost in the labyrinth of thought:
 
**innocence.**
 
But innocence has its own danger.
 
It can become ignorance.
 
Compassion without awareness may become helplessness.
 
Love without understanding may become submission.
 
Peace without justice may become silence before oppression.
 
And therefore the Noble Savage also needed the Monster.
 
He needed someone who would ask questions when his innocence became complacency.
 
He needed someone who would challenge the structures that produced suffering.
 
He needed someone who would say:
 
Love is not enough if we refuse to understand why people suffer.
 
Compassion is not enough if we remain silent before injustice.
 
Peace is not enough if it is built upon fear.
 
Faith is not enough if it prevents inquiry.
 
And knowledge is not enough if it destroys compassion.
 
Perhaps this was the beginning of my real education.
 
Not the education that produces degrees.
 
Not the education that produces titles.
 
Not even the education that fills libraries.
 
But the education that teaches one human being how to hold contradiction without immediately destroying one side of it.
 
### **When They Met Again**
 
That evening, something changed.
 
The Monster rose.
 
He looked toward the Noble Savage.
 
But instead of attacking him, he paused.
 
For the first time, there was no war.
 
There was recognition.
 
The Monster saw that the Noble Savage had survived everything.
 
He had survived disappointment without becoming cynical.
 
He had survived ignorance without becoming arrogant.
 
He had survived pain without becoming cruel.
 
He had preserved something the Monster himself had almost lostâthe ability to love without demanding a philosophical justification for love.
 
And the Noble Savage looked at the Monster.
 
Perhaps he saw something too.
 
He saw that the Monster was not simply darkness.
 
He saw the wounds beneath his anger.
 
He saw that behind every question was often a desire for truth.
 
Behind every rebellion was perhaps a desire for dignity.
 
Behind every intellectual attack was sometimes a longing to protect something precious.
 
The Monster was not fighting because he hated the world.
 
Perhaps he was fighting because he loved the possibility of a better world too intensely.
 
That realization changed everything.
 
The Monster did not have to destroy the Noble Savage.
 
The Noble Savage did not have to silence the Monster.
 
They could sit together.
 
They could listen.
 
They could argue.
 
They could disagree.
 
They could remain contradictory.
 
And still belong to the same human being.
 
Perhaps maturity is not the disappearance of contradiction.
 
Perhaps maturity is learning how to live with contradiction without allowing it to become destruction.
 
The Monster had always wanted victory.
 
The Noble Savage had always wanted peace.
 
Now they could seek understanding.
 
That may be the beginning of wisdom.
 
### **The Intervention of Silence**
 
But something else made this encounter possible.
 
A human presence.
 
An angel-like presence, if I may use that word without turning it into mythology.
 
Someone whose influence did not come through loud instruction.
 
There are people who teach by speaking.
 
There are others who teach by listening.
 
And there are a rare few who teach through silence.
 
Meaningful silence is not emptiness.
 
It is a language.
 
Sometimes a person remains silent because they have nothing to say.
 
But sometimes they remain silent because what they are saying cannot be reduced to words.
 
That silence can become an intellectual intervention.
 
It can make us uncomfortable.
 
It can force us to examine ourselves.
 
It can create a space in which our own thoughts become audible.
 
Perhaps that was what happened to me.
 
I had spent years constructing arguments against the world.
 
Suddenly, without being directly instructed, I began questioning the person who was constructing those arguments.
 
What if the problem is not always the world?
 
What if sometimes the problem is the way I look at it?
 
What if my resistance to the world has itself become a prison?
 
What if my insistence upon intellectual independence has made me emotionally dependent upon conflict?
 
What if I have become so accustomed to fighting that peace itself has begun to appear suspicious?
 
These are uncomfortable questions.
 
But meaningful encounters are often uncomfortable precisely because they do not leave us where they found us.
 
Sometimes another human being does not change your life by giving you answers.
 
Sometimes they change it by making you ask better questions.
 
And sometimes the greatest intervention is silence.
 
A meaningful silence.
 
A silence that does not abandon you.
 
A silence that accompanies you.
 
A silence that gives you enough space to hear your own forgotten voice.
 
Perhaps that was what had happened.
 
The Monster had heard something.
 
The Noble Savage had heard something.
 
And somewhere between them, Figar had begun to listen.
 
### **The World as Prison and Garden**
 
For a long time, the world appeared to me as a prison.
 
Perhaps I was not entirely wrong.
 
Human civilization has constructed many forms of imprisonment.
 
There are political prisons, social prisons, economic prisons, religious prisons and psychological prisons.
 
There are prisons without walls.
 
A person can be imprisoned by poverty.
 
Another can be imprisoned by privilege.
 
One can be imprisoned by fear of public opinion.
 
Another by the desire for public approval.
 
One can be imprisoned by dogma.
 
Another by excessive skepticism.
 
Even intelligence can become a prison when it begins to believe that it has understood everything.
 
I had perhaps built my own prison from resistance.
 
I wanted to remain free, and therefore I fought.
 
I fought intellectually.
 
I fought morally.
 
I fought philosophically.
 
I fought against the obvious and sometimes against the invisible.
 
But somewhere along the way, I forgot an important truth:
 
**Freedom is not merely freedom from something. It is also freedom for something.**
 
Freedom from oppression must become freedom for dignity.
 
Freedom from dogma must become freedom for inquiry.
 
Freedom from hatred must become freedom for love.
 
Freedom from fear must become freedom for living.
 
Otherwise, rebellion itself becomes another form of imprisonment.
 
That evening, for the first time in a long time, I wondered:
 
What if the world is not only a prison?
 
What if it is also a garden?
 
What if the same world that produces cruelty also produces kindness?
 
The same society that manufactures oppression also produces resistance?
 
The same human being who can destroy can also create?
 
The same mind that invents weapons can write poetry?
 
The same hands that can hurt can heal?
 
Perhaps existence is not divided as neatly as we imagine.
 
Perhaps good and evil do not live in separate countries.
 
Perhaps they are neighbours.
 
Perhaps they sometimes live under the same roof.
 
Perhaps every human being carries a little forest inside.
 
There are wolves there.
 
There are flowers.
 
There are poisonous plants.
 
There are streams.
 
There are storms.
 
There are birds that sing even after the night has become unbearably dark.
 
The mistake is not that the forest contains monsters.
 
The mistake is believing that we are only the monsters.
 
And perhaps the opposite mistake is believing that we are only noble.
 
### **The Meeting of Ethics and Love**
 
Our conversation moved through ethics.
 
What is good?
 
What is evil?
 
Who defines morality?
 
Can morality exist without religion?
 
Can religion exist without morality?
 
Can political systems remain humane?
 
Can human beings possess power without becoming prisoners of power?
 
These questions have no simple answers.
 
But perhaps the purpose of philosophy is not always to provide answers.
 
Sometimes philosophy teaches us how to ask better questions.
 
And poetry does something similar through another language.
 
Poetry does not always explain life.
 
It reveals it.
 
A poet may take an ordinary moment and make us see it differently.
 
A philosopher may take an ordinary assumption and make us question it.
 
A compassionate human being may take an ordinary silence and make us feel understood.
 
Perhaps all three are forms of the same human desire:
 
**to see beyond the surface.**
 
The Monster wants to see beyond appearances.
 
The Noble Savage wants to feel beyond appearances.
 
And perhaps wisdom begins when seeing and feeling stop fighting each other.
 
### **Religion, Politics and the Human Being**
 
Religion entered our conversation too.
 
Religion has often been treated as an answer to the deepest questions of existence.
 
But perhaps religion also creates questions.
 
Who are we?
 
Why are we here?
 
What do we owe one another?
 
What is justice?
 
What is forgiveness?
 
What is death?
 
What survives us?
 
And politics asks another set of questions.
 
Who possesses power?
 
Who makes decisions?
 
Who benefits?
 
Who is excluded?
 
What is justice within society?
 
What does freedom mean when resources are unequal?
 
These questions are different, yet they intersect.
 
The spiritual life asks about the human soul.
 
The political life asks about human society.
 
But the same human being inhabits both.
 
That is why separating them completely is difficult.
 
A person may pray in solitude and still have responsibilities toward society.
 
A person may speak about revolution and still need compassion.
 
A person may defend tradition and still need humility.
 
A person may reject tradition and still need wisdom.
 
The Monster and Noble Savage therefore appeared again.
 
One demanded justice.
 
The other demanded compassion.
 
One demanded truth.
 
The other demanded humanity.
 
And perhaps both were right in what they were seeking, even when each became wrong in the way he sought it.
 
### **The Danger of Becoming Only One Thing**
 
Human beings love simple identities.
 
We like to say:
 
I am rational.
 
I am spiritual.
 
I am progressive.
 
I am traditional.
 
I am rebellious.
 
I am peaceful.
 
I am intellectual.
 
I am emotional.
 
But perhaps every such identity becomes dangerous when it becomes complete.
 
A human being is never only one thing.
 
I can be rational in one moment and emotional in another.
 
I can be courageous and afraid.
 
I can be generous and selfish.
 
I can be wise in one situation and foolish in another.
 
I can love someone and disagree with them.
 
I can oppose an idea without hating the person who holds it.
 
The human being is a moving contradiction.
 
Perhaps that is not a defect.
 
Perhaps it is our nature.
 
The Monster wanted consistency.
 
The Noble Savage wanted authenticity.
 
Life demanded complexity.
 
And perhaps the real self exists somewhere inside that complexity.
 
### **The Discovery of Integration**
 
There was a time when I wanted to choose between Figar and Arif.
 
Between the thinker and the human being.
 
Between the Monster and the Noble Savage.
 
Between rebellion and compassion.
 
Between intellect and innocence.
 
But perhaps I no longer need to choose.
 
Perhaps Figar can think while Arif feels.
 
Perhaps Arif can love while Figar questions.
 
Perhaps the Monster can protect the Noble Savage.
 
Perhaps the Noble Savage can humanize the Monster.
 
This does not mean that contradiction has disappeared.
 
It means that contradiction has become dialogue.
 
And dialogue is very different from war.
 
War seeks victory.
 
Dialogue seeks understanding.
 
The Monster had always wanted victory.
 
The Noble Savage had always wanted peace.
 
Now they could perhaps seek understanding.
 
That may be the beginning of wisdom.
 
### **The Singer of the Heart**
 
And somewhere in this entire experience, another realization emerged.
 
There are people who become part of our intellectual history without writing a single page in our books.
 
They enter our lives and alter the rhythm of our thinking.
 
They may never know the full extent of their influence.
 
They may speak one sentence.
 
They may remain silent.
 
They may simply exist differently.
 
Yet something within us changes.
 
Perhaps that is what it means when someone becomes the singer of the heart.
 
A singer does not necessarily change the world.
 
Sometimes a singer changes the way one person hears the world.
 
The melody does not remove suffering.
 
It changes our relationship with suffering.
 
It does not erase darkness.
 
It teaches us that darkness too can contain stars.
 
Perhaps the person who inspired this transformation did not give me answers.
 
Perhaps they gave me something more valuable:
 
**the courage to reconsider my questions.**
 
And perhaps that is the deepest form of influence one human being can have upon anotherânot to occupy their mind, but to awaken something within it.
 
### **A Temporary Peace**
 
I say âfor the time beingâ because I do not trust permanent declarations about the human soul.
 
Tomorrow the Monster may return.
 
He may become angry again.
 
He may look at the world and see hypocrisy.
 
He may question institutions.
 
He may reject easy answers.
 
And the Noble Savage may again retreat into innocence.
 
That is acceptable.
 
I am not writing the story of a final transformation.
 
Life does not work that way.
 
There is no final chapter while we are alive.
 
We change.
 
We return.
 
We regress.
 
We learn.
 
We forget.
 
We remember again.
 
Perhaps every transformation is temporary until it becomes a habit.
 
And perhaps every habit must occasionally be challenged by a new transformation.
 
So I do not claim that I have defeated the Monster.
 
Nor do I claim that the Noble Savage has finally enlightened him.
 
I simply say that they met.
 
And this time, they did not fight.
 
Sometimes that is enough.
 
### **The Student of Life**
 
I have often called myself a student of life.
 
I like that identity because it protects me from the arrogance of completion.
 
A student can change his mind.
 
A student can admit ignorance.
 
A student can ask.
 
A student can listen.
 
A student can be wrong without believing that his entire identity has collapsed.
 
The greatest danger in intellectual life is perhaps not ignorance.
 
It is certainty.
 
Ignorance says:
 
**I do not know.**
 
Certainty sometimes says:
 
**There is nothing left to know.**
 
The first can begin a journey.
 
The second can end one.
 
I would rather remain a student.
 
I would rather continue asking.
 
I would rather discover tomorrow that something I believed yesterday was incomplete.
 
I would rather be corrected by life than protected by my own ego.
 
Perhaps this is why every encounter matters.
 
Every person becomes a possible teacher.
 
Every disagreement becomes an opportunity.
 
Every silence becomes a text.
 
Every wound becomes a question.
 
Every moment of beauty becomes an invitation.
 
### **Beyond Time and Space**
 
When I look back at that meeting, I no longer remember the physical details with the same intensity.
 
I remember the movement of thought.
 
I remember the feeling that two intellectual worlds had begun to overlap.
 
I remember how a conversation that began casually became something deeper.
 
And I remember the strange sensation that we had somehow left the ordinary world.
 
Perhaps that is why I describe it as a journey above time and space.
 
Human consciousness has its own geography.
 
There are places within us that have no coordinates.
 
There are memories that belong nowhere.
 
There are encounters that cannot be measured by duration.
 
A conversation may last three hours and leave no trace.
 
Another may last twenty minutes and remain with us for years.
 
Time measures duration.
 
It does not measure significance.
 
Space measures distance.
 
It does not measure intimacy.
 
Perhaps our spheres met not because we agreed on everything, but because we were willing to enter each other's intellectual space without destroying it.
 
That is rare.
 
And therefore precious.
 
### **The Road Home**
 
When we finally rose from the table, the night had become quiet.
 
The dhaba looked almost different.
 
The same tables.
 
The same chairs.
 
The same road.
 
The same darkness.
 
But I was carrying a different world inside me.
 
I stepped outside.
 
The air was cool.
 
Somewhere in the distance, a vehicle moved along the mountain road, its headlights appearing briefly and then disappearing around a bend.
 
I watched them vanish.
 
And suddenly I thought of our conversation.
 
Life is perhaps like that road.
 
We see only a small portion of it.
 
The rest disappears around the bend.
 
Yet we continue.
 
Not because we know where the road ends.
 
But because something within us asks us to move.
 
I smiled.
 
The Monster was still there.
 
The Noble Savage was still there.
 
Figar was still there.
 
Arif was still there.
 
None of them had disappeared.
 
And perhaps they did not need to.
 
I had spent years imagining that one must conquer the other.
 
Now I understood that perhaps they had been waiting for reconciliation.
 
The Monster did not need to die.
 
He needed a heart.
 
The Noble Savage did not need to disappear.
 
He needed a voice.
 
And Figar did not need to choose between them.
 
He needed to become the place where they could meet.
 
That night I walked away carrying no victory.
 
Only a strange peace.
 
A peace that did not come from solving life.
 
It came from accepting that life may never be solved.
 
Perhaps we are not equations.
 
Perhaps we are poems.
 
And a poem is not required to provide a final answer.
 
It only has to open something within us.
 
A door.
 
A window.
 
A memory.
 
A wound.
 
A possibility.
 
As I walked, I thought about all the people who had entered my life and left something behind.
 
Some left arguments.
 
Some left wounds.
 
Some left laughter.
 
Some left questions.
 
Some left silence.
 
And a very few left a new way of looking at myself.
 
Perhaps every human encounter is a mirror.
 
Some mirrors show us the face we present to the world.
 
Others show us the face we hide from ourselves.
 
And the rarest mirrors show us both.
 
That evening had been such a mirror.
 
The Monster had looked at the Noble Savage.
 
The Noble Savage had looked at the Monster.
 
And I had stood between them.
 
For the first time, I understood that neither was the whole truth.
 
The truth was somewhere in their meeting.
 
Somewhere in the space between knowledge and innocence.
 
Between rebellion and tenderness.
 
Between reason and affection.
 
Between the desire to change the world and the desire simply to love it.
 
Perhaps this is what growing older really means.
 
Not becoming certain.
 
Becoming capable of living with uncertainty.
 
Not knowing everything.
 
Learning how much remains unknown.
 
Not winning every argument.
 
Learning when an argument is less important than a human being.
 
Not destroying every illusion.
 
Learning which illusions give beauty to existence.
 
And not becoming so intelligent that we forget how to be kind.
 
### **The Monster and the Noble Savage Were One**
 
Perhaps the greatest realization of all is the simplest.
 
The Monster and the Noble Savage were never two people.
 
They were never even two complete personalities.
 
They were fragments of one human existence.
 
The Monster carried my questions.
 
The Noble Savage carried my tenderness.
 
The Monster protected my freedom.
 
The Noble Savage protected my humanity.
 
The Monster taught me to resist.
 
The Noble Savage taught me to embrace.
 
The Monster taught me not to surrender my mind.
 
The Noble Savage taught me not to surrender my heart.
 
And perhaps life requires both.
 
A mind without a heart can become cold.
 
A heart without a mind can become vulnerable.
 
Intellect without compassion can become arrogance.
 
Compassion without critical thought can become helplessness.
 
Courage without tenderness can become brutality.
 
Tenderness without courage can become submission.
 
The human being needs a conversation between these opposites.
 
Perhaps that conversation is what we call consciousness.
 
Perhaps consciousness itself is not a kingdom ruled by one voice.
 
Perhaps it is a parliament of contradictions.
 
And wisdom is not the silencing of those voices.
 
Wisdom is learning how to make them speak to one another.
 
### **The Journey Continues**
 
I do not know where this journey will lead.
 
Perhaps tomorrow I will once again become the Monster.
 
Perhaps the world will again appear unjust, absurd, hypocritical and difficult.
 
Perhaps I will once again question everything.
 
Perhaps I will once again argue.
 
Perhaps the Noble Savage will once again remind me that not everything needs to be defeated.
 
Perhaps the Monster will remind him that not everything should simply be accepted.
 
And perhaps they will continue talking.
 
That is enough.
 
I no longer seek a final victory between them.
 
I seek coexistence.
 
I seek integration.
 
I seek a life in which thought does not destroy feeling and feeling does not silence thought.
 
A life in which rebellion can coexist with compassion.
 
A life in which questioning can coexist with wonder.
 
A life in which knowledge can remain humble.
 
A life in which love does not require the abandonment of reason.
 
Perhaps that is the real voyage.
 
Not from ignorance to knowledge.
 
Not from darkness to light.
 
But from fragmentation toward wholeness.
 
And so I continue.
 
Not as Monster alone.
 
Not as Noble Savage alone.
 
Not merely as Figar.
 
Not merely as Arif.
 
But as the unfinished human being who carries all of them within himself.
 
I continue as a student.
 
A student of people.
 
A student of silence.
 
A student of contradiction.
 
A student of love.
 
A student of thought.
 
A student of failure.
 
A student of beauty.
 
Above all, a student of life.
 
And perhaps somewhere beyond the boundaries of time and space, where identities become less important and the human soul becomes visible in its simplest form, the Monster and the Noble Savage are still sitting together.
 
They are no longer enemies.
 
They are talking.
 
Perhaps they are laughing.
 
Perhaps they are listening.
 
Perhaps, for the first time, neither is trying to enlighten the other.
 
Perhaps they have finally discovered what I spent so many years trying to understand:
 
**They were never two.**
 
**They were always one.**
 
And perhaps this is what the mysterious journey of life finally teaches usâthat we are not required to destroy one part of ourselves in order to become another.
 
We are asked to understand.
 
To reconcile.
 
To listen.
 
To grow.
 
To remain unfinished.
 
Because the moment we believe that we have finally understood ourselves, life opens another door.
 
Another person appears.
 
Another silence arrives.
 
Another question rises.
 
Another meeting begins.
 
And once again, we leave the familiar geography of the earth and travel somewhere above time and space.
 
Perhaps that is the beauty of being human.
 
We are always becoming.
 
Always arriving.
 
Always departing.
 
Always meeting ourselves again in someone else.
 
So the story of the Monster and the Noble Savage does not end at the dhaba.
 
It begins there.
 
It continues in every conversation.
 
In every disagreement.
 
In every act of compassion.
 
In every rebellion against injustice.
 
In every moment when knowledge bows before love.
 
In every moment when love finds the courage to question.
 
And perhaps, one day, when all the arguments have exhausted themselves and all the identities have become silent, the two will sit together again.
 
The Monster will look at the Noble Savage.
 
The Noble Savage will look at the Monster.
 
And neither will ask:
 
âWho won?â
 
Because there will be nothing left to win.
 
Only something left to understand.
 
And perhaps they will smile.
 
Perhaps the night will be quiet.
 
Perhaps the stars will appear above them.
 
Perhaps somewhere a river will continue flowing without asking where it is going.
 
And perhaps I will finally understand that the river, too, never chose between its banks.
 
It needed both.
 
One gave it direction.
 
The other gave it shape.
 
Together they allowed it to move.
 
Perhaps human beings are like that.
 
We need our contradictions.
 
We need our questions and our answers.
 
Our darkness and our light.
 
Our rebellion and our tenderness.
 
Our Monster and our Noble Savage.
 
For I am still a student of life.
 
And life, in its infinite generosity, has not yet finished teaching me.
 
Perhaps it never will.
 
And perhaps I would not want it any other way.
 
Because somewhere above time and space, the Noble Savage and the Monster were always one.
 
Perhaps they were waiting only for us to meet again.

When Monster Meets Noble Savage Again
Figar Arif


There are meetings that happen in places, and there are meetings that happen beyond
places. The first kind is easy to understand. Two people sit across a table, exchange
greetings, speak about ordinary things, laugh at familiar jokes, discuss the weather, work,
society, friends, politics, or perhaps some incident of the day, and eventually leave. Such
meetings begin and end within the boundaries of time. We remember where they happened,
when they happened, and sometimes even what was said.
But there is another kind of meeting. It may begin in an ordinary place, at an ordinary hour,
among ordinary people, and yet something extraordinary may happen within it. And
somewhere between one thought and another, two human beings discover that they are no
longer sitting in a dhaba, a room, a garden, or anywhere upon the physical earth. They have
entered another geography. The geography of consciousness. Perhaps our meeting was
one such meeting.
The kind of questions people ask without expecting that the answers will become important.
But human beings are strange creatures. Sometimes the deepest revolutions begin with the
simplest greetings. A question was raised. Another question followed. An idea encountered
another idea. And then, almost imperceptibly, conversation stopped being conversation. It
became a journey. At first, it walked. Then it ran. Then, without warning, we began to fly.
We began from our respective intellectual territories. Each of us carried our own history, our
own convictions, our own doubts, our own experiences, and perhaps our own prejudices.
We moved from one subject to another, sometimes deliberately and sometimes without
direction.
We discussed ethics, Religion, Politics, Morality, Philosophy, Poetry, human nature, and
whatnot. The dhaba was still there, but we were no longer entirely there. Our bodies
remained at the table. Our minds had travelled elsewhere. We had taken an aerial journey.
For a while, our intellectual spheres moved parallel to each other. Each had its own orbit, its
own direction, its own history. Yet gradually, almost imperceptibly, the distance between them
began to disappear.
The Monster
For a long time, I had imagined my intellectual existence as a movement between two
opposite poles. One I called the Monster. The other I called the Noble Savage. The names
are deliberately contradictory. Perhaps that contradiction is the whole story.
The Monster is the part of me that refuses to accept the world as it is.He is suspicious of
inherited morality. He questions authority. He challenges conventions.
He is restless before injustice. He does not easily bow before established truths.
He is sometimes arrogant, sometimes angry, sometimes excessively rational, and
occasionally destructive in his insistence upon freedom.
The Noble Savage is different. He is the innocent part of me. He believes in love before
argument, compassion before ideology, human dignity before political identity. He does not
possess an elaborate philosophy because perhaps he does not need one. He knows some
things instinctively. He knows that a wounded person needs compassion. He knows that
beauty can exist without explanation. He knows that nature does not need a theory in order
to be beautiful. He knows that silence can be meaningful. For years, I imagined that these
two personalities were fighting each other. And I, somewhere between them, kept calling
myself Figar and Arif, as though two names could contain two different worlds. But perhaps I
was mistaken. Perhaps the Monster and the Noble Savage were never enemies. Perhaps
they were two incomplete attempts to describe the same human being.
The Birth of the Monster
My Monster did not appear suddenly.
He was born slowly. He was created by questions and circumstances. Every time I
encountered an injustice that had been normalized, he became stronger. Every time I saw
hypocrisy disguised as morality, he became louder. He was not satisfied with inherited
answers.
He wanted to know.
●
Why?
●
Why should a person obey?
●
Why should one truth be considered sacred while another is condemned?
●
Why should morality belong exclusively to institutions?
●
Why should religion become a boundary between human beings rather than a bridge
between them?
●
Why should politics consume compassion?
●
Why should knowledge make us arrogant rather than humble?
●
Why should civilization call itself civilized while repeatedly producing violence?
The Innocence of the Noble Savage
The Noble Savage was never interested in winning arguments. He was interested in
remaining human. He did not have a library of philosophical references. He did not need
Nietzsche, Rousseau, Gandhi, Iqbal, Marx, Foucault, or anyone else to tell him that suffering
mattered. He simply felt it. When someone was hurt, he wanted to help. When someone
cried, he wanted to listen. When someone was lonely, he wanted to sit beside them. But
innocence has its own danger. It can become ignorance. Compassion without awareness
may become helplessness. Love without understanding may become submission. Peace
without justice may become silence before oppression. And therefore the Noble Savage
also needed the Monster.
He needed someone who would ask questions when his innocence became complacency.
He needed someone who would challenge the structures that produced suffering.
He needed someone who would say: Love is not enough if we refuse to understand why
people suffer.
When They Met Again
That evening, something changed. The Monster rose. He looked toward the Noble Savage.
But instead of attacking him, he paused. For the first time, there was no war. There was
recognition.
The Monster saw that the Noble Savage had survived everything. He had survived
disappointment without becoming cynical. He had survived ignorance without becoming
arrogant. He had survived pain without becoming cruel. He had preserved something the
Monster himself had almost “lost the ability” to love without demanding a philosophical
justification for love. And the Noble Savage looked at the Monster. Perhaps he saw
something too. He saw that the Monster was not simply darkness. He saw the wounds
beneath his anger. He saw that behind every question was often a desire for truth. Behind
every rebellion was perhaps a desire for dignity.
The Monster did not have to destroy the Noble Savage.
The Noble Savage did not have to silence the Monster.
They could sit together.
They could listen.
They could argue.
They could disagree.
They could remain contradictory.
And still belong to the same human being.
Perhaps maturity is not the disappearance of contradiction.
Perhaps maturity is learning how to live with contradiction without allowing it to become
destruction.
The Monster had always wanted victory.
The Noble Savage had always wanted peace.
Now they could seek understanding.
That may be the beginning of wisdom.
The Intervention of Silence
Meaningful silence is not emptiness. It is a language. Sometimes a person remains silent
because they have nothing to say. But sometimes they remain silent because what they are
saying cannot be reduced to words. That silence can become an intellectual intervention. It
can make us uncomfortable. It can force us to examine ourselves. It can create a space in
which our own thoughts become audible. Perhaps that was what happened to me.
Meaningful encounters are often uncomfortable precisely because they do not leave us
where they found us. Sometimes another human being does not change your life by giving
you answers. Sometimes they change it by making you ask better questions.
And sometimes the greatest intervention is silence.
A meaningful silence.
A silence that does not abandon you.
A silence that accompanies you.
A silence that gives you enough space to hear your own forgotten voice.
The World as Prison and Garden
For a long time, the world appeared to me as a prison. Perhaps I was not entirely wrong.
Human civilization has constructed many forms of imprisonment. There are political prisons,
social prisons, economic prisons, religious prisons, and psychological prisons. There are
prisons without walls.
A person can be imprisoned by poverty. Another can be imprisoned by privilege. One can be
imprisoned by fear of public opinion. Another by the desire for public approval. One can be
imprisoned by dogma. Another by excessive skepticism. Even intelligence can become a
prison when it begins to believe that it has understood everything.
Freedom is not merely freedom from something. It is also freedom for something.
The Meeting of Ethics and Love
Our conversation moved through ethics.
●
What is good?
●
What is evil?
●
Who defines morality?
●
Can morality exist without religion?
●
Can religion exist without morality?
●
Can political systems remain humane?
●
Can human beings possess power without becoming prisoners of power?
These questions have no simple answers. But perhaps the purpose of philosophy is not
always to provide answers. Sometimes philosophy teaches us how to ask better questions.
And poetry does something similar through another language. Poetry does not always
explain life. It reveals it.
A poet may take an ordinary moment and make us see it differently. A philosopher may take
an ordinary assumption and make us question it. A compassionate human being may take
an ordinary silence and make us feel understood.
Perhaps all three are forms of the same human desire: To see beyond the surface.
Religion, Politics and the Human Being
Religion entered our conversation too. Religion has often been treated as an answer to the
deepest questions of existence. But perhaps religion also creates questions.
Who are we?
Why are we here?
What do we owe one another?
What is justice?
What is forgiveness?
What is death?
What survives us?
And politics asks another set of questions.
Who possesses power?
Who makes decisions?
Who benefits?
Who is excluded?
What is justice within society?
What does freedom mean when resources are unequal?
These questions are different, yet they intersect. The spiritual life asks about the human
soul. The political life asks about human society. But the same human being inhabits both.
That is why separating them completely is difficult.
Both were right in what they were seeking, even when each became wrong in the way he
sought it.
The Danger of Becoming Only One Thing
Human beings love simple identities. Every such identity becomes dangerous when it
becomes complete. A human being is never only one thing.
I can be rational in one moment and emotional in another.
I can be courageous and afraid. I can be generous and selfish.
I can be wise in one situation and foolish in another.
I can love someone and disagree with them.
I can oppose an idea without hating the person who holds it.
The human being is a moving contradiction. Perhaps that is not a defect. Perhaps it is our
nature.
The Discovery of Integration
There was a time when I wanted to choose between Figar and Arif.
Between the thinker and the human being.
Between the Monster and the Noble Savage.
Between rebellion and compassion.
Between intellect and innocence.
But I no longer need to choose.
Figar can think while Arif feels.
Arif can love while Figar questions.
Monster can protect the Noble Savage.
Noble Savage can humanize the Monster.
This does not mean that contradiction has disappeared.
It means that contradiction has become dialogue. And dialogue is very different from war.
The Singer of the Heart
And somewhere in this entire experience, another realization emerged. There are people
who become part of our intellectual history without writing a single page in our books.
They enter our lives and alter the rhythm of our thinking.
They may never know the full extent of their influence.
They may speak one sentence.
They may remain silent.
They may simply exist differently.
Yet something within us changes.
The person who inspired this transformation did not give me answers. They gave me
something more valuable: The courage to reconsider my questions.
That is the deepest form of influence one human being can have upon another: not to
occupy their mind, but to awaken something within it.
A Temporary Peace
I say this for the time being because I do not trust permanent declarations about the human
soul.
Tomorrow the Monster may return. He may become angry again. He may look at the world
and see hypocrisy. He may question institutions. He may reject easy answers. And the
Noble Savage may again retreat into innocence. That is acceptable.
I am not writing the story of a final transformation. Life does not work that way. There is no
final chapter while we are alive.
●
We change.

We return.

We forget.
We remember again.

A student can ask.

I stepped outside. The air was cool. Somewhere in the distance, a vehicle moved along the

Perhaps the greatest realization of all is the simplest. The Monster and the Noble Savage

The Monster carried my questions. The Noble Savage carried my tenderness. The Monster

The Journey Continues: End shall never come

As the unfinished human being who carries all of them within himself. I continue as a

Title: Delving for beauty
Content:
What does beauty mean?
A pretty face or the soul unseen?
Acceptance of flaws, or being bee's knees?
Something within or something to please?
Is it in the bird or its flight?
In the mind or our sight?
Is it veiled or something we see?

Well, for some it is the flower , for some
it is its scent.

Title: ज़रा सी बात
Content:
“ज़रा सी बात”

क्यों जरा-जरा सी बात पर आँखें भर आती हैं?
क्यों हँसने का कोई मौका नहीं छोड़ना चाहते हैं?
क्यों बेकरारी पल भर का सुकून नहीं देती?
किसी बात के इत्मीनान से मन भर जाता है।

भागदौड़ भरे जीवन से फुर्सत पाना चाहते हैं,
फिर इन फुर्सत के पलों में अकेले क्यों हो जाते हैं?
सब कुछ है हमारे पास,
क्या सचमुच सब कुछ है हमारे पास?
बस इन्हीं दो बातों के बीच उलझ कर क्यों रह जाते हैं?

क्यों हर मंज़िल पर पहुँचकर
एक नई तलाश शुरू हो जाती है?
क्यों अधूरी-सी ख्वाहिशें
हर खुशी पर भारी पड़ जाती हैं?
क्यों अपने ही सवालों का
कोई जवाब नहीं मिलता?
क्यों दिल की खामोशियों को
कोई अल्फ़ाज़ नहीं मिलता?

शायद ज़िंदगी का मतलब
हर प्रश्न का उत्तर पाना नहीं,
बल्कि हर दिन मुस्कुराकर
खुद को फिर से अपनाना है।

जो है, उसे महसूस करना ही
सबसे बड़ी दौलत है।
बाकी तो समय की धूल है,
जो आती है और गुजर जाती है।

कवयित्री— पूनम झा
By- Poonam Jha

Name: Maushumi Lata Padhi
Title: The Sixth Month
Content:
The Sixth Month 

Three years of dreams, 
three months of turmoil,
seven years to finally sign off. 

Brick by brick, 
she built her life. 
Chaos to peace, 
she realised—
love is not what we lose,
but that which endures within. 

But day in, day out, 
the hushed murmurs shout, 
surrounded by jaundiced eyes, 
pricked by social thorns. 
She smelled the roses 
and owned her garden. 

Her life was in harmony, 
but her daily social groups, 
dotted with their family tales, 
peppered with domestic concerns, 
at times stirred a note 
of her old desire that did not flower. 

Three decades gone, 
a common friend chanced upon 
memories of his wedding day, 
for which they had lovingly chosen 
a score of eternal love songs— reopening hidden gems of the past. 

More news trickled in, 
and with it, 
a vulnerability not seen before—
a rare crack in her armour, 
a silent tremor
she tried to ignore. 

Sleek cell in hand,
the nudge made her search 
which turn his life had taken—
new dreams forged, 
new paths travelled, 
both blooming afar. 

With reunions on the rise,
a tiny desire to talk, 
a call to connect,
for old shared times’ sake, 
the ship had anchored, 
a hello was fine.

Offline had been her ally, 
knowing where her worth lay. 
But social media laid its bait, 
as the past began to steal in. 
An unusual quiet pull
led her to reach out. 

Over six months, at times, 
her first love haunted her feed. 
She sought an old friend far away.
Both having sailed diverse seas, 
scripting success shores apart— 
a green dot to heal a grey past. 

A couple of odd notes, 
a natural human call. 
But the tides had changed,
the waves had no echo. 
She went with the flow,
feeling lighter than before. 

Blessed with boundaries, 
the lyrics of her life 
made her song bloom.

Name: Nusha Jamila
Title: Celestial Misfortune
Content:
What are stars?
Mere little blinks scattered
Over a canvas of paint so dark;
Yet still they dazzled her.
        No matter they typically are sparse,
        Or often so very guttered,
        But within her they lit an intense spark,
        Albeit fleeting, always a spur.
    
"Just wait," she promised,
"I'll come see you one day."
And wait, she did. And did
In faith, that one day she just may.
        What is life but a comet –
        A cold rock in darkness astray;
        And its companion, time, never honest.
        Both hand-in-hand only betray.
    
Betrayed was she,
Her faith in painful shards,
As the fact was forgone to her
That it was forbidden to want the stars.
        No matter the ploy or the plea,
        Forced was she behind habitual bars,
        Her dreams deserted to an endless defer,
        With only the remnants of brutal scars.
    
Alas! The fate of her starlight desires –
The cosmos reduced them to pitiful satires.
Only a blink, and there it was, the Moon,
Within her palms, unsullied and out of cocoon.
        Oh so bright and so unfairly pure,
        And made all else swoon for sure.
        Yet no, neither the Moon nor Mars she fancied,
        Only those little blinks were all she'll ever need.
    
Deemed was she an ungrateful wretch,
Merely for daring to deny this "boon".
Was she truly at fault, akin to all they allege?
Doubts emerged, her senses less and less attune.
        And so she gradually teetered to the edge,
        As nights wore on beside "her Moon",
        Beneath the dome so mockingly etched
        By fluorescent stars so sham, her utter misfortune.

Name: Theodore Perking
Title: An escape into Eternity
Content:
Against the crashing waves of the crooked sea 
There stands a boat and a sailor trying to flee 
A boat that has never seen ground in days 
And a sailor who never wants to return to the old ways 

The boat mercilessly gets thrashed by waves
While the sailor prepares his own grave 
For he knows that the boat won't last long 
But he wants his dear life to prolong 

The boat sailing in the sea with its Hull cracked
With all of its parts broken and sacked 
It sails the storms barely surviving
Wishing for its doom like its conniving

While the sailor proudly sailing 
Never to return with no one trailing 
Looking at the sea with eyes of hope 
Tying the mast tight with a rope 

For the sailor had a history of cruelty 
Of both mind and heart that he looked for an opportunity
To escape the night with his old boat
No matter how long it stays afloat

The battered boat with cracks and holes
had no one by his side to console 
For he too had seen through lots of storms 
And didn't want to go on anymore 

Alas the water starts devouring the boat 
And the sailor begins to lose his hope 
But despite that he stands confident as he sees 
A bright light coming from the above with a soft breeze

Name: Jahnavi Muralidhar
Theme: Regret, wrong decisions, moving on, forgiving yourself, mistakes
Title: I was wrong.
Content:
I took a decision, and it seems to be wrong
Maybe it wasn't wrong at all, because I wasn't happy about the other decision either
And I wasn't happy with anything. My heart desires only what I do not have
It seeks what I have no means of getting, it wishes for the forbidden
But then, my heart swells with regret, and it feels like a mistake
I feel like I regret everything now. Then what do I do?

Waves of crashing sorrow won't leave my heart alone, like those in the ocean
And unlike the rocks in the ocean which bear the waves, my body's not a rock
And I tremble with the sorrow, I feel myself shake and shiver, my head hurts
I feel like I made a mistake, and now the roof's collapsing and its time to deal with it
Everything hurts, why did I even do this? I blame every misfortune on that
If I had not done that, then maybe things would've been different
And maybe things would've been better
And maybe I would've been happier
Endless worries which spawn by seemingly nothing and beat my heart til' its bruised and bleeding free.

Hey, it's okay.

I've seen you at your worst, I've seen the number of days you've cried
All the days you had to hold your tears back, and not let your lips tremble
All the times you had to shout back, just to feel like you own a piece of your life
All the dreams and the despair, all the meals you've skipped
How people shout at you, and leave, and in the quiet of the night, you sit there knowing you haven't eaten anything and that you'll lose more weight
In the unsettling quiet that comes after everything is over and done with
I've seen you at your worst and your best
And hey, it's okay.

Maybe having seen you all this while, I've developed some empathy
It's really okay. Even if you mess up a thousand times
Even if everyone gives up, even if everyone turns their backs on you
Even if everyone hates you, I'll still be here
I'll take your hand in mine even if its bleeding and scarred and treasure it
I don't know the way forward, but I won't give up on you

Oh, everything is messed up
"This is the final boarding call for all passengers from CJB to DEL. All passengers should now be on board through gate 2..."
Long after the flight has departed and I'm still standing here
Long after the sound of the flight taking off, and long after the whirr of the plane
Long after everyone's left, and I'm standing alone at the empty airport
I wonder if I messed up

I don't have a plan anymore
I keep wandering around like a child lost at a fair
I wish for someone to take my hand and guide me because I can't guide myself
But hey, its okay, we're going to get through this
Just fuck it all, blow a candle, start over again like its a new birthday

Somehow my life is full of every monster and every despair and now I feel like
I'm the reason behind it all, I'm the root cause
My whole plan, a dream I had for the future, everything collapsed in a day
It's okay, erase it all, start over again, we'll fill the board with something else
You did whatever you could with whatever you knew, and its okay

Even if we have nights where we have waves of that crushing sadness come back
Even if we have times we want to bang our head against a wall
Even if we have times where we curse ourselves
We can't look down, yes, its really okay.

Name: Hensi Chelani
Title: The Life I No Longer Run From
Content:
I spent my life
searching for peace

in quiet rooms,
finished pages,
prayers whispered
before sleep.

Then I met a man
with a cricket bat
and a promise.

Cool as an unhurried afternoon,
he worked again 

And again,
And again,

until failure became practice
and ambition, a way of waking.

One evening,
he takes my hand,
then opens my diary.

He skips nothing.

Not the blue of ordinary days,
not the red of restless words,
not the green margins
where small doodles
grew like wildflowers.

“Every word means something,”
he said.

I almost laugh.

I have spent years
explaining myself
to people who wanted
only the summary.

He reads my spine
without breaking it.

He sees the certificate,
the medal in its plastic sleeve;
proof that sleepless nights
had become something valuable.

He smiles & says: “Keep going.”

And I finally understand that 
peace is not silence.

It is someone
with storms of his own,
Someone who still knows
how to hold your rain;

someone who works for victory,
accepts defeat,
and remains gentle.

He holds me
like a book being bound carefully,
so no page escapes.

“More,” he says.

More poems.
More pages.
More life.

And I made my choice:
I will stop searching.

Peace is not a place
where nothing hurts.

It is the hand
I reach for
when it does.

It is being read completely 
and still being held.

So I choose this:

the unfinished pages,
the early mornings,
the cricket grounds,
the man who keeps trying
when no one is watching.

I choose a life
I no longer need
to run from.

Name: Jahnavi Muralidhar
Theme: Defiance, rebellion, following your own path, courage, Dionysus
Title: Dionysus
Content:
I'll change my career path a million times
I'll eat chicken and eggs if that's what I want
I'll transfer colleges and wear crop tops
I'll go alone to places if I have no one else
I'll eat alone every day if that's what it is
Your gaze, which used to imprint on my soul,
Even after you looked away, caused me unease
A hole burned into my being by your judgement
Now stare at me all you want, and I don't care

Dionysus took me with him to paradise
Have I drunk from the well, or have you?
I'll get intoxicated and dance in public if I want
Because we're on a floating rock in space
Were you there to wipe my tears when I cried?
Did you ask me to eat when I used to skip meals?
Did you hold my hand in the heat while I was alone?
And if not, don't ask me the 6 Ws, let me live
If I can live life my own way, turning to ash is okay

Your momentary, fleeting gaze full of judgement
Used to etch itself on my soul. But the truth is,
I'm the one who has stayed for it all, have you?
I'll stay loyal to the unending flame inside me
That kept it bright for my eyes even in the dark.
My resilience, which saved me over and over.
I'm no longer locked in the bars of your gaze.
So turn up the music, and let's get drunk tonight
Because I'm my own slave, and I do what I like.

Name: Shawna Agrawal
Title: Blooming in Mud
Content:
The city of Gorapur a place where people lived a happy and contended life. It was well administered and all thanks to King Raghunath who treated his people well and made sure that they were happy. Queen Madhumati a women with true beauty always cared for her people. 
Raghunath made sure that his people are protected. He had made sure to build up his relations with other kings as well who genuinely honored him. One of the kings was king Tarkash of city Rampur a neighboring city of Gorapur. Both the cities were like family. 
King Raghunath had everything but he was concerned about his successor as he had no one to look after him. The King and the Queen prayed a lot to get the auspicious blessing and it took no time when Queen gave birth to a adorable princess Kirtimukhi.
The whole city including Rampur city celebrated the birth of princess. 
King Raghunath, a man of pride was not only disappointed but it also grew his anxiety and he walked away from celebration. When Madhumati noticed this she said, " Everyone are celebrating what is bothering you"? 
He griped his fist and said, "It's Kirtimukhi. We were blessed with daughter not son. Who will rule the city after me. Daughters are no rulers"
"Our Daughter is our pride she will be Queen someday and will be better ruler than us" Said Madhumati comforting Raghunath. 
Hearing this Raghunath went to king Tarkash and said, "today I decide that my daughter Kirtimukhi will marry your Son  Arjun". Let the two cities become one through this alliance. 
Hearing this Madhumati became shocked and decided that her daughter won't be sacrificing. 

Kirtimukhi was blooming like a flower but what she missed was her fathers Raghunath affection who was always critical. She tried to become her Son and so practiced swords was well versed in her scriptures but all what Raghunath could say, "Daughters are not Rulers, only if I had a Son".
In no time Kirtimukhi grew up to be a wonderful princess. 
Raghunath decided to make it formal and called King Tarkash for wedding engagement. With sudden engagement alliance Kirtimukhi was aghasted and decided to call it of. 
Raghunath was against this decision but Kirtimukhi said, "I always tried to be your son but you never considered me worthy of becoming your successor. I want to compete with Arjun and if he defeats me I would marry him. But if not you would make me your successor"
Seeing the determination Raghunath gave in and announced the competition. Arjun who was always fond of Kirtimukhi decided to play along. The competition was just about 3 questions
1. Who is faster wind or mind? 
2. Who is your biggest enemy? 
3. Why is marriage important? 
Arjun said, "Wind is faster than mind, you are your own enemy and marriage is important to make your family grow"
Kirtimukhi smiled and said, "the speed of mind is faster as you imagine faster than wind, your afflictions are your biggest enemy and marriage is about love and union of souls. It is important to love for marriage". Everyone cheered as Kirtimukhi won. King Raghunath realized his daughter is worthy to be a good ruler. 
This is how Kirtimukhi bloomed in mud. 

Note: The story is about the challenges that even today every girl faces. She is been undervalued, stereotyped and constantly looked down. I hope you enjoy it

Title: Woh Pita hi hota hai
Content:
*एक पिता के जीवन पर*

कैसे करूँ बयां मैं जीवन एक पिता का,
जिसे कभी मैंने रोकर, थक कर सोते नहीं देखा।

तमाम मुश्किलों भरी ज़िन्दगी में भी
सबको कली जैसा रख,
मैंने पिता को खार के बिस्तर पर सोते देखा।

हमारी तमाम महंगी ख्वाहिशों को

पर पिता को एक लम्हा भी न मिले बच्चों के लिए,

Name: Sreedevi
Title: पढना सीखते बच्चे
Content:
### पढ़ना सीखते बच्चे

ज़िन्दगी को कहाँ पढ़ते हैं?
नहीं सिखाते है उनको प्रश्न पूछना
क्यों नहीं कोई आज तक पूछ पाया ?
छह साल की छोकरी आम की टोकरी भरकर क्यों लाई है?
क्या वो स्कूल गयी थी ?
क्या टोकरी उसे भारी नहीं लगती ?
नन्हें से हाथों की ऐसी क्या मजबूरी थी ?
जो आम की टोकरी उसे लानी पड़ी
मुख्तखोरी का आलम तो देखो
उसकी टोकरी के आम को तो चूसना है
पर उससे उसके दाम नहीं पूछना है।

माना एक कविता है
पर क्या कविता ज़िन्दगी की व्याख्या नहीं है ?
पढ़ लो और अगली कविता पर बढ़ लो।
कविता में हो रही घटना को
आम बनाया जा रहा है
जिसे सही ठहराया जा रहा है।

इस कविता को ध्वनि वर्ण और शब्द की तरह पढ़ने वालों
भेजो अपनी छह साल की छोकरीयों को
सर पर भरी हुई आम की टोकरियों को रखकर
बाज़ार में एक दिन के लिए
फिर इसे छह साल की बच्चियों की कक्षा में पढ़ाना
छह साल की छोकरी भरकर लाई टोकरी
छह साल की बच्ची को  मां का सहयोग करती बच्ची कहकर  पल्ला न झाड़ ले
पर कविता मनोरंजन नहीं है।
कविता सवाल करती है मुझसे तुमसे हम सबसे
छह साल की बच्ची की विवशता का जवाब कहाँ है?

Name: rittik bora
Title: Privilege
Content:
A palace,
built behind fragile walls,
a crown passed down
upon stones we never laid.

We inherited
the path,
but not the eyes
to question it—
the crown,
not the spine to carry it.

Empty footsteps
wandering through its halls,
until the mirror asks:
who is walking?

Heirs of the past,
or architects of the future?

Let the mirror strip the mask,
until nothing borrowed remains.

A privilege we pass along—
a voice
for those who come next,
not a path to follow,
but a compass to guide,
a gate left open,
and the courage
to lay their own stones.

Name: Theodore Perking
Title: Almost enough
Content:
I wish I could understand why we sunder,
Why our incomplete conversations become a bother,
Always having less time when we meet,
And getting less with each time we speak.

It's like a person catching a glimpse of the sun,
While drowning under the weight of uncertainty.

I try to think of what I could have done
To let you into my life, where we could have some fun,
But I just become trapped in my own limitations,
And stuck in a world of simulations.

Name: rittik bora
Title: A Walk Towards Freedom
Content:
Beneath a lightless sky,
Where darkness had taken hold,

Faces turned into masks,
Where truth became bankrupt,
And lies bought every prize.

I locked myself behind closed doors,
Shivering in the cold,
Where breathing grew too heavy
To carry me forward,

And liberation
Became a mountain to climb.

Deep within the abyss,
I chose an unseen path,
A walk taken alone,
To find the child I had lost—
To smile again,
And dance
To the beating rhythm of being alive.

Still,
The shadow trails behind—
A reflection of what I refuse to become,
Toward the freedom I once buried.
