Name: Kiran Dhaware
Title: वो कौन थी?
Content:
वो कौन थी?

आज नींद आँखों पर, कुछ ज़्यादा ही मेहरबान थी,
आवाज़ देकर जगाने वाली,  वो नहीं थी।

सुबह की किरण भी
खिड़की पर आ खड़ी थी,
पर घर के कोनों में
वो रौनक़ नहीं थी। 

नाश्ते में तो देर हो गई,
घड़ी की सुइयाँ भी भाग रही थी,
“जल्दी कर, ठंडा हो जाएगा…”
बोलने वाली, वो झिड़की नहीं थी। 

रोज़ की हड़बड़ाहट में
कमरा उलट कर बैठी थी,
चीज़ तो सामने ही थी,
बस उसे ढूँढने वाली, वो नज़र नहीं थी।

घर से निकली,
तो दरवाज़े पर ठिठक गई थी,
“अपना ख़याल रखना…”
कहने वाली, वो परवाह नहीं थी।

अजीब था…

जिन बातों को रोज़ सुनकर
कभी-कभी अनसुना कर देती थी,
आज उन्हीं बातों के बगैर
मुझे बेचैनी-सी हो रही थी।

रसोई से आती खुशबू में
उसके हाथों की गरमाहट थी,
वही चूड़ियों की खनक से
घर की धड़कन बजती थी।

उसकी डाँट में फ़िक्र,
तो ख़ामोशी में ममता थी।
 इन्हीं छोटे-छोटे एहसासों से,
घर की साँसें चलती थीं।

आज महसूस हुआ
वो घर का हिस्सा नहीं थी,
मुझे ज़िंदगी देने वाली
मेरी माँ… पूरा घर ही थी।

Name: Aryya Khasnobis
Title: Laila
Content:
“So, what do I call you then? Jamaal, or Laila?”

It has been quite a long night. Perhaps, the longest one since I met Aanika. I have spent the night at Aanika’s house. We have been dating a lot these days because of the increasing affection that has grown between us over the past few months. We had talked a lot by then, enough to know each other, but never did I think of this coming up in our chats. Over a cup of freshly brewed coffee and the tilting rays of the early sun, it’s my turn to explain my side of the truth.

“I know what you are thinking right now!”

“Oh, really? Tell me then.”

“That I am crazy!”

“Aren’t you?”

“No.”

“That’s exactly what I wanted to hear.”

Startled, I look at Aanika. I know her. She’s open-minded, big-hearted. But is she this much cool about seeing her current boyfriend pretending to be a lady in front of a crowd of 40 drunk people, in a remote bar where she never planned to visit in the first place?

“Aanika. I wanted to tell you before.”

“But you didn’t, Jamaal.”

“How does it feel to date a drag queen, Aanika?”

With the sudden drop of silence, I can see her smile.

“A bit awkward? Yes. But deep down in my heart, I know there’s always a reason. A reason for you to be happy. In the end, it doesn’t matter what you are. What matters is who you are, Jamaal.”

“I am not sure if everybody thinks alike.”

“You know it takes a lot of courage to do what you do, Jamaal. You know it, right?”

“When I first met you, I never thought you had such strong opinions on feminism! I guess you are far cooler than what I thought.”

“How does it feel, Jamaal?”

“Feel what?”

“To be a woman. To be a different self! Being Laila?”

“I wore a red gown the first time I staged a performance. Red like wine. I didn’t used to have such a late line-up then. People never used to wait for my show like they did yesterday. Sexist comments used to fly around. Criticism had become a sincere companion. Still, I didn’t give up.”

“But why?”

“I used to feel the glare in their eyes. The unwanted hunger to swallow me.”

“Why did you invite something which you knew would never have been acknowledged by society?”

“Because Laila is not just a name, Aanika. Laila is a pretence of being my real self.”

“A real self?”

“Someone who doesn’t need to hide behind the crude discrimination of a specific gender. Someone who can be brave, bold and beautiful. Someone who can promote an equality-demanding personality and inspire a woman to be like her.”

“All this at the expense of so much pain, Jamaal? You are a man acting as a girl at night to inspire us? At the end of the day, we all are equal!”

“Equal? Do you know women spend, on average, two and a half times as many hours as men on unpaid domestic and care work, Aanika? As of 2025, 102 countries had never had a woman as their Head of State or Government. And nearly one in three women have experienced physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Let apart the millions of young girls growing up without access to education, never encouraged by their parents. They don’t get out of their houses. So, now then, are we equal?”

Aanika can’t help but smile at me.

“How do you know all this?”

“Because one fine day, a so-called Jamaal decided to be Laila."


(End)

Name: sweta vaishnav
Title: “मैंने ख़ुद को चुना.…।”
Content:
“मैंने ख़ुद को चुना.…।”

चलते समय की नदी के साथ,
बढ़ती उम्र की सीढ़ियाँ चढ़ते हुए
सिर्फ़ चेहरा ही नहीं बदलता,
अनुभवों की धूप और संघर्षों की वर्षा में
मन भी कुंदन-सा तपकर निखर जाता है।

जीवन के कुछ रिश्ते बरगद की छाँव बनकर
जीवन भर सुकून देते हैं,
तो, कुछ रिश्ते
पेड़ की सूखी पत्तियों की तरह
समय की पहली हवा में ही बिखर जाते हैं।
और कुछ ऐसे भी होते हैं,
जो बिछड़ जाने के बाद भी
स्मृतियों की शाखाओं पर ठहरे रहते हैं,
हर मौसम में चुपचाप याद आते हैं।

तब समझ आता है—
हर हाथ उम्रभर थामने के लिए नहीं होता,
कुछ लोग साथ निभाने नहीं,
बल्कि जीवन का सबसे बड़ा पाठ सिखाने आते हैं।

माँ हमेशा कहती हैं—
"यदि रिश्ता बच सकता हो,
तो उसमें अपनत्व का जल, धैर्य की मिट्टी,
विश्वास का बीज और समझ का प्रकाश अवश्य देना।

रिश्ता तभी फलता है,
जब दोनों ओर से उसे सहेजा जाए।"

शायद इसलिए
मैंने हर विवाद में शब्दों का शोर नहीं चुना,
क्योंकि कई बार मौन की गरिमा
हज़ार तर्कों से अधिक प्रभावशाली होती है।
मौन, पराजय का नहीं,
परिपक्वता का सबसे सुंदर परिचय होता है।

लेकिन माँ ने यह भी सिखाया—

किसी को मनाने की व्याकुलता न करें,
किसी की स्वीकृति की याचना न करें,
जो मेरे अपने हैं,
वे मेरे मौन की भाषा भी पढ़ लेते हैं।

और जिन्हें मेरी उपस्थिति का मूल्य नहीं,
उन्हें मनाने से पहले
मैंने स्वयं को अपनाना सीख लिया है।

क्योंकि अंततः,
जीवन की सबसे बड़ी उपलब्धि
दूसरों की स्वीकृति नहीं,
स्वयं की स्वीकृति है।

जिस दिन मैंने ख़ुद को स्वीकार लिया,
उसी दिन मैंने जाना—
भीतर की संतुष्टि और आत्मसम्मान वटवृक्ष की जड़ों-सा अटल हैं।
और तभी मैंने सचमुच ख़ुद को चुन लिया।

कवयित्री : श्वेता वैष्णव 
By : Sweta Vaishnav

Name: Naina Pandita
Title: Letters from the Past
Content:
Letters from the Past 

Sometimes I sit and think about those days when you would go to the UK or the US to visit my brother, your son, while I stayed back in India.

There was no WhatsApp then. No email. No mobile phone to call you whenever I wanted. I waited for the long international calls every Sunday as I hung around the landline phone. 

There will still your weekly letters; I still remember how I used to wait for them.

Whenever the postman came, I would wonder if there was something from you. And when I saw that familiar envelope with your handwriting, I would feel so happy.

I knew your handwriting even before I saw your names.

I would open the letter carefully and read it slowly. I didn't want to miss a single word. Sometimes I would read it again because, in those few pages, I felt close to both of you.

Your letters were never just letters to me.

They told me about your journey, about how you were doing, what you were thinking, and the things you wanted to tell me. There was always some advice, some concern, and so much love.

I especially miss your handwriting now.

There was something comforting about seeing your words on paper. As I read them, I could almost hear you speaking to me. For a little while, the distance between us did not seem so great.

Today, both of you are gone, and I miss you in ways I cannot really explain.

There are so many times when I wish I could sit with you and talk about my life. I wish I could tell you what has happened over the years. I wish I could hear your advice again.

And sometimes, I simply wish a letter from you would arrive.

Just one.

I would give anything to see that familiar envelope again.

I would hold it in my hands for a long time before opening it. I would look at your handwriting and probably smile through my tears.

I know that letter cannot come now.

But I still have your old words, your memories, and everything you taught me.

Maybe that is why those letters mean so much to me today. At the time, I thought I was simply reading a letter from my parents.

I did not realise I was keeping pieces of you with me for the rest of my life.

Mum and Dad, I miss you both terribly.

But wherever I go, whatever I do, a part of you will always be with me.

Your words are still in my heart.

And they always will be.

With all my Love 💕

Name: Acharya shikha chandel
Title: Poem
Content:
हाँ, मैं स्त्री हूँ

हाँ, मैं स्त्री हूँ,
घर का चूल्हा-चौका भी करती हूँ,
दूध निकालना भी जानती हूँ,
बच्चों की उँगली पकड़कर
उन्हें चलना भी सिखाती हूँ।

घर-परिवार की जिम्मेदारियाँ
हँसकर निभाती हूँ,
पर अपनी पहचान को
कहीं पीछे नहीं छोड़ती हूँ।

मैं खेत की मिट्टी को भी समझती हूँ,
और किताबों की खुशबू को भी,
संस्कारों को सीने से लगाती हूँ,
तो अपने सपनों को भी जीती हूँ।

मैं माँ हूँ, बहन हूँ, बेटी हूँ,
किसी की पत्नी, किसी की सहेली हूँ,
पर इन रिश्तों से पहले
मैं अपने अस्तित्व की पहेली हूँ।

मेरी आवाज़ को कमजोरी मत समझना,
मेरी चुप्पी को मेरी हार मत समझना,
मैं सहना जानती हूँ,
पर अन्याय के आगे झुकना नहीं जानती।

मैं हाथों में पूजा की थाली भी रखती हूँ,
और जरूरत पड़े तो हक़ की आवाज़ भी उठाती हूँ।
मेरी शक्ति केवल शब्दों में नहीं,
मेरे कर्मों में दिखाई देती है।

मैं अपनी संस्कृति पर गर्व करती हूँ,
अपने संस्कारों को आगे बढ़ाती हूँ,
और आने वाली पीढ़ी के हाथों में
शिक्षा की मशाल थमाती हूँ।

हाँ, मैं स्त्री हूँ—
मुझे किसी के सहारे की पहचान नहीं,
मेरी अपनी उड़ान है,
मेरे अपने आसमान हैं।

मैं रुकूँगी नहीं,
मैं झुकूँगी नहीं,
मैं अपने सपनों के साथ चलूँगी—
क्योंकि हाँ, मैं स्त्री हूँ,
और स्त्री होना ही मेरी शक्ति है।
आचार्य शिखा चंदेल   
एकल विद्यालय 
(लेखिका, समाजसेविका)

Name: Dr. Abdul Salam Khan
Title: “मैं ही हिंदुस्तान हूँ”
Content:
ना राम, ना रहीम, ना हिंदू, ना मैं मुसलमान हूँ,
हिंदी है बोली मेरी, हाँ, मैं ही सच्चा हिंदुस्तान हूँ।
मुझमें समाई यमुना-गंगा, प्रेम-सी पावन मेरी धरती,
नर्मदा, कृष्णा, कावेरी, गोदावरी मुझमें बहती।
केसर के फूलों से बासित-शोभित मेरे शीश हैं,
विवेकानंद की चरण-पादुका गौरवमयी आशीष है।
सीना है चौड़ा मेरा विंध्य, हिमालय, अरावली से,
शोभित मेरी ओढ़नी है अलग-अलग भाषा-बोली से।
पूर्व में पुरी के जगन्नाथ का मंगलाचरण विस्तार है,
पश्चिम में एलोरा, अजंता धर्म-संस्कृति के आधार हैं।
हाँ, मैं हूँ हिंद—ना राम, ना रहीम,
ना मैं हिंदू, ना मुसलमान हूँ।
हिंदी है बोली मेरी, हाँ, मैं ही तो सच्चा हिंदुस्तान हूँ।

Name: Basil Benhur Tigga
Title: Nocturnal Hour
Content:
Nocturnal Hour
By
Basil Benhur
It was around midnight. The room lay swallowed in darkness, saved only by a single electric lamp casting a warm circle of light across the desk. Resting in the glow were just two items: a closed diary bound in black leather and a solitary fountain pen. Outside, muffled rumbles of thunder and the low howl of the wind rattled against the walls.  
A man stepped up to the desk, pulled out the wooden chair, and sat down. He opened the diary, exposing two crisp white pages before him. Uncapping the fountain pen, he set the lid on the desk and held the nib hovering over the paper. He hesitated, probing the darkest corners of his mind for even the faintest glimmer of inspiration. Then, accompanied by a distant crack of thunder, an idea struck. A slow grin curled across his lips, and he began to write.
"It was sometime around midnight. A man sat on the edge of the bed, the soles of his shoes resting against cold floor tiles. The room was almost entirely in shadow, saved only by the faint light filtering through the window curtains.  
A gust of wind seeped through the window frame, making the curtains sway. Slats of light shifted across the wall, jolting the man from his trance. Snapping back to reality, his gaze fell upon a dark pool creeping steadily toward his feet, and he hastily pulled them back. Only then did he register the warm, slick sensation coating his right fist. Clutched tightly in his fingers was the largest knife from the kitchen set, dark liquid dripping from the blade.  
Slowly, his eyes drifted to a shape twitching on the floor. Lying not far from him was his beloved, her life ebbing away with every passing second as her hand clutched uselessly at her abdomen. Five times in rapid succession, the blade had driven into the exact same spot.  
The man remained frozen, his chest heaving as a relentless thought echoed in his mind: 'This is what you get for talking too much, you fool!'  
He stared until the body fell completely still. When the silence registered, panic shattered his control. He bolted upright, his shoe splashing into the spreading crimson pool. Every trace of evidence had to be erased. Shoving the bloody knife into his inner jacket pocket, he yanked out a handkerchief and began frantically wiping nearby surfaces—a book, a vase, a glass. But as he scrubbed the glass, he froze. It was smearing red. He was wiping it with his drenched, bloody hand.  
Dread settled in. He had visited this apartment nearly every day for six months; he could never erase his touch from this place. His situation was hopeless. The glass slipped from his grip and shattered against the floor.  
Stumbling to the window, he threw back the curtains and shoved the panes wide open. Thunder rumbled across the dark alley below. Swinging his legs over the sill, he gripped the metal drainpipe and began a precarious descent. The wild wind whipped across the brickwork, threatening to tear his fingers from the slick rust. Halfway down, a blinding flare of lightning lit the sky, followed by a loud roar of thunder. His wet hands slipped. He pitched backwards into midair, crashing violently onto the pavement below.  
Agony radiated through his body. Nearby, a dog began to bark wildly. Convinced he had fractured his spine, he groaned and forced himself up, searing pain shooting through his left knee. Turning his back on the growling beast, he limped out into the main street, moving beneath the glow of streetlamps. 'I just need to reach my apartment, and everything will be fine,' he repeated to himself.  
The dog bounded out of the alley, its aggressive barks echoing down the quiet street. Lights flickered awake in nearby windows. 'Stupid dog,' he cursed. Limping into the shadows beneath an unlit streetlamp, he pulled the knife from his jacket and waited. As the dog rounded the corner, he drove the blade straight into its skull. The animal whined, and with a fierce yank, he plunged the steel into its chest until silence reclaimed the street.  
Rain began to pour, washing over his face and rinsing away the blood. Looking down at his second kill of the night and of his life, a strange realisation crept over him. He felt no remorse; he felt invincible. Taking life made him feel godlike, possessing the absolute power to destroy without consequence. Intoxicated, he threw his arms wide into the storm, letting the torrential downpour pelt his face.
Lowering his arms, he spotted a ground-floor window glowing faintly at the end of the lane. Limping forward like a drunkard, fear completely dissolved, he vaulted the low boundary wall and reached the covered porch. Rain poured off his clothes. Lowering the knife to his side, he raised his left fist and knocked thrice on the heavy wooden door.
Knock! Knock! Knock!"  
The writer paused, his pen hovering in midair over the page. He turned his head toward the door leading to the drawing room. He could have sworn he heard knocking at his own door. Outside, the storm raged on, wind and rain beating against the glass.  
He looked down at his last written words: “Knock! Knock! Knock!”  
With a quiet sigh, he set the pen between the pages of his diary, pushed himself up from his chair, and stepped into the dark drawing room. Guided only by the faint light spilling from his study, he navigated past the sofa to the front door. He unlocked the knob and pulled it open. Outside, the porch was empty, illuminated only by flashes of lightning over the pouring rain. He stepped back, pulled the door shut, and turned the bolt.  
Navigating his way back into the warmth of his study, he returned to his desk, sank into his chair, and picked up his pen.  It was at that exact moment he noticed something wrong.  The pen felt cold... and wet.  
His gaze dropped to the manuscript, eyes widening. Tiny water droplets splattered across his fresh handwriting, the moisture bleeding into the paper and blurring the dark blue ink.  The realization arrived with sudden, paralyzing horror.  
With a sharp, abrupt movement, he turned around. Standing behind him was a man, rain dripping from his jacket, his mouth stretched into a wide grin. Held firmly in his grip was a flashing steel blade.  
The writer opened his mouth to scream, but the blade moved faster. Cold steel bit deep across his throat before a sound could escape. Clasping both hands over his neck to stem the warm surge, the writer fell from his chair, collapsing onto the floorboards as the darkness swallowed him whole.  

**************************************************************************

Name: Aryya Khasnobis
Title: A Date With Laila
Content:
|| A date with Laila ||

“So, what do I call you then? Jamaal, or Laila?”

It has been quite a long night. Perhaps, the longest one since I met Aanika. I have spent the night at Aanika’s house. We have been dating a lot these days because of the increasing affection that has grown between us over the past few months. We had talked a lot by then, enough to know each other, but never did I think of this coming up in our chats. Over a cup of freshly brewed coffee and the tilting rays of the early sun, it’s my turn to explain my side of the truth.

“I know what you are thinking right now!”

“Oh, really? Tell me then.”

“That I am crazy!”

“Aren’t you?”

“No.”

“That’s exactly what I wanted to hear.”

Startled, I look at Aanika. I know her. She’s open-minded, big-hearted. But is she this much cool about seeing her current boyfriend pretending to be a lady in front of a crowd of 40 drunk people, in a remote bar where she never planned to visit in the first place?

“Aanika. I wanted to tell you before.”

“But you didn’t, Jamaal.”

“How does it feel to date a drag queen, Aanika?”

With the sudden drop of silence, I can see her smile.

“A bit awkward? Yes. But deep down in my heart, I know there’s always a reason. A reason for you to be happy. In the end, it doesn’t matter what you are. What matters is who you are, Jamaal.”

“I am not sure if everybody thinks alike.”

“You know it takes a lot of courage to do what you do, Jamaal. You know it, right?”

“When I first met you, I never thought you had such strong opinions on feminism! I guess you are far cooler than what I thought.”

“How does it feel, Jamaal?”

“Feel what?”

“To be a woman. To be a different self! Being Laila?”

“I wore a red gown the first time I staged a performance. Red like wine. I didn’t used to have such a late line-up then. People never used to wait for my show like they did yesterday. Sexist comments used to fly around. Criticism had become a sincere companion. Still, I didn’t give up.”

“But why?”

“I used to feel the glare in their eyes. The unwanted hunger to swallow me.”

“Why did you invite something which you knew would never have been acknowledged by society?”

“Because Laila is not just a name, Aanika. Laila is a pretence of being my real self.”

“A real self?”

“Someone who doesn’t need to hide behind the crude discrimination of a specific gender. Someone who can be brave, bold and beautiful. Someone who can promote an equality-demanding personality and inspire a woman to be like her.”

“All this at the expense of so much pain, Jamaal? You are a man acting as a girl at night to inspire us? At the end of the day, we all are equal!”

“Equal? Do you know women spend, on average, two and a half times as many hours as men on unpaid domestic and care work, Aanika? As of 2025, 102 countries had never had a woman as their Head of State or Government. And nearly one in three women have experienced physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Let apart the millions of young girls growing up without access to education, never encouraged by their parents. They don’t get out of their houses. So, now then, are we equal?”

Aanika can’t help but smile at me.

“How do you know all this?”

“Because one fine day, a so-called Jamaal decided to be Laila."

(End)

Theme: A Victorian Tale of Love, Healing and Letting Go
Title: THE GARDEN BEYOND THE WINTER
Content:
Author's Biography 
Piya Poppy Rathbone (pen name) is a multifaceted creative soul born in Kolkata, India, and currently residing in Russia. A professional international fan artist, pet photographer, poet, singer, music teacher, short story writer, children’s book editor, animal rescuer, and event manager, -.She is the recipient of numerous prestigious accolades, including Global International Artist of the Year 2024, the Jamini Roy Achievement Award, Vinci Honor Award, USA Book of World Records, American Merit Council honor, Tagore Award, Dream Pride Award, and many more from esteemed institutions such as 4T Success Academy, Manikarnika Art Gallery, Delhi Art International, and CAA Talent Hunt 2021. She also serves as President of Vladimir Putin’s Society in Moscow and Administrator of the “We Stand with Mr. Vladimir Putin Society..Four of her anthologies have already been published worldwide.

Author’s Note
THE GARDEN BEYOND THE WINTER is a five-chapter short story created with the utmost respect, admiration, and gratitude for the timeless qualities of maturity, dignity, humility, and quiet strength.
The character of Inspector Mirov is an original fictional creation inspired by my admiration for the distinguished screen presence and aristocratic persona of the legendary Spanish actor Sir Julio Peña Muñoz. The character, setting, relationships, and events presented in this story are entirely fictional and form part of my artistic interpretation.
Please note that this narrative is a dedicated tribute to the legendary classical twentieth-century actor Sir Julio Peña Muñoz and is entirely separate from and unrelated to the contemporary Spanish actor Julio Peña Fernández, who shares a similar name.
This story is my artistic way of bringing Sir Julio Peña Muñoz's elegant, aristocratic presence into a world of Victorian honour, tenderness, healing, and enduring devotion. Rather than placing him within a narrative of tragic departure, I wished to imagine a journey in which a wounded heart learns to release its fear and once again welcome happiness.
For me, letting go does not mean letting go of the person one loves. It means letting go of the fear that prevents one from accepting the love that remains.
Sir Julio Peña Muñoz remains a cherished source of artistic inspiration throughout my creative journey, standing alongside the great traditional masters of the silver screen who have profoundly inspired my work: Sir Basil Rathbone, Sir Christopher Lee, Sir Peter Cushing, Sir Alan Rickman, Sir Alberto de Mendoza, and Sir Telly Savalas.
Never forgotten.

THE GARDEN BEYOND THE WINTER

Chapter 1:
A Victorian Tale of Love, Healing and Letting Go

Peregrine Vale arrived at Blackthorn Hall on a rainy afternoon in January.

The country road was almost hidden beneath a veil of silver rain, and she drew her woollen cloak more closely around her shoulders as she hurried towards the great iron gates, protecting the parcel beneath her arm.

Inside was an old volume of poetry she had borrowed from Inspector Mirov several weeks earlier.

She had meant to return it sooner.

But life, she had discovered, had a habit of delaying even the simplest intentions.

When she reached the stone portico, she lifted the brass knocker.

Before she could strike, the door opened.

Mirov stood before her.

He wore a dark waistcoat beneath his black coat, and his silvering hair was slightly disordered, as though she had interrupted him in the midst of his work. His expression, ordinarily severe, softened when he saw her.

“Miss Vale.”

“Inspector Mirov.”

His eyes fell upon the parcel.

“You have walked here in this weather merely to return a book?”

Peregrine smiled.

“I feared you might think I had stolen it.”

“I should have preferred that explanation.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because it would have meant you enjoyed it sufficiently to keep it.”

For a moment, neither spoke.

Then Mirov stepped aside.

“Come in before the rain makes a ghost of you.”

Peregrine entered.

The warmth of the hall surrounded her, carrying the faint fragrance of burning cedar and beeswax. Portraits of stern-faced ancestors watched from the walls, while an enormous grandfather clock marked the hour with solemn precision.

Mirov took the parcel from her.

“You need not have troubled yourself.”

“I wanted to.”

Those three words unsettled him more than they ought to have done.

He had spent years hearing people speak of duty, obligation and necessity. Very few ever spoke of desire without wanting something in return.

“You have read it?” he asked.

“Twice.”

“And?”

“I think the poet was rather unhappy.”

A faint smile touched his lips.

“Most poets are.”

“Perhaps because they spend too much time writing about what they lack.”

The smile vanished.

Peregrine immediately noticed.

“I beg your pardon.”

“There is nothing to pardon.”

But his voice had changed.

She did not pursue the matter.

Instead, she glanced towards the library.

“You have a fire?”

“Always.”

“Then perhaps I may stay until the rain passes?”

Mirov hesitated only briefly.

“Of course.”


---
Chapter 2:

The rain continued until evening.

Peregrine sat beside the library fire while Mirov worked at his desk. At first they spoke very little. Yet the silence between them was not uncomfortable.

She read.

He wrote.

The fire crackled.

Outside, the rain whispered against the windows.

Eventually Peregrine closed her book.

“May I ask you something?”

“You may.”

“Why do you live here alone?”

His pen stopped.

Mirov looked towards the fire.

“Habit.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” he admitted. “It is merely the answer I have given myself.”

Peregrine studied him quietly.

“Do you dislike company?”

“No.”

“Then why avoid it?”

He rose and walked towards the window.

For several moments he watched the rain.

“Because,” he said at last, “there are certain kinds of happiness a man learns to fear.”

Peregrine was silent.

She understood that this was the first honest thing he had told her.

“Perhaps,” she said gently, “the fear belongs to the past.”

Mirov turned towards her.

“And perhaps the past knows more about happiness than we do.”

“Perhaps.”

She smiled.

“But it does not know everything.”

Something in her expression made him look away.

When Peregrine finally departed that evening, Mirov accompanied her to the door.

The rain had stopped. A few stars had appeared between the clouds.

“Thank you,” she said.

“For what?”

“For letting me stay.”

Mirov regarded her thoughtfully.

“I think I should thank you.”

“For returning your book?”

“No.”

His voice was quieter.

“For making this house feel less silent.”

Peregrine smiled.

Then she descended the steps and disappeared through the gates.

Mirov remained at the doorway long after she had gone.

For the first time in years, he found himself listening for footsteps that were no longer there.


---

Chapter 3:

After that evening, Peregrine began visiting Blackthorn Hall more frequently.

At first, she came for books.

Then for tea.

Eventually, neither required a reason.

There was an ease between them that neither attempted to name. Peregrine would sit beside the library window with her embroidery while Mirov read his correspondence. Sometimes they spoke for an hour; sometimes scarcely at all.

And Mirov discovered something he had almost forgotten.

He enjoyed another person's presence.

He began to look forward to afternoons.

He began to notice the weather.

He began, quite unwillingly, to hope.

Yet hope frightened him.

One January morning, Peregrine found him standing in the conservatory.

The garden beyond the glass was covered in frost. The roses were bare, their branches dark against the pale winter sky.

“You never come here in winter,” she observed.

“There is nothing to see.”

Peregrine stepped beside him.

“There is always something to see.”

She pointed towards the rose bushes.

“They are not dead.”

“They appear to be.”

“They are sleeping.”

Mirov gave a quiet laugh.

“You have decided to become a botanist?”

“No. Merely an optimist.”

“An occupation I have never understood.”

“I had noticed.”

She smiled.

His expression soon became serious.

“Peregrine…”

She waited.

“I have been thinking.”

“That can be dangerous.”

He almost laughed.

But then his face grew solemn.

“You should not become accustomed to me.”

She frowned.

“Why?”

“Because I am not the man you believe me to be.”

“Then tell me who you are.”

He looked away.

“I am a man who has spent years believing that happiness is a temporary visitor. A man who has mistaken fear for wisdom. A man who has convinced himself that solitude is strength.”

Peregrine said nothing.

Mirov continued.

“I have thought that if I never allowed myself to love again, I could never suffer again.”

“And has it worked?”

He looked at her.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I have suffered anyway.”

The words seemed to surprise him.

Peregrine placed her hand gently against the cold windowpane.

“Then perhaps you have been protecting yourself from a danger that no longer exists.”

Mirov lowered his eyes.

“I am afraid.”

“I know.”

“I do not know how to stop.”

“You do not have to stop being afraid all at once.”

He looked at her.

“You only have to stop allowing fear to make your decisions.”

The conservatory became silent.

Outside, a single snowflake landed upon the glass.

For years Mirov had believed that healing meant forgetting.

Perhaps he had been wrong.

Perhaps healing meant remembering without trembling.


---

Chapter 4:

Spring arrived slowly.

The snow disappeared from the garden, and the first green shoots appeared beneath the roses.

Mirov began to walk there again.

One afternoon, Peregrine found him kneeling beside the oldest rose bush, carefully removing the dead branches.

“You were right,” he said.

She smiled.

“About the roses?”

“About winter.”

He rose and brushed the soil from his gloves.

“I thought everything had ended because nothing was blooming.”
“And now?”
He looked towards the garden.
“Now I think some things simply require patience.”
Peregrine's eyes softened.
“And perhaps courage.”
“Yes.”
He paused.
“Perhaps courage most of all.”
That evening, they walked beneath the newly flowering trees.
Mirov spoke of the years he had spent hiding from happiness—not because Peregrine demanded his confession, but because he finally wished to give it.
He spoke of regret.
Of fear.
Of guilt he had carried long after it had ceased to serve any purpose.
When he finished, Peregrine did not tell him that the past did not matter.
She simply said:
“Your past matters. But it does not have the right to decide what comes next.”
Mirov stopped walking.
For a long moment he looked at her.
Then he took her hand.
Not desperately.
Not possessively.
Simply with gratitude.
“I believe,” he whispered, “I have been waiting for someone to tell me that.”
Peregrine smiled.
“Then believe it.”
And for the first time, Mirov did.

---
The Garden Beyond the Winter

Chapter 5:

That summer, Blackthorn Hall changed.

The windows remained open until late evening. Music occasionally drifted through the drawing room. The servants laughed more freely, and the neglected garden became beautiful again.

Mirov himself seemed transformed—not into another man, but into the man he had always been beneath his fear.
He still loved solitude.
He still valued silence.
But solitude was no longer his hiding place.
One evening, beneath the old rose arbor, he turned to Peregrine.
“I have spent so long believing that loving someone meant eventually losing them.”
Peregrine looked at him quietly.
“And what do you believe now?”
“That love is not a promise against sorrow.”
She waited.
“It is the courage to live despite it.”
A smile appeared upon her lips.
“And are you still afraid?”
Mirov considered the question.
“Yes.”
Peregrine raised an eyebrow.
“Then nothing has changed?”
“Everything has changed.”
He smiled.
“I am afraid—and I shall love anyway.”
Peregrine's eyes filled with warmth.
Mirov gently took her hand.“I cannot promise you that life will never hurt us.”
“I would never ask you to.”
“I cannot promise that tomorrow will resemble today.”
“Nor would I wish it to.”
He looked towards the roses.
“Then perhaps I have finally understood what I was trying to let go of.”
“What?”
“The belief that happiness must be surrendered simply because it cannot be guaranteed.”
Peregrine leaned closer.
“And what will you do with happiness now?”
Mirov smiled.
“For once…”
He looked at her.
“I shall welcome it.”
The evening breeze moved softly through the roses.
The garden that had once seemed lifeless was overflowing with colour.
And Mirov understood at last that the winter had never truly been in the garden.
It had been within him.
He had not needed to forget his past.
He had not needed to erase his grief.
He had only needed to stop carrying it as a prophecy of the future.
Beside Peregrine, beneath the roses, he finally allowed himself to believe that a heart could remember its wounds and still choose happiness.

And so they remained beneath the summer sky—not because either belonged to the other, but because they had freely chosen to walk the same path.

For Mirov, that was enough.

More than enough.

It was the beginning of everything he had once believed he could never have again.

Love. Hope. And a life beyond the winter.

And perhaps that was what letting go truly meant:

Sometimes letting go does not mean letting go of the person you love. It means letting go of the fear that prevents you from accepting the love that remains.

THE END 🌹📜

My Lady of the Dreamy Nights!

Thou art, oh, so beautiful, my lady, like the mesmerizing, wondrous twinkling star
 My lady doth enchant, captivate, and put me into a trance
 I stretch my hands towards thee, yet seem so far!
 I know thou canst only be my dream, for just a glance

Thou canst never be mine, but even in my dreams thou floatest away, out of my reach?
 I bathe in thy heavenly luminance afar and to thee offer my worship now,
 My ravishing lady of the sparkling, dreamy nights, thy elegance, thy charm, thy pristine celestial splendor doth bewitch
 Oh, my ethereal, angelic damsel, thou hast stolen my heart, never to return; take my bow!

Thy sublime loving caress draws me nearer
 With thee residing in my heart, I am richly blessed
 Oh, my lady, as thy spell turns deeper and dearer
 Banishing any gloom, in life's every trough, every crest

The very substance of ambition is merely the shadow of a dream
 My ambition lies in the mere desire even to touch thy soul or its shadow, setting my life agleam!

Name: SOUMASISH SAHA
Title: THE CHASE OF TIME
Content:
Chapter 1

   Aniruddha, exhausted, walked along the railway tracks, wiping away tears. He had taken the final decision of his life — after a little while he would end himself. Sitting on the rails, he began to remember the beautiful moments of his life. Suddenly, the beautiful face of his daughter floated before his eyes. He quickly took his wallet from his pocket and looked at the photograph of his family; a few tears fell onto his daughter’s picture.
   Aniruddha was the only earning son of a simple middle-class family. His father had worked as a caretaker at a paper mill and had struggled hard to educate him. He had taken a loan from the bank to send Aniruddha to college. When Aniruddha graduated, his father lost his job at the mill. Worried about how to repay the large bank loan, his father suffered a heart attack and died. After his father’s death, the entire burden of the family — including the bank loan — fell on Aniruddha’s shoulders. Fortunately, Aniruddha found a job at an IT company in Kolkata as a software engineer, earning about twenty-five thousand. With that salary he somehow managed the heavy burden. He then married Moushumi, who worked seasonally as a primary-school para-teacher. They had a beautiful daughter named Anamika. Aniruddha loved his daughter more than himself. But again, a dark shadow descended on the family. Aniruddha’s mother was diagnosed with blood cancer, and he spent all his money on her treatment. Unable to find a way out, he mortgaged his ancestral home and took out another huge loan from the bank—this time for an amount far greater than before. Aniruddha loved his mother dearly, and he fought desperately to save her. He repeatedly sought treatment for her, paying for chemotherapy and blood transfusions whenever possible. But unrest began to grow within his family. He and his wife argued constantly about taking such a large, mortgaged loan. On one side were his daughter's school expenses; on the other, his mother’s mounting medical bills; and all the while he was crushed by the calculations and burden of the enormous bank loan.
   Finally, the day came when Aniruddha, unable to repay the debt, was forced to leave his ancestral home. He moved into a rented house, and the unrest between him and his wife reached a breaking point. Yesterday Moushumi took their daughter and left for her father’s house as she left, she declared she would divorce him. The turmoil at home spilled into his work life. For several days he had been late to the office and taking frequent leave; today his boss berated him for failing to complete the project on time, fired him, and threw a resignation letter in his face.
   Crushed and devastated, Aniruddha realized there seemed to be no way out. He would never be able to repay the bank; he might even end up in jail. His wife was leaving him, and his mother’s condition was worsening by the day—she might not have much time left. From every direction he felt defeated, and in a world that had turned against him, there appeared to be only one escape: death!
   “Poo... Poo...” Aniruddha heard the distant whistle of a train. Quickly, he slipped his wallet into his pocket and lay down on the railway track. On the opposite track, a stray dog wandered aimlessly. Suddenly, it stopped, fixed its eyes on Aniruddha, and began barking furiously, as though trying to prevent him from committing this dreadful act.
   The train drew nearer, its approach trembling through the rails beneath him. Aniruddha felt the vibrations travel into his body. His heart pounded violently inside his chest. It would all be over in just a few moments. Then, at last, he would be free from this torment forever.
   Even with death rushing so close, fear no longer touched him. Unable to restrain the weight of that final moment, he closed his eyes, trying to quiet his restless mind. His daughter’s face surfaced before him, vivid and fragile, and tears slipped silently from the corners of his eyes.
   "It's not your time yet, Aniruddha! Get up."
   A voice came from the side. Aniruddha’s eyes opened. He noticed that the dog standing across from him had also stopped barking.
   "Get up, Aniruddha. It’s not your time yet. There’s no point in lying on the track. Get up."
   Aniruddha looked around and saw a man in a black coat and pants sitting on a milestone a short distance away. The man was holding a gold-plated watch in his hand, gazing at it intently, his head bowed as he examined the time. The moment Aniruddha sat up on the track, the man lifted his eyes toward him and smiled. There was a strange expression on his face, as though he had known Aniruddha for a long time.
   Then, the man stepped down from the milestone came and sat beside him. He fixed Aniruddha with a devilish stare.
   Aniruddha noticed that the man’s eyes glowed bright red, like blood. Startled, Aniruddha asked, “Who are you?”
  "My name is KAAL!... I can see everyone's death. And I'm seeing that it is not your time yet, Aniruddha — you will not die so soon."
   Aniruddha felt a flush of confusion. Was the man mocking him, or was something wrong with him? What did he mean, "I can see death" and "it's not your time yet"? And how did the man know his name? Aniruddha asked, tense, "How did you know my name?"
   The train whistle shrieked, growing louder and closer. The locomotive was only a few meters away. Aniruddha turned to the man and said, "You move off the track. Let me die in peace."
   "Why won't you understand, Aniruddha? Your time is not yet."
   "What are you talking about? Who are you? Get away from me or you'll die with me."
   "No, Aniruddha, I won't die! It is not your time yet. Do you see that dog in the line next to you?" The man raised a finger, pointing. "That dog's time has come — death is already hovering over its head."
   In a moment, the crossing switch on the railway line shifted. The train that had been heading straight towards Aniruddha turned aside and moved onto the next track. A dog was walking along the line, and as soon as it saw the train approaching, it began to run. But it could not match the speed of the train. It collided with the front of the engine, slipped beneath the iron wheels, and was torn into two pieces. Blood spurted out, splashing across Aniruddha’s shirt.
   Horrified by the sight, Aniruddha sat up with a jolt. The man sitting beside him glanced at his face and then began to smile.
   “I told you, Aniruddha—you wouldn’t die. Do you believe me now? My work here is done. See you…”
   With those words, the man stood up and left. Aniruddha sat in silence for a while.
   Then he called out, “Listen, mister, what’s your name?” But when he turned his head, there was no one there.
   On the railway track before him the two halves of the dog’s body are floating in a pool of blood. Its eyes bulged grotesquely, as if they were staring straight at Aniruddha. Shuddering with fear, he turned his face away and made his way down the tracks toward the road.

Chapter 2

   Aniruddha was walking along the road, his mind replaying the events of the day. He thought most about that man. Who was he? How did he know Aniruddha? What name he told to him? Suddenly, Aniruddha’s eyes fell on a bench a little ahead. There he was—the same man. Black coat, black pants… Yes, it was him. Aniruddha began walking toward him.
   The man was sitting on bench, holding a gold-plated watch. He was staring at the watch intently. Aniruddha went up and said: "Hey mister, what's your name?"
   The man looked up slowly, “Hey, Aniruddha, you’ve arrived! Come sit… sit here,” he said, pointing Aniruddha to sit next to him
   Aniruddha sat and compelled by a mixture of curiosity and unease, asked again, “What is your name?”
   The man’s reply came soft but certain. “My name is Kal Aniruddha!... I can see death.”
   Aniruddha’s face flickered with disbelief and recognition both. “Oh yes, Mr. Kaal!... Why have you been saying the same thing over and over again since then—time-death, death-time? Tell me, who are you? Are you God?”
   The man’s voice hardened with a strange authority. “I am not God, Aniruddha! I am Kaal! The one to whom God has given time. He may live only that allotted time, and then death will devour him. When his time comes, I will come to take him. I went to take that dog on the railway track, because his time had come. And you’ve seen...”

   Shaken by his outburst, Moushumi fled the room, wiping her eyes. Aniruddha glanced once at his daughter’s face.
   “Her time has come, Aniruddha,” Kaal said.
   Aniruddha glared. “Even if I die, I will never let this happen. Do what you want.”
   “I have nothing to do, Aniruddha. You must do what needs to be done. You have four minutes.” Kaal glanced at the clock. “To save the girl, you must kill someone else in her place. Kill someone, and I will extend your daughter’s life.”
   “Okay.... But this is the last time.”
   “For the last time,”
   Aniruddha and Kaal stood in the corridor. Aniruddha kept peeking at the doors of each room as they passed. A nurse was pushing an old man in a wheelchair; the man coughed weakly. Aniruddha looked at Kaal’s face. Kaal said, “Pneumonia patient. He’ll live at most a month and a half.”
   Aniruddha turned away. They stopped before another room. A patient’s leg was bandaged and suspended from the ceiling by a rope. Aniruddha looked at Kaal again.
   “He committed suicide by jumping from the third floor of his house,” Kaal said, “But he didn't die, he just broke his leg. Two years later, he'll do the same thing again. Then it's a sure shot..."
   “Damn,” Aniruddha whispered, and moved on to the next room. He saw patient after patient: each one seemed destined for a short life. He disliked them all. At last, he leaned over the railing of the second-floor corridor.
   "You can see him, Aniruddha." Kaal pointed his finger down at the boy who had the accident. “Young, Long life ahead—his time hasn’t come yet. If you kill him, your daughter’s life will lengthen too.”
   "If you kill him, his death will be considered an accident. You will not be at fault here. You have two minutes, and fifty-one seconds left Aniruddha. Decide" Kaal disappeared.
   Aniruddha understood there was no time. He rushed down the stairs, pushed open the ICU door, and entered. Inside, the boy lay unconscious on the bed. Aniruddha realized this was the golden opportunity to do what he had to do. He stepped in front of the boy’s head and slowly removed the oxygen mask from his mouth. The boy began convulsing on the bed, gasping for air. Aniruddha’s hands trembled. His eyes flickered with uncertainty. 
   What was he doing?
   The ECG machine beside the bed beeped louder and louder as the boy’s heart rate edged closer to a flat line. Aniruddha’s conscience pulled him back. With sudden force, he thrust the oxygen mask back onto the boy’s face. The boy’s frantic movements stilled, and his breathing steadied. On the ECG, the heart rate climbed back to normal.
   Tears streamed down Aniruddha’s face. He loathed himself. What a mortal sin he had nearly committed. Would he truly kill a young boy to save his daughter’s life? This boy, too, had a family. And Aniruddha, himself a father, had almost stooped to such a despicable act for the sake of his own child.
   “Leave it, Aniruddha! … You can’t.”
   Aniruddha turned and saw Kaal standing on the opposite side of the bed.
   “I knew you couldn’t do it, Aniruddha. It’s alright…”
   Aniruddha is going to say something, but Kaal stopped him.
   “Time doesn’t stand still for anyone, Aniruddha. But there is one last way to save your daughter. Do you know what it is?”
   Aniruddha slowly looked up at Kaal.
   “What you were going to do yesterday morning, you have to do again. But this time, for your daughter.”
   Aniruddha wiped his eyes. He understood what Kaal was trying to say. Aniruddha could even give his life for his daughter.
   “Another thirty seconds, Aniruddha, then—”
   Before Kaal could finish, Aniruddha left the room alone. He began climbing the stairs and reached the roof of the hospital building on the fifth floor. Outside, rain had started pouring with thunder and lightning. Drenched in the rain, Aniruddha stood before the roof wall. Slowly, he climbed onto it. Lightning split the sky with a deafening crack. Thunder roared somewhere close ahead.
   Aniruddha was fearless; there was no trace of fear on his face. He turned once to look back. Kaal was standing there, the ticking of his watch sharp in the silence between the thunderclaps. Kaal glanced at the watch and said:
   “Another ten seconds, Aniruddha. Hurry up and do what you have to...”
   Aniruddha looked down. Two ambulances stood on the road below, washed in rain. But the road itself was empty—people must have taken shelter from the storm.
   He didn’t wait any longer. Closing his eyes, his daughter’s face flashed before him. His legs felt weightless. And then—he jumped.
   In the ICU, Aniruddha’s daughter regained consciousness. As soon as she opened her eyes, she clung to her mother. Her first question was: where was her father? At that, her mother began searching for Aniruddha. She said:
   "Dad was here, I don’t know where he went… I can’t see him."
   Meanwhile, Aniruddha fell on the floor of the hospital compound. He opened his eyes and saw Kaal standing before him, smiling brightly.
   Kaal said with a laugh, "Get up, Aniruddha, we have to go now."
   Aniruddha stood, taking a long look around. Then he said, "Will you take me, Kaal?"
   "Weren’t you asking on the street, why you were the only one who could see me? Now you have your answer, don’t you?"
   "I understand… because it is my time too. Let’s go then. What more is there? I have gained much in life; I have lost much. Now I am free from all the sorrows and pains of my entire life, forever. Let’s go. I will go wherever you take me."
   "Don’t you want to meet the one you did all this for?"
   Aniruddha looked at Kaal’s face.
   "Go meet the girl once, and then come back…"
   Aniruddha’s eyes filled with tears at the thought of meeting his daughter. He said:
   "No… if I see her before leaving, my heart will break. Let her remain as she is. She has her mother to look after her. Her father is dead now. What more is there to say… I only want her to be well, forever."
   "Your daughter opened her eyes and asked about you first, Aniruddha. Why don’t you want to meet her?"
   Aniruddha’s eyes filled with tears. Kaal took him to stand in front of the ICU. From outside the door, Aniruddha saw his daughter sitting up in bed. Everything seemed fine to her. Her mother was on one side of the bed, and on the other side stood a doctor, explaining the medicines to Moushumi.
   At that moment, his daughter noticed Aniruddha standing at the door. "Baba... Baba..." she called out, raising her hand toward him. Both Moushumi and the doctor turned to look outside.
   Aniruddha was startled. He asked Kaal, "Can she see me? How?... But I’m—"
   He looked at Kaal, who was smiling. Moushumi gestured for Aniruddha to come inside.
   Kaal said with a smile, "Go. Your daughter is calling you. Go..."
   Aniruddha stepped in and embraced his daughter, kissing her forehead as tears streamed down his face. He asked softly,
   "Is everything alright? You don’t feel pain anywhere, do you?"
   The doctor beside them interrupted: "Excuse me... please don’t hold her so tightly. The wound on her head is still raw. Too much pressure could cause the bleeding to start again. Are you, her father?"
   Aniruddha released her gently and answered, "Yes..."
   The doctor asked, "Where have you been all this time?"
   Aniruddha said: “Me?... This... I mean... that... above... I mean...”
   Moushumi said: “How did your clothes get wet?”
   Aniruddha said: “Oh, that means... outside... that...”
   Moushumi said: “What’s going on outside?... Were you getting wet in the rain?”
   Aniruddha said: “Actually, I... I went to look for the doctor.”
   The doctor said: “You went out looking for me? Why?... I was in my room right there.”
   Aniruddha said: “Oh, sorry, I didn’t notice.” He looked at Kaal. He couldn’t understand what was happening. Kaal was standing on the other side of the door, smiling.
   The doctor handed Aniruddha a prescription paper and said: “Please bring these medicines from the counter. It’s time to give her (gesturing to his daughter) medicine.”
   Aniruddha said: “Yes, yes, I will bring it right away.” Saying this, he left the room. Then he came to the corridor and said to Kaal: “What is going on? How can they all see me?... Why are you laughing?”
   Kaal said: “Why can’t they see you?”
   “You mean?... You said you would take me?”
   Kaal pointed to the prescription in Aniruddha’s hand and said: “Who will bring those medicines? Are you trying to escape your daughter’s responsibility?”
   “I don't understand anything you're saying, Kaal! You came here to take me. I'm already dead, right? So, what's the delay? Come and take me now.”
   “Well... it seems you're in a hurry to go. Are you really dead, Aniruddha?”
   Aniruddha froze. “Didn't I die? I jumped from the fifth floor. Didn't I die?”
   Just then a ward boy pushed a trolley down the corridor. Aniruddha stepped in front of him and pleaded, “Hey brother, wait — listen.”
   The man stopped the trolley and stared at Aniruddha. He studied his face.
   “Can you see me?” Aniruddha asked.
   The man looked surprised. “See you? What do you mean?”
   “I mean I’m standing here, talking to you. You can see me properly, right?”
   “What do you mean... why can't I see you? Are you a ghost or something?” the man retorted.
    Aniruddha blinked, stunned by the question. “Can you really see me? You're not drunk, are you?”
   Kaal watched him and laughed.
   The man said to Aniruddha, “It's 10:30 now — we don't get drunk before 11:30. But you're not drunk, are you? What nonsense are you talking?” Annoyed, he pushed the trolley and walked away.
   “What is this?” Aniruddha couldn’t understand anything.
   Kaal placed his hand on Aniruddha’s shoulder and said, “Let’s take you somewhere.”
   “Where?”
   “Let’s see.”
   Kaal led Aniruddha and stopped him in front of a room. Inside, a gentleman was sitting on a stool while a junior doctor tied a bandage around his head. The man seemed quite familiar to Aniruddha. The gentleman looked outside and saw him.
   “Hey!... You?”
   The man stood up and held Aniruddha’s hands. At that moment, Aniruddha recognized him. It was the doctor who had nearly been murdered by an assailant in his own home—the very man whose life Aniruddha had saved.
   Aniruddha said, “Sir, you…? (glancing at the bandage on his head) Are you seeing a doctor? Are you alright? … 
   “Yah I’m okay now but you are here? … What are you doing here?”
   “Yes, I actually…”
   “Truly, what you’ve done for me… What would have happened to me if you hadn’t come then. Hey, your hand is cut.”
   “Actually …”
   "Just a minute... Hey, Samaresh... Samaresh..."
   A junior doctor came out of the room to respond. "Yes, sir?"
   "This man's hand is cut. Please take him and get it dressed."
   "Okay, sir," the junior doctor said, holding Aniruddha's hand. "Please come in, sir."
   "No, no, it's alright," Aniruddha said, embarrassed. "I can do it myself."
   "It's okay," the doctor replied. "I'm sorry, what was your name?"
   "Aniruddha, sir."
   "Yes, yes, Aniruddha Babu, please come inside. Don’t worry, this entire hospital is mine."
   Hearing this, Aniruddha looked at the doctor in surprise. The junior doctor dressed Aniruddha’s wound. The doctor placed his hand on Aniruddha’s shoulder and said:
   "Don’t worry, Aniruddha Babu, I didn’t tell the police anything about you. I told them I fought with that man myself and saved my life, and that he fell from the railing while trying to escape. I didn’t mention your name."
   "Thank you, sir," Aniruddha said.
   The doctor replied: "They have their eyes on my property. I knew something like this would happen. I had a hunch beforehand. So now I’ve informed the police officer and arranged security for myself."
   "Oh, very good. So now you have nothing to fear."
   "No!... Didn’t you say whom you came here to see? Do you have a patient with you?"
   "Yes, I mean, my daughter had a little accident, so she’s admitted here. I’m here to—"
   The doctor hesitated and asked, "What happened to the girl? Is it something serious?"
   "No, no, nothing serious. She’ll be released in a little while."
   "Oh, okay, okay, let it go. It’s scary to think about all the things that have happened during the day. Hey, Samaresh… please call Mala once."
   The junior doctor, Samaresh, called someone. The receptionist madam came running up from the floor below.
   "Sir, are you calling me?"
   The doctor said, "Yes, Mala, come. He"—placing his hand on Aniruddha’s shoulder—"is someone very close to me. His daughter is admitted in the ICU over there. I will pay all her bills."
   Aniruddha was surprised and said, "Hey, what are you saying, sir? Why would you pay my bill?"
   The doctor stopped him and said, "Don’t take a single penny from him."
  "Okay, sir," the receptionist madam said and left.
   The doctor then said to Aniruddha, "Didn’t I tell you that one day I would definitely repay you for this kindness? Let’s go and see your daughter now."
   The doctor took Aniruddha to see his daughter in the ICU. There, Moushumi told him about his mother’s illness. The doctor promised Aniruddha that he would have his mother treated in this hospital and that he would bear all the expenses. Aniruddha’s face turned red with shame.
   While leaving, the doctor asked Aniruddha: “What do you do, Aniruddha Babu?”
   Aniruddha replied that he had worked in an IT company but had lost his job. The doctor told him there was no need to feel bad about it. His brother was the owner of a large IT company in Kolkata, and he would speak to him about Aniruddha and arrange a job for him very soon. Saying this, he left.
   Meanwhile, Moushumi came crying and hugged Aniruddha. She admitted her mistake and told him that she had been wrong in judging him. Their daughter had always wanted to go to her father. She had decided to return to Aniruddha today, but this disaster had intervened. Moushumi said she would go back to him now, with their daughter. Tears of emotion flowed from Aniruddha’s eyes.
   Kaal beckoned to Aniruddha from outside the ICU door. Aniruddha told Moushumi he was going to the reception and left the room.
   In the corridor, Kaal asked Aniruddha: “What?... Now you get your old life back, Aniruddha, right? Are all the bad times over?”
   Aniruddha clasped Kal’s hands tightly and said: “Truly, Kaal, if you hadn’t been here today, who knows where I would have ended up? How wrongly I judged you. I completely mistrusted you. But today, you have transformed my life entirely. You did something I could never have imagined. You truly have the power to change people’s lives and destiny.”
Kaal replied: “I haven’t changed anything about you, Aniruddha. It was your time, and you changed it yourself. I only showed you the way. You walked that path on your own. You changed your time, Aniruddha. The Aniruddha whose days were going badly yesterday is in a better place today. So, what do you understand?”
“What?”
“No one can stop time, Aniruddha. But people can change time. If you can use that time instead of running after it, you will see that you can achieve a lot in life. So instead of blaming yourself for bad times, use time and see how you can make that bad time better. And yes, in this world, the lifespan given by God to a person is only as long as the time he has. No one knows what will happen tomorrow. So, enjoy the time you have in life with all your heart. Don’t waste it.
   You love your family very much, Aniruddha. As a father, what you have done for your daughter today is truly undeniable. Your family needs you very much now, and you need your family too. Stay with them always. They will also stand by you in your troubles now.
   So, it’s time for me to go now, Aniruddha. I’m going. You be well.”
“Yes, see you again...”
   “No!... not again, Aniruddha. Don’t you understand the meaning of meeting me?”
   Kaal placed his hand on Aniruddha’s shoulder.
   “Be well, Aniruddha....”
   With these words, Kaal walked toward a dark part of the corridor and, after a short distance, disappeared into the shadows.
   Aniruddha returned home with his wife and daughter. Moushumi came and bowed before her mother-in-law.
   The next day, Aniruddha took his mother to the hospital and had her admitted. There, the doctor told Aniruddha’s mother the story of her son’s heroism—how Aniruddha had risked his own life, fighting the assailant alone to save him. Hearing this, Aniruddha’s mother’s face glowed with pride for her son.
   A few days later, on the doctor’s advice, Aniruddha joined his brother’s IT company. His mother, who had been battling a deadly disease, eventually recovered.
   Aniruddha’s life was once again filled with happiness and joy.

Chapter 8

   Few days later …
   A gentleman sat at a bus stop beneath the canopy on the side of the road. He wore a checked shirt, black formal pants, polished black shoes, a watch, and glasses, with an office bag tucked under his arm. He kept glancing at his watch again and again. It was nine fifty-five. His office is across the street.
   “Ashutosh Babu!”
   The man looked up when someone called his name.
   "Your time has come ... now move on." Saying this, Kaal sat down next to the man on the bench at the bus stop. The man looked at Kaal in surprise.
   The man asked Kaal, "Yeah... but how did you know my name?"
   Kaal pointed to the man's ID card with his eyes and said, "That's how I saw it, your name is written on that ID card."
   The man had his ID card hanging around his neck. The man said, "Oh, I see. Yeah, time has come but I get into the office at exactly ten. I'm really strict about this..."
   "Wow... I see you value time very much, that's nice."
   "By the way, your name?" The man extended his hand to Kaal for a handshake.
   Kaal shook hands with the man and said, "My name is Kaal."
   "Kaal means season?... Which season?... Rainy season or autumn?... Summer season or winter?... Ha, ha, ha." The man started joking with Kaal. But Kaal didn’t like it at all. Kaal looked at the man.
    
   The man, realizing that Kaal didn’t like his humor, said, "Hey, don’t be angry, Kaal babu, I’m actually a bit of a humorous person... But what kind of name is this 'Kaal'? I’ve never heard of anyone like that before. What’s your .full name?"
   Kaal got a little annoyed and said, "Antim Kaal."
   "Antim Kaal—The last time?... What kind of name is that?"
   Kaal was about to say something when the man asked, “So, what do you do?”
   Kaal replied, “When someone’s time is up, I come to take them. And now I’m…”
   The man interrupted, “Time is up? What time is up?” As he said this, he looked at his watch. It was ten o’clock, with two minutes left. The man said:
   “Well, listen, Kaal Babu, I am a life insurance agent by profession. Do you want to get any insurance?”
   Kaal asked, “Insurance?... Should I get insurance?”
   “Yes… a new scheme has come into the market. If you die, your family will get 1.5 crore. Tell me, should I prepare this scheme in your name?”
  “Wow… that’s a pretty good scheme. Then you need to do this scheme first.”
   “Yes, of course. I already have an insurance policy of 2 crore in my name. Suppose I die, then all the money will be transferred to my wife’s account.”
   “Oh, I see… your wife is going to be rich very soon.”
   “Ha, ha, ha…” The man laughed. “You’re quite funny, Kaal Babu.”
   “Your time has come Ashutosh Babu, now go ahead. Don’t be late at all.”
   The man looked at his watch and saw that it was ten o’clock. He said, “Yes, .yes, you are right, it is time for me.” Then he stood up from the bench.
 
“See you, Kaal babu.”
   “Yah, see you.”
   “You should think carefully about the scheme. If you decide to take it….” The man took out a card from his pocket and handed it to Kaal. The card had his name, office address, and phone number written on it. “Give me a call on this number or come to my office over there.” He pointed across the street.
   “Okay, okay… You move on, I’ll see you again very soon. You move on, Asutosh babu, I’ll stay here.”
   “Oh, you’ll stay here?” The man turned around and walked onto the street while speaking to Kaal. “Then I’ll….”
   Suddenly, a private car slammed on its brakes and stopped right in front of him. Had it been any closer, it would have hit him. He jumped in fear.
   “Are you trying to kill me?” he shouted at the driver. The driver got out, cursing, his face peering out of the window.
   The man stood in the middle of the road, looked at Kaal at the bus stop, and said, “You see, Kaal babu, what a rude lot these people are. They don’t watch out for anyone. If they could, they’d run people over without a second thought. You can’t walk safely on the streets because of their reckless driving.”
   Kaal, sitting at the bus stop, laughed hysterically after hearing him.
   “See you, Kaal Babu.” Saying this, the man stood in the middle of the road and waved at Kaal.
   Kaal, seated at the bus stop, also waved back at the man. His red eyes sparkled.
   As the man turned his face and headed toward his office, a speeding truck from the opposite direction crushing him to death.
