Name: Saikat Kumar Maji
Title: The Country I Carry
Content: Every morning at six, before the sun had properly risen, Saikat unlocked the little tea stall beside the railway crossing. The stall was nothing special. A blue plastic sheet for a roof. A wooden counter darkened by years of tea stains. Three aluminium kettles. Six glass jars filled with biscuits. A small radio that worked only when it felt like it. But there was one thing Saikat never forgot. Every morning, he folded the national flag carefully, placed it on the cleanest part of the counter, and touched it with his fingertips before beginning his day.One morning, a schoolboy noticed.“Uncle, why do you do that every day? “Saikat smiled. “Because it is my country. “The boy laughed. “I know that. But what does a flag have to do with your tea shop? Saikat poured tea into a glass. “Everything. “The boy was not convinced. “Did you fight for the country? “Saikat shook his head.“No.”“Then what did you do? “Saikat looked across the railway tracks. “Nothing big.”He paused.“Maybe that is why I remember. Saikat had never been a soldier.He had never stood on a stage.His name had never appeared in a newspaper.He had simply lived.For thirty-five years, he had opened his stall before sunrise and closed it after the last local train had passed.He had given free tea to railway workers during winter.He had kept an umbrella at the stall for passengers caught in sudden rain.When a student's examination fee was short by a few hundred rupees, Saikat quietly paid it.When a migrant worker lost his wallet, Saikat gave him enough money to reach home.When an old woman came to the station every Sunday to meet a son who had stopped returning, Saikat kept a cup of tea ready for her.“Why do you help everyone?” the boy once asked.Saikat laughed.“I don't help everyone.”“Then?”“I help whoever is standing in front of me.”Years passed.The schoolboy grew up.He left the village for college.Then came a job in another city.Then another city.Then another.Like millions of young people, he became busy.His country slowly became something he saw on television.A map in a textbook.A flag during national holidays.A word people shouted during cricket matches.One evening, twenty years later, he returned to his hometown.The tea stall was still there.But Saikat was sitting behind the counter, thinner now, his hair completely white.The boy, now a grown man, smiled.“Uncle, you still remember me?”Saikat looked at him for a few seconds.Then his eyes lit up.“The boy who asked why the flag belonged in a tea shop.”They laughed.The man sat down.“Do you still believe that?”Saikat looked at the flag.“Yes.”“Why?”Saikat remained silent for a while.Then he pointed toward the railway crossing.A group of workers were repairing the tracks.A woman was buying vegetables from a roadside seller.Two children were running to school.A police constable was standing in the heat, controlling traffic.A farmer on a bicycle was carrying sacks of rice.An ambulance crossed the road.A train passed.Thousands of lives.Thousands of struggles.Thousands of ordinary people.Saikat said quietly,“A country is not only its borders.”The man listened.“It is the railway worker who repairs the track so someone reaches home safely.It is the teacher who teaches a child even when the salary comes late.It is the farmer who wakes before sunrise so another family can eat.It is the nurse who stays awake beside a stranger.It is the driver who takes an ambulance through traffic.It is the person who refuses a bribe even when nobody is watching.It is the student who studies because tomorrow belongs to them.”He touched the flag.“A country is made of people who do small things honestly.”The man looked down.“Then loving your country means...?”Saikat smiled.“It means caring about what happens to people you may never meet.”The words stayed with him.That night, he returned home and opened his old suitcase.Inside were photographs from school, certificates, a broken wristwatch—and an old notebook.On the first page, written in a child's handwriting, were four words:**I LOVE MY COUNTRY.**He stared at them for a long time.As a child, he had thought loving his country meant feeling proud.As an adult, he finally understood.Love was not only pride.Love was responsibility.The next morning, he went to a government school near his home.He asked the headmaster one question.“What does the school need?”The headmaster mentioned broken desks.So he helped repair them.A month later, he noticed several children were missing classes because they did not have proper books.He bought books.Later, he joined a group cleaning the pond near the village.Then he started helping elderly people fill out online government forms.None of these things made the news.No one gave him a medal.No one called him a hero.But one morning, while walking past the school, he saw a little girl standing beneath the national flag.She was singing.Her voice was small.A little shaky.But she sang with everything she had.The man stopped.For the first time, he understood what Saikat had meant.The flag did not belong to soldiers alone.It belonged to the farmer.The teacher.The worker. The student. The mother. The child. It belonged to everyone who carried this country forward in whatever small way they could. That evening, he returned to Saikat's tea stall. But the stall was closed. The next day, it was still closed. And the day after that.Only then did he learn that Saikat had passed away peacefully in his sleep.On the counter, beneath the old radio, the national flag was folded neatly.Beside it was a piece of paper.There was only one sentence.**“I could not give my country everything. So I tried to leave every person I met a little better than I found them.” The man read it twice.Then he folded the paper carefully. Years later, whenever someone asked him what patriotism meant, he never spoke about shouting louder, waving a flag higher, or proving that one country was better than another.He simply said:“Love your country enough to make it better—even when nobody is watching.”Because a nation is not built only in parliament halls, battlefields, or history books.Sometimes, it is built quietly—in a classroom,on a farm,beside a railway track,inside a hospital,at a small tea stall,and in the heart of an ordinary personwho decides,every single day,to care.That is the country we inherit.And that is the country we carry.

Name: Dipanwita Dey
Title: The House Of Cards We Called Home
Content:
I never realized until I noticed
a part of me had dissolved
in the intoxication of you.
That missing piece was never mine
it had always belonged to you.

I never noticed
how my sleep slipped away
into an ocean of thoughts
I couldn’t solve.

I wrapped myself in your thoughts
thoughts that were not all true.

I lost a part of me
just to preserve the image of you,
etched deep in my heart,
in my soul,
in my mind.

I waited for an eternity
for the silence to break,
for the smile that never stayed.
I clung to the last sweet melody
that still echoes in my ears.

I couldn’t break the wall
you built around yourself
to protect your heartbreak.
A thousand times I tried and fell,
But the longing to be called yours
kept me chasing a million ways, 
to hold on to a beautiful delusion I built in my fairytale. 

I wish I could have a glance of your mysterious world.
Instead,
I built a house of cards,
believing it could be our forever home
never noticing how it crumbled each day.
Still, I kept collecting the pieces,
like a hopeless soul
thinking it had found its forever place.

I never realized
until I emptied myself
just to carry your broken pieces as mine.
I never realized
I let you leave your fingerprints on my heart,
knowing they would haunt me
until my last breath.

I lost a piece of myself
just to keep the forever you.

Name: Shrushti Rathva
Title: The Love I Left Behind
Content:
Five years ago, Niharika Sharma had trusted one person who meant more than anyone in the world.

Avyansh Mathur, her best friend, her secret crush, her everything.

Until he turned her world and biggest secret into the worst nightmare of her life which she could have never imagined in her life. The betrayal.

It had started with a prank, she always believed that her ansh would do anything but wont hurt her ever.

As for Niharika she always believed ansh also had feelings for her because the way he noticed something no one ever did, and the way he only let her call ansh because only aside from her anyone can call him anything expert that its like the right only belonged to her 

It was a summer festival and Niharika was backstage preparing for her dance when she heard a few people talking about some surprise she thought maybe it was for someone so she ignored it. 

Once she was on stage she saw the screen behind her turned on 

She her private messages appeared where she indirectly hinted she was in love with ansh

But the very next second a videos come up where ansh confess that she is so childish and very immature and no one in right mind would be her partner 

The entire auditorium exploded with laughter 

And ansh? He stood there silent 
Watching her break because he knew all this will come up 

“Turn it off,”she whispered 

He just stood there watching her with a smirk but it wiped off as soon as a slap was landed on his cheek by none other than Niharika.

The whole crowd fell silent and niharika spoke yes i have loved you before you were my everything but you know what some people don't deserve that just like you i hate you avyansh mathur 

For the last time Niharika looked at the boy she loved and something inside her died.

That night, she deleted his number and completely ignored him for 2 months and left for dehradun 
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5 years later

she was standing in the office of Spanish fashion, staring at the man she had spent five years trying to forget 

Fate brought her back to him when she was signed up for Paris fashion week by this company as it was a huge opportunity  for her to turn down so she accepted it and now here she was in front of him again.

Avyansh Mathur CEO  of ikansh fashion 

Tall, muscular and more sharp and cold but the eyes they held something he counsel decipher 

Finally he said 

Congratulation Niharika 

She smiled professionally 

Thankyou Mr Mathur and i will give my best 

His expression tightened 

She waited and spoke after a minutes shall we start mr mathur as i w have to go  through alot to understand styles and models 

He nodded and for the next three weeks strangers disguised as professionals at least from her side while avyansh was trying his best to stay neutral

They just worked like every other boss and employee but even after ansh bringing her favorite milkshake and food while bringing regular for other employees.

One evening, after fourteen-shoot, avyansh found Nihartika packing her makeup brushes 

“You are leaving without dinner “

“I am not hungry” she said while packing

“You haven't eaten since noon”

She looked up

“Thankyou mr mathur for your worries but i am okay “ 

He handed her a smiley french fries just the way she loved she looked at him than at fries and than said “tahnkyou once again mr mathur but sorry i cant eat this i am not kid anymore”

That day he knew how badly he hurt her because refusing smiley fries.

At reunion party when some friends spoke about that incident she blanked out still but reacted nothing but for him it was like someone stabbed him again and for the first time he did what she never thought would happen he came in the middle of the crowd k wheeled on both legs and hold his ears just how he used to apologies back than.

for everyone it was shock because the avyansh mathur doesnt kneel in front of anyone and one test escapade her eyes which didn't went unnoticed by him and spoke “even though i dont deserve your forgiveness but indeed to say this whatever i did is not forgivable and i dont deserve but i am extremely sorry for that hope so one day you forgive me.

And that went viral in their old college group again 

For the first time in five years, Niharika opened that group.

Hundreds of messages had appeared.

“Is that Avyansh Mathur?”

“He actually knelt ? The same guy who did that to Niharika?”

She stared at the screen for a few seconds before locking her phone.

She didn't care about the video.

Or at least, she wanted to believe she didn't.

But she couldn't stop thinking about the look on his face.

There had been no arrogance.

No smirk.

No trace of the boy who had stood silently while her world fell apart.

Only regret.

And somehow, that scared her more than his hatred ever could.

The next morning, she found a cup of coffee waiting on her desk.

Her favorite.

But there was no note.

No message.

Nothing.

She looked toward Avyansh's cabin.

She picked up the coffee.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

He heard her.

His fingers stopped moving over the keyboard.

But he didn't look up.

“You're welcome, Niharika.”

She froze.

It was the first time in five years he had said her name like that.

Softly.

Without ownership.

Without expecting anything.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Paris Fashion Week preparations became more intense. 

Niharika worked harder working on her skills day and night constantly standing and moving 

Avyansh noticed every little thing.

The way she stayed late.

The way she checked every outfit twice.

The way she quietly helped junior models who were nervous.

She had changed.

And he was proud of her.

One night, Niharika found him alone in the studio, surrounded by design sketches.

“You're still here?”

“So are you.”

She smiled faintly. For a moment, it felt familiar. Too familiar.

“You always wanted to design internationally.”

“I did.”

“You achieved it.”

“Not everything I wanted.”

Her smile faded.

“Why didn't you explain?”

His expression changed.

“About that night?”

She nodded.

“Because I was a coward. I thought it was just a stupid prank. The guys convinced me it would be funny. They said you'd laugh once everyone knew about your crush.”

His voice cracked.

“I knew you were going to be embarrassed. I knew you would hate it. But I never imagined…”

He stopped.

“You didn't stop it.”

“No.”

“You watched.”

“Yes.”

“You smiled.”

His eyes lowered.

“I did.”

Niharika swallowed.

“That is what hurt the most.”

“I know.”

“No, you don't.”

She stepped closer.

“You knew I loved you. You knew I trusted you. You knew you were the only person I had told everything to.”

Her eyes filled with tears.

“And you used the one thing I was most afraid of against me.”

Avyansh didn't defend himself.

“You're right.”

That answer somehow hurt more.

“I waited for you to come after me,” she whispered.

His eyes lifted.

“I waited for you to say it wasn't true. I waited for you to explain. I waited for you to come to my house and tell me you were sorry.”

His jaw tightened.

“But you never came.”

“I did.”

She stared at him.

“What?”

“I came to your house that night.”

She went completely still.

“You weren't there.”

“My mother told me you had left for Dehradun.”

“I had.”

“I stood outside your house for almost an hour.”

Niharika's lips parted.

“Why didn't you call?”

“I had your number.”

“You deleted it.”

“Not until that night.”

She stared at him.

“I was angry. Ashamed. And scared that if I saw you again, I'd hate myself even more.”

He paused.

“So I left.”

Neither spoke.

Five years of anger suddenly felt much heavie

The day before Paris, Niharika received a phone call.

Her mother.

She smiled while talking.

When she ended the call, she turned around and found Avyansh standing behind her.

“Everything okay?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She hesitated.

“My parents want me to come home after Paris.”

His expression remained neutral.

“That sounds nice.”

“They're looking for someone for me.”

His face went still.

Niharika noticed.

“Someone?”

She nodded.

“Marriage.”

For the first time in years, Avyansh looked genuinely shaken.

But he only said—

“I hope he's good to you.”

Niharika stared at him.

“That's all?”

“What else should I say?”

“I don't know.”

He smiled sadly.

“Whatever I want to say doesn't matter anymore.”

She looked at him for a long moment.

Then I walked away.

Paris changed everything.

The fashion week show was a success.

Niharika stood backstage after the final walk, watching the lights fade.

She had done it.

The dream she once thought was impossible had finally become real.

Everyone celebrated.

Avyansh stood at the far end of the hall.

Watching her 

Proud.

But preparing to let her go.

When she finally approached him, he handed her a small box.

“What is this?”

“Open it.”

Inside was a tiny silver bracelet.

A small letter was attached.

Niharika unfolded it.

For the girl who taught me that love isn't about protecting someone from the world.

It's about never becoming the reason they need protection.

Her eyes blurred.

She looked at him.

“I don't deserve to give you this.”

“Then why did you?”

“Because I wanted you to have something that didn't come with an expectation.”

He stepped back.

“No forgiveness. No second chance. Nothing.”

Niharika looked down at the bracelet.

“Just a goodbye?”

He smiled.

“If that's what you want.”

She looked at him.

And she realized something.

The boy she had loved five years ago had been selfish.
But the man standing in front of her was finally willing to love her without asking her to belong to him.

And perhaps that was the difference between loving someone and actually being ready for them.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Three months later.

Niharika was back home.

She had started working on her own beauty and fashion project.
Life was moving forward.

One evening, Niharika was sitting on her balcony when her phone rang. The number was unknown.

“Hello?”

Silence.

Then a familiar voice whispered, “Hi, Nihu.”

Her heart skipped.

“Avyansh?”

“Yeah.”

She smiled despite herself. “Why did you call?”

“I just wanted to hear your voice.”

She closed her eyes. “That's dangerous.”

“I know.”

After a pause, he said, “I'll be in Dehradun next week. I won't meet you unless you want me to.”

“You've changed.”

“I had to. Losing you once taught me what regret feels like. Losing you again 
would teach me what acceptance feels like.”

Her smile faded.

“Avyansh…”

“I won't ask you to forgive me, love me, or give me another chance.”
She looked at the bracelet around her wrist.

“Then what do you want?”

His voice softened.

“One coffee.”

She laughed quietly. “And if I say no?”

“Then I'll drink it alone.”

“You still hate drinking coffee alone.”

“I've learned to live with it.”

She looked up at the night sky before finally saying, “Fine. One coffee.”

His breath caught. “When?”

“Saturday.”

“Okay.”

“Avyansh?”

“Hmm?”

“Don't be late.”

A smile touched his voice.

“Never again.”

Saturday came.

Niharika reached the café first.

Five minutes later, the door opened.

Avyansh walked in.

He stopped when he saw her.

She was wearing a simple white dress.

Her hair was open.

And around her wrist was the bracelet he had given her.

His eyes fell on it.

She noticed.

“Don't look so surprised.”

“You're wearing it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She smiled.

“Because you were right.”

“About?”

“Sometimes people deserve a second chance.”

His heart pounded.

“But…”

She raised a finger.

“Don't get excited.”

He laughed.

“I wasn't.”

“You absolutely were.”

“Okay. Maybe a little.”

She shook her head.

Then she looked at him seriously.

“I haven't forgotten what happened.”

“I know.”

“I may never completely forget it.”

“I know.”

“And trusting you again won't happen overnight.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“But I'm willing to try.”

Avyansh stared at her.

“Are you sure?”

“No.”

He laughed softly.

“That's honest.”

“But I want to find out.”

He looked down, trying to hide the emotion in his eyes.

Then he reached across the table.

He didn't hold her hand.

He simply placed his palm on the table between them.

An invitation.

Nothing more.

Niharika looked at his hand.

Then slowly placed hers over it.

His fingers trembled.

Just once.

And she smiled.

“You know something?”

“What?”

“You were always my safe place.”

His eyes became wet.

“But you stopped being one.”

“I know.”

“Maybe…”

She squeezed his hand.

“Maybe we can build a new one.”

He looked at her.

“Together?”

She smiled.

“Slowly Ansh.”

And for the first time in five years, Avyansh couldn’t hold it in anymore. He 
hugged her and cried. She let him, holding him tightly.

He simply held her hand carefully, as though he had finally understood its value.

Because sometimes, love doesn’t return as the same story.

Sometimes, it returns as two people who have grown, hurt, healed, and learned how to choose each other again.

And this time—

Niharika didn’t choose the boy who had once been her everything.

She chose the man who had finally learned how to become worthy of being her something.


The End

Name: Jahnavi Muralidhar
Theme: Letting go, dropping expectations, realising a relationship won't serve you
Title: Let go and fall
Content:
You and I, we're holding on to either ends of a rope.
Society tells me I should love you, I should respect you
Because you're the one keeping me safe from the world
And you hold on tight to the rope, determined to keep me close
To shelter me from the world, that I can move forward, but only within your gaze
And I myself can feel your affection sometimes, in your persistence
How you keep holding onto the rope, even if I tell you to let go, even if I scream at you
I can feel your warmth and your sincerity in the way you hold on, your arms trembling with anxiety
And therefore, I want us to try again

But it seems to be that no matter how much I try, something isn't quite right
I tell you "please loosen your hold, and don't hold me that tight, don't twist it that way"Because you're cutting into my arm and my arm might start to bleed
But you just hold on even tighter. Maybe you're just anxious, that I might go away
That the loosening of your hold might mean that you lose me forever
But that isn't an excuse for you to act the way you do, is it? Why can't you trust me?
You twist the rope in just the way you know hurts the most, a memory of me trusting you weaponized against me and myself
and I can't do this anymore
And all the wounds you've caused me through the years are all in my battered hand
Wounds that just won't heal, because you've cut too deep. I won't say I'm an angel
Because I'm not an angel, I'm human too. And some days when you twist the rope, I twist it right back at you where I know it'll hurt you
Maybe I want you to feel a fraction of what I have felt
But even if I do that, it just hurts my hand too. Our relationship, which the society said is holy, and pious, why is it like this?I ignore the seething pain in my hand, just to hurt you more
But it doesn't give me the peace that I thought it would. And now at night, I'm looking down at you, at the rope in my hand, and wondering what went wrong again

Two radically opposite people. One who is so in love it makes them anxious
And one is hurt by that anxiety every single day. Isn't this gap between intent and action way too wide? It's so wide that it cuts me like a knife
Can you please set me free, I don't want to try anymore
No matter how many times we try, and take it slow, and I tell myself, its okay if we're different, we're going to try again, somehow, we're back here again
You with your hand trembling with anxiety, and me with eyes that look caged
Can you please set me free then, I just can't try anymore

The sanctity and love which was supposed to be here, which I never felt
My heart beats with anxiety at the rope trembling with yours
I tell you, "let's try again, here's what I need." but you twist my hand where it hurts
And now, I just look away, I can't bear to meet your eyes again

I'll drop the rope, and along with that, all expectations for you
We're family by blood but you never felt like my family by the way you act
Some relationships just aren't meant to be
I dropped the rope, I stopped trying to get you to act a certain way
Only if I hold onto the rope, I keep telling you "no, don't twist it! it hurts."I can't make you who you're not. So I let go
And now I'm free.

Name: Shreyasee das
Theme: Echoes of the soul,A journey from outside world to inside,The Sun,Epic, Ego
Title: The Shadow and the sun
Content:
*THE SHADOW AND THE SUN*
_Where Kurukshetra Lives Inside_
_By Shreyasee_

There is a place inside every human
Where Kurukshetra never ended.

Not a field of arrows,
But a field of identities.

On one side stands the world
With all its names, its trophies, its wounds.

On the other stands the soul,
Naked, silent,
Needing no applause to exist.

And between them,
On a chariot that has lost its way,
Stands a man born of the Sun,
Yet living in shadow.

His name is Karna.
Not the Karna of Hastinapur.
The Karna who lives inside us.

He was the Sun who needed a cloud to prove his light.

Sutaputra, they called him,
And he believed it.

Then a curse became his scripture,
Then a crown became his soul.
Angraj, they called him,
And he became a slave to that name.

That is his tragedy,
Not that he was denied,
But that he never denied the denial.

He gave and gave and gave,
His armor, his earrings, his friendship, his life,
But he never took.

Never rest.
Never peace.
Never the simple knowing,
I am enough.

And his loyalty,
That fire-like loyalty to Duryodhan that poets praise?

It was never to Duryodhan.
It was loyalty to his own wound.

Duryodhan did not give him friendship.
He gave him identity.
He said, I make you King.
And for a man who had been called Sutaputra all his life,
That one word became oxygen.

He was not protecting Duryodhan on the battlefield.
He was protecting the only man who had ever given him a name that did not wound.

Is this not us?
Are we not all loyal to those who gave us a name?
To the company that gave us a designation,
To the lover who gave us worth,
To the degree that gave us pride?

We call it loyalty,
But it is slavery to our own ego.

The fire to prove,
But not the power to become the living proof.

Truth has no figure.
Truth has foundation.

A lamp is not true because its light travels far.
It is true because its oil is deep.

THE SCIENCE OF THE SUN

The Sun rides a chariot pulled by seven horses.
They are not horses.
They are light itself, broken into seven colors.

Violet - The Crown.
The highest thought.
In Karna, clouded by the need to be seen as great.

Indigo - The Third Eye.
The eye that sees within.
Karna never opened it.
He saw himself only through the eyes of others.

Blue - The Throat.
The courage to speak truth that liberates,
Not truth that proves.

Green - The Heart.
Love.
In Karna, an ocean, but a wounded ocean.

Yellow - The Will.
The fire to become.
In Karna, the fire to prove he was a warrior,
But never the power to sit quietly and know,
I am a warrior even when no war exists.

Orange - The Creation.
Skill.
The greatest archer in all the land,
Yet a slave to his own skill.

Red - The Root.
Foundation.
Which Karna never had.
His root was never in his soul,
But in his support,
In a curse, in a crown, in a friendship.

When seven horses run in seven directions,
The chariot does not move, though the horses run fast.

Immense speed. Zero arrival.
Born from the Sun, yet never reaching the Sun.

There are two Suns.

Prakash Surya - The Outer Sun.
It gives light to all, but burns itself.
It needs a world to see it.
This is the Karna in us.

Bodha Surya - The Inner Sun.
It does not give light.
It is Light.
It has no sunrise, no sunset.
Its seven horses have become one white fire.
It needs no witness.
This is the Shreyasee in us.

Life is a pilgrimage from Prakash to Bodha,
From seven colors to One,
From proving to being,
From mud to lotus.

A lotus is born in mud.
It does not curse the mud.
It uses the mud to bloom above it.

That was the true aim of the epic,
Not to show who won,
But to show how every soul,
Even the most wounded, can become a lotus.

Even Karna.

THE MEETING

An empty field.
No conches. No armies.
Only two souls.

SHREYASEE:

What word is this, forgiveness, upon thy tongue, O Angraj?

Thou art called noble, great of soul.
Dost thou not know what every child knows?
The light of the Sun can never be bound.

Its hue may shift,
Saffron at dawn, white at noon, blood-red at dusk,
And so its shadow changes shape.
But light remains light.

Thou art but a form of shadow, Karna.
And shadows do not live long where true light reigns.

Thou namest Draupadi guilty.
But is that guilt hers, or is it thine own longing wearing her face?

Thou hast built a palace upon dust.
Thy Guru's curse became thy foundation.
Sutaputra became thy scripture.
But true brilliance needs no crutch.
True valor walks on its own feet.

In what pride callest thou thyself Suryaputra,
When thy seven steeds run scattered?
Thy violet craves a crown, thy red has no root.
How shall thy chariot ever find the Sun?

And thy troth to Duryodhan,
Is it love for a friend,
Or love for the throne that gave thee a name?
Had he not cried Angraj in that sabha, wouldst thou still have loved him?

Speak true, O Sun in chains,
Thou art loyal not to Duryodhan, but to thine own wound.

KARNA:

Peace!

Thou speakest of light as one who has read of fire,
But never been branded by it.

Infinite blaze of the Sun no mortal flesh can bear.
It is shadow that makes the Sun's wrath into a mother's love.
Without shadow, the Sun is but death.

As shadow is part of body, so night is part of Sun.
Man sees the Sun not by light, but by the shadow in his own eye.
Light dwells within, but shadow is the tongue that tells the world of the Sun.

Ego is man's identity.
Without ego, there is no Om.
Without I, there is no beginning.
Ego is Lakshmi. It gives man legs to walk this earth.
And that same ego, when washed in sacrifice, rises as Om.

My friendship is my Dharma.
My seven horses know but one road, the road of my word.
And a word is a mountain.
A mountain waits for none, but it never moves.

SHREYASEE:

True, light is never sundered from shadow.
But without body, where is shadow, Karna?
Without self, where is ego?

Thy brilliance, thy valor, it is a web, O great weaver,
Woven of illusion.
For it is not knit to thy soul.
Thou bearest it as burden and callest burden duty.

Thou hast become slave to thine own gift.
But the Sun is slave to none, not even to its own shining.

What warrior art thou, who needs a war to know he is warrior?
What Sun art thou, that needs a cloud to prove it shines?

Look, every man today has thy fire,
The fire to prove.
But where is the power to become the living proof?

True Suryaputra is not he whose horses run swift,
But he whose horses run together.

Take that name away, Angraj.
Who art thou?

KARNA:

Existence is as a mountain.
A mountain has weight and echo too.
But a mountain waits for none.

SHREYASEE:

But beneath every mountain, Karna,
Beneath every mountain there burns a volcano.

If it should erupt,
What then remains of mountain?
What then remains of its weight, its echo, its identity?

KARNA:

We shall meet again, someday.

SHREYASEE:

We shall see.
When thy seven become One.

The curtain falls.
But inside the reader, the play just begins.

To the reader who is Karna:

Thou hast become Sun for the world,
But hast thou become Sun for thyself?

Thy seven horses are running,
But do they run together?

From mud to lotus,
From proving to being,
That is thy journey.

FOR THE WORLD - THE HEALING

This is not a poem only about Karna.
This is medicine for the modern world.

If humanity understands this one truth,
That the seven horses must run together,
Then many wounds of the world are healed.

Depression ends, because a man stops asking the world, Am I enough?
And begins to say to himself, I am enough.

Anxiety ends, because the chariot no longer runs in seven directions to prove itself.

War of ego in offices ends, because we stop protecting the name that gave us identity, and start protecting truth.

When a child reads this, he will never be slave to Sutaputra, never be slave to Angraj.
He will know, I am neither my insult nor my crown. I am Atma.

When a leader reads this, he will not give people only designations and salary.
He will give them belonging, and freedom from proving.

When a lover reads this, she will not ask, Do you make me worthy?
She will say, I am lotus. Even in mud, I bloom.

The global benefit of this poem is simple:
From competition to completeness,
From comparison to coherence,
From Prakash that burns the world to Bodha that heals it.

If one reader in a hundred understands that his seven horses must become One white fire,
Then his home becomes peaceful, his work becomes worship, his love becomes liberation.

That is why the epic was written.
Not for who won Kurukshetra,
But for how Kurukshetra inside us can end.

May every Karna become Sun.
Not for the world.
For himself.

Name: Amit Mohan
Title: Echoes of the Unspoken
Content:
The corridors of City Hospital never truly slept. Even in the dead of night, they pulsed with a quiet rhythm, the hum of machines, the shuffle of rubber soles on polished floors, the low murmur of nurses exchanging notes under dimmed lights. The air carried the scent of antiseptic and exhaustion, hope and heartbreak, all tangled into one.
Through it all moved Dr. Aarav Mehta.
At 38, he had the steady hands of a seasoned surgeon and the quiet eyes of a man who had seen too much. He walked with the kind of calm that wasn’t learned in medical school, it was earned through life, through loss, through the quiet strength it took to keep going when the ground beneath you had cracked. Three years ago, cancer stole his wife, Naina. She had been his anchor, his laughter, the quiet in his chaos. Her death hadn’t broken him, but it had hollowed something inside, a silence he never spoke of, but carried with him in the way he looked out windows too long or paused a second longer before answering.
Still, every morning, he woke up and showed up, for Rhea.
His seven-year-old daughter was his heartbeat now, the one reason he remembered how to smile. She had her mother’s eyes and a stubborn streak that sometimes made him laugh out loud, even on the hardest days. The world saw him as composed and collected, but Rhea knew better. She was the only one who saw the softness in his silence, the way he tucked her in just a little tighter on stormy nights.
In the hospital, Aarav was a figure of quiet strength. Patients trusted him. Colleagues respected him. He didn’t say much, but when he spoke, his words felt like a warm hand on a cold shoulder, steady, grounding, kind.
And perhaps that was what first caught Dr. Meher Sharma’s attention.
She had noticed him before, always in motion, always present, always just out of reach. There was something about the way he listened, not just with his ears, but with his whole presence. Something about the way he seemed untouched by the noise around him; as if he held some secret the rest of the world had forgotten.
She didn’t know his story. Not yet. But something told her it was worth discovering.
Dr. Meher Sharma was a pediatric surgeon, sharp, precise, and deeply compassionate. Her hands worked with the kind of care only a mother could understand, and her heart beat for the smallest patients in the hospital’s most fragile wards. She was respected, admired, often called the calm in the storm during emergencies.
At home, her world seemed picture-perfect. Her husband, Karan, a gentle-natured software engineer, adored her with quiet constancy. Their five-year-old son, Vihaan, was a whirlwind of joy and mischief, the sun around which her universe revolved. By every standard, her life was full. But sometimes, even perfection leaves echoes, soft, persistent emptiness that creeps in between the smiles, in the pauses of a busy day, in the silence just before sleep. Meher never spoke of it, not even to herself. It wasn’t unhappiness, it was something quieter, more elusive. A longing she couldn’t name.
She noticed Dr. Aarav Mehta during one of those long, bleary-eyed hospital shifts that stretch into each other without end. At first, he was just another colleague. But slowly, she began to notice things, how his presence brought a strange kind of stillness to the chaos. How his kindness wasn’t loud but constant. He remembered the names of janitors, always had a spare cup of coffee for overworked nurses, and spoke about his daughter, Rhea, with such deep affection that it made something stir inside her chest.
Their conversations began, as they often do, in small, innocent ways, discussing medical cases, shared responsibilities, late-night consults. But beneath the clinical exchanges, something unspoken grew, like a current under still water.
"You have a beautiful way of seeing the world," Meher said once, during a quiet tea break in the staff lounge. Her voice had surprised even her, softer than intended.
Aarav looked up, a faint smile playing on his lips. “It’s the only way I survive it.”
From then on, they found each other during moments in between, short pauses between surgeries, hurried lunches in quiet corners, or those rare minutes after a difficult shift when neither of them wanted to go home just yet. They talked about music, parenting, grief, and the absurd little things that only fellow doctors understood. Meher was struck by the gentleness in him, how every gesture was thoughtful, never careless. He never touched her hand. Never leaned in too close. There were no forbidden words, no reckless confessions. And yet, what grew between them felt deeper than desire. It wasn’t an affair. It wasn’t temptation. It was something rarer. Sacred, even. A quiet companionship. A shelter of souls. But Meher lived in quiet fear.
It crept in during the in-between moments, when her phone buzzed with Karan’s name while she was sitting in the hospital garden, mid-laughter at one of Aarav’s perfectly timed, dry remarks. Her laughter would fade too quickly, her back would straighten, and her fingers would hesitate before answering. She wasn’t cheating. She reminded herself of that often, like a prayer. But still, she was hiding. And it wasn’t just a secret; it was a person. Him. Aarav.
One afternoon, as sunlight filtered through the neem trees and the scent of hospital coffee lingered faintly in the air, Aarav turned to her. His tone was soft, without judgment.
“Why do you always look over your shoulder when you smile at me?”
Meher’s breath caught. She didn’t look at him. She stared at the chipped edge of the garden bench, then whispered, “Because if I don’t... I might fall.”
There was a long silence, gentle and heavy.
Aarav looked away then, his jaw tightening with something like resignation. “Then maybe we should stop climbing.”
They tried. They really did.
                                                         --------------x--------------
For a few days, they kept their distance, passing each other in the corridors with polite nods, keeping conversations clinical, limiting messages to essentials. But it was hard to stay away from someone who felt like home in a world that rarely offered softness. He understood her without needing her to explain. She saw his grief, not as something to be pitied, but something to be held gently. There was no rush, no agenda, no recklessness between them, just the quiet pull of two people who had learned how to carry pain with dignity.
And sometimes, the heart doesn’t seek excitement or escape. Sometimes, it just longs to be understood.
Then, the earth moved.
At first, it was just a tremble beneath their feet, subtle, almost like a passing truck. But within seconds, it turned violent. The ground heaved, the walls groaned, and the very foundation of the hospital screamed in protest.
A massive 7.8 magnitude earthquake had struck the city.
The corridors of City Hospital, once filled with calm precision, descended into chaos. Floors buckled. Walls cracked open like dry earth. Ceiling tiles crashed down. Lights flickered, then died. Alarms blared, machines shrieked, and somewhere close, a child screamed in sheer terror. Dust billowed through the air, thick as smoke, choking lungs and stealing vision.
In the madness, Aarav saw Meher, frozen for half a second in the middle of the hallway, her eyes wide with disbelief.
“Meher!” he shouted, reaching her just as a deafening crack split the air above.
He pulled her toward a narrow corridor, away from the ICU wing, as the ceiling behind them gave way in a roar. Debris rained down like a storm of stone and steel. A hospital bed flew past. Glass shattered. Somewhere, someone cried out in pain. Aarav shielded Meher with his body, bracing them both against a supporting wall. The building shook again, harder this time, like the earth was trying to rip itself apart. Then, the power cut.
And everything fell into darkness.
No light. No sound.
Just dust, silence, and the terrifying uncertainty of who had survived.
When Meher opened her eyes, the world was dust and darkness.
Blood traced a slow line down her temple, warm against the coldness of her skin. The air was thick, unbreathable. Every breath was effort. Every sound felt muffled, like the earth had swallowed their voices whole. Aarav was beside her, bruised, bleeding, but alive. He had shielded her with his body, arms still wrapped protectively around her, as if instinct alone had chosen who he would save. They were trapped and buried beneath tons of concrete and steel. The collapse had sealed them in a hollow pocket of space, just enough room to breathe, to shift slightly, to feel the steady thrum of each other’s pulse in the silence.
No phones. No lights. No idea if help would come. No guarantee they’d live to see the sun again. But in that darkness, they had each other. And for a while, that was all that existed. Time bent. The hospital, the world above, their responsibilities, all fell away. What remained were whispered words, cracked voices, and two souls laid bare.
“I never meant for this to happen,” Meher said, her voice breaking, barely more than a breath.
“Neither did I,” Aarav replied, searching for the faint outline of her face. “But it did. And I’m not sorry for knowing you.”
She turned her face slightly toward him. “Do you think I’m a bad person?”
In the silence that followed, he reached for her hand. For the first time.
A gentle hold. Nothing more. Nothing less.
“No,” he said softly. “I think you’re someone who loved beyond the lines the world gave you. Even when you weren’t allowed to.”
And so, in that broken, buried place, they talked. Of their children, Rhea and Vihaan. Of the dreams they had set aside for duty, of the quiet ache of carrying lives not entirely their own. Of love that had bloomed not in rebellion, but in the tender, empty spaces life had forgotten to fill.
There were no more lies left in the rubble.
“I wish we met in another life,” Meher whispered, her voice barely holding.
Aarav closed his eyes, a single tear slipping into the dust. “We did,” he said. “It was these fifteen hours. And in this life… that’s enough.”
Fifteen hours passed.
Each breath came harder than the last. The dust had settled in their lungs, thick and punishing. It tasted like concrete and loss. They spoke less now, too tired, too dry-mouthed. Their fingers stayed entwined, not for comfort anymore, but for the quiet reassurance that they were still there. Still alive.
Somewhere, beyond the rubble, faint sounds echoed, voices, metal shifting, urgent calls for silence. Rescue teams.
Hope.
But hope felt distant. Like sunlight behind storm clouds. Like a name you once knew but couldn't quite remember.
They held on.
To breath. To memory. To each other. And then, light.
A narrow shaft broke through the darkness, cutting across the dust like a silent promise. Voices grew louder, closer. The shifting of debris turned to deliberate movement. And then, hands. Dozens of them, pulling, lifting, reaching through the stone and steel to bring them back.
They were pulled from the wreckage, limp, broken, but alive.
Blankets were thrown around their trembling shoulders. Oxygen masks pressed to dust-stained faces. Medics shouted instructions. Stretchers wheeled toward flashing ambulances. Everything moved fast, the world a blur of motion and noise. Meher, disoriented, scanned the chaos. Her vision blurred, but she searched anyway, until she saw him. Across the crowd. Aarav. Bloodied, exhausted, eyes barely open. But looking straight at her. Their gazes locked. No words passed between them. None were needed. Just a nod. A promise. And then they were carried away in opposite directions, into different ambulances, different realities, different lives.
But something unspoken remained between them. 
Not a goodbye. Not an ending. Just... the truth.

                                                            --------------x--------------

One month later, life at the hospital had resumed its relentless rhythm, sterile lights, clipped footsteps, quiet urgency. The earthquake had left cracks in the walls, but deeper ones in the people who had survived it. Meher moved through her shifts like someone trying to fit back into a life that no longer fit quite the same. She smiled, she operated, she went home to Karan and Vihaan, held them closer than she used to. But something had changed. A part of her was still buried under that rubble, tucked away with fifteen hours of truth she couldn’t speak aloud.
Then, one evening, she opened her locker. Among the usual mess of files and spare gloves, a single folded note rested quietly on top of her coat. No envelope. No name. But the handwriting stopped her breath. She’d memorized it in the dark. With trembling fingers, she unfolded the paper and read:
We were never wrong. Just misplaced in time.
I will remember these fifteen hours as the most honest hours of my life.
Be happy. Love your family.
And know, somewhere, someone is always silently grateful that you exist.
                                                                                                              – A
She stood there for a long time, note pressed to her chest, eyes closed.
It wasn’t a plea.
It wasn’t a promise.
It was closure. Gentle. True. Enough.
And though she would never say it out loud, a small part of her would carry those fifteen hours for the rest of her life, tucked between the pages of her memory like a pressed flower from a forgotten season.
A love that never asked to be more than what it was.
Real. Brief. And unforgettable.
That night, Meher cried quietly beside her sleeping husband. Not out of loss or regret, but for a love that had lived without demands, without possession or promises, yet filled with a truth deeper than most people ever experience.
Years passed. They never met again.
But every time Meher walked past the old garden bench at the hospital, she would smile softly, because sometimes, carried by the wind, she could still hear Aarav’s laughter. It felt like a gentle reminder of those fifteen hours, brief, but unforgettable.
And far away, on quiet nights, Aarav would look up at the moon and silently tell himself, “Fifteen hours… that’s all we had. But it was enough to last a lifetime.”
                                                          --------------x--------------

Name: Moumita Pal Das
Title: Two parallel lines
Content:
We never met, the two parallel lines
We  cross every common path,
Every distorted emotion we have,
But we never met.
We ran beside each other in silence,
Close enough to feel the warmth,
Far enough to never touch.
Our shadows almost tangled at dusk,
Yet the light always pulled us apart.
We shared the same sky of questions,
The same storms of unspoken words,
The same quiet wish at midnight
That one day, lines might forget themselves.
But we never met.
Only learned how closeness can ache,
How distance can look like fate,
And how some stories exist
Not to collide—
But to run on, side by side,.....Endlessly.

Name: Zainab Saba
Title: Unspoiled
Content:
Unspoiled


“No, Mom! You can’t do this to me!”

“It’s just for one day, dear. Trust me, you’ll be alright.”

And with that, the door shut on my face. I knew no amount of protesting or pounding on the door would budge Mom.

Even the privilege of being ‘daddy’s princess’ would not work this time, because Dad was away on a business trip.

To give you a little context, I am the only child of my parents.

Dad is fully aware of this huge blessing he has in the form of a beautiful daughter. He always lets me have my way, buys me the things I want, no matter how expensive they are, and hands me his card whenever I want to go partying with my friends. He never questions me, never stops me, and never holds me accountable. On my last birthday, when I turned 20, he even gifted me my dream car — a Lamborghini Revuelto!

But, Mom! She is the complete opposite of my Dad. She is always stopping me from partying and spending money, tells me to go out and earn for myself so that I “understand what hard work looks like,” and is always arguing with Dad over me, telling him he has “spoiled” me. She even calls me things like “a reckless, prodigal brat”!

I can endure all of this with Dad by my side. He somehow always seems to calm her down whenever she flares off at me.

But when Dad is away, Mum seizes the golden opportunity to “un-spoil” me. She literally forces me into humiliating tasks like cleaning my room, making my bed, doing dishes, and even mopping the floor!

All this while the maid is in the house!

I can never understand why I have to do these, and also, why Mum does these degrading chores when we have dozens of servants for everything that needs to be done.

“You must know basic household chores,” she always says, and I disagree.

This time, a strange idea has come to her mind.

She has handed me a note of ₹100 and has kicked me out of the house, telling me I must spend one whole day with this meagre amount.

Last night, when she discussed this challenge with me, I rolled my eyes. I thought this was just another episode of her trying to make me “feel about those who aren’t as privileged as I am”. Or about those who cannot afford to live a “wealthy, carefree life” like me.

But this morning, when she actually led me out of the house and handed me the note, I was pissed off.

I was so mad that I tore the note into pieces and blew the shreds in the air. Then, I stomped down the driveway of our villa and headed towards the gate.

It takes about 10 minutes to reach the gate from our mansion. A little to the right of the gate is our grand auto gallery housing nearly 20 expensive cars that are owned by our family, including my personal Lamborghini Revuelto.

Towards the left of the gate — a good distance off — there are about four small huts inhabited by our servants and their families.

This is the one thing I don’t like about my home. I have often asked Dad to have them evicted. Why do they have to live in our area? Those lazy, dirty, slumdogs.

I would have convinced Dad, had Mum not come in between. She simply won’t have it. She says that if they’re evicted, she too would leave the house and never come back.

I don’t understand why Mum has to lower her standards to theirs? Why can’t she just live her life and enjoy the privilege of being the mistress of such a huge estate? Why does she have to care for every pauper in sight?

We are not responsible for every needy person, are we? I mean, if you are needy, just move your lazy behind and go get some work!

As I neared the gate, I caught a glimpse of a boy, about 10 years old, peering through the glass gates of our auto gallery.

I immediately recognized him. He was Bunty, the nephew of one of our maids. He didn’t live with us but often came to visit. He was crazy about cars, and Mum had once told me that his favorite too was the Lamborghini Revuelto.

I had laughed so hard at that. Poor him! He could not even afford its tire in his dreams!

I had secretly prohibited our maid from letting him in, but she had complained about it to Mum, and she had been so furious at me.

Now was my chance to get even.

I stormed towards him, and before he could run away, I smacked the back of his head hard. He recoiled, his hand clutching his head where I had hit him.

“Get out of my house!” I screamed.

Without a word, he walked down towards the gate, turned to the right, and was gone.

His calm demeanour aggravated me even more, and I ran after him, but he was out of sight.

I kept walking down the road, mad and fuming, kicking at every stone that came my way, and sending cats and dogs yelping.

I felt in my pockets for my phone. It was not there. I had left it behind, and it was no use going back for it because Mum simply won’t let me in.

“Just like you wouldn’t let that boy in…,” something inside me whispered.

I ignored.

My wrist watch showed 8 a.m. It was about 14 hours more before I would be let back into the house.

I was beginning to feel a little bit hungry now. Delicious smells of different kinds of breakfast rising from the street stalls and dhabas were only adding fuel to the fire.

But I would never eat from those cheap, unhygienic street foods. I belonged in expensive restaurants and luxurious cafeterias.

So what if I don’t have money at the moment? I’m a VIP, the daughter of the greatest business tycoon in the country. Everybody knows me. I can eat for free and tell them I’ll pay later.

With these thoughts, I reached the doorstep of one of my favourite cafés. Clearing my throat with an air of confidence, I entered.

While I sat at a table going through the menu, the familiar waiter came to take my order. He smiled at me.

“Why is Ma’am alone today? Where are your friends?” he asked.

“Shut up and just take my order,” I snapped.

He stopped smiling.

After placing the order, I said in a casual tone, “Um, just wanted to let you know I don’t have money right now. I’ll pay later.”

He looked up with raised eyebrows.

“Sorry?”

“I don’t — ”

“We don’t accept payments “later”, ma’am. You know that very well.”

“Make an exception for me. You know very well who I am.”

“That doesn’t matter. Rules are the same for everyone.”

“Don’t mess with me. I am warning you — ”

“Ma’am, this is not your father’s property. If you cannot maintain the decorum, please leave.”

And he walked away.

I stormed out of the stupid café, burning with fury. With nowhere to go—because I couldn't have my friends see me in this condition— I kept walking down the street, across the park, and into different neighbourhoods.

Anger and resentment started taking a toll on my mind, and I felt weak and hungry. 

The watch showed 11:45 a.m. when I finally walked into a local dhaba being managed by two men who appeared to be brothers.

I asked for a puri. They handed it to me, but before I could take a bite, they asked for money.

“I don’t have it now. But I’ll — ”

The puri was snatched from my hand. “What do you mean you don’t have it now? We are not giving out charity; we are selling.”

I was shocked. How could someone be so cruel? My head felt dizzy.

“Please, bhaiya, I need some food. I haven’t eaten anything since morning.”

“So what? We are not responsible for every needy person, are we? I mean, if you are needy, just move your lazy behind and go get some work!”

I left the dhaba and staggered on.

Suddenly, my head spiralled, and I stumbled to the side of the road. My vision blurred.

As I fell, I heard a concerned voice, “Appi!” and felt a small but strong hand trying to keep me from falling. Then, everything went black.

                                                                     -----

When my eyes opened, I found myself inside what looked like a hut. A small boy was bent over me with a worried look on his innocent face. He held a bottle of water in his hand from which he had been sprinkling some drops on my face.

There was no mistaking him. The face was very familiar — Bunty, the nephew of my maid.

Seeing me open my eyes seemed to relieve him.

He said softly, “Are you alright, Appi? You suddenly fainted near my balloon stall.”

I got up slowly, my face red with shame, guilt, and regret.

“I’m alright,” I said, smiling feebly.

“You don’t seem to be. Have you eaten anything since morning?”

I shook my head.

“That’s why! Look at the time. It’s past noon.”

He got up and disappeared into the next room. In a few minutes, he came back carrying a plate of two chapatis, a bowl of dal, and two boiled eggs.

He set down the plate before me, and in an apologetic voice, he said, “I’m sorry, Appi. I couldn’t prepare a better breakfast. It’s the end of the month, and we are out of rations.”

I didn’t say anything. I couldn’t. It was no use.

Without a single word, I began eating, while he got busy arranging the odds and ends that were scattered on a large trunk placed at one end of the room.

As I ate, I felt small. Like a pitiful servant who had been caught red-handed trying to steal a gold coin from the King’s treasury.

The noble king stood before me, towering and tall.

His majestic presence numbed me, and I shuddered at the thought of being ordered to the gallows. But the beneficent king had pardoned me.

He knew I was poor, destitute. And so, he had ordered that I be given a box of gold coins.

“Go and build yourself a good life,” he had said, “and steal no more.”

                                                                    ----

From time to time, Bunty would cast a glance at me and ask if I needed anything.

I shook my head every time. What could I need? Hadn’t he given everything already?

In twenty minutes, I stood up feeling much better.

“Thank you, Bunty, for everything,” I said.

“Don’t mention it,” he replied, smiling. “Do you need anything else?”

“Yes,” I said in a small voice. “I need fifty rupees, if you could spare. I will return tomorrow, I promise.”

A surprised look came into his eyes, but his head nodded, “Of course.”

He went to the next room and was back in a few seconds with a note of fifty in his hand.

He extended it to me and with a playful wink, he said, “An ocean is thirsty today?!”

I smiled.

How could I tell him oceans go dry when it doesn’t rain? If I were an ocean, he was the rain from the heavens.

Taking the note from his hand, I bid him goodbye.

I didn’t thank him. That word couldn’t even begin to encompass how indebted I felt towards him.

I didn’t say sorry. It was too small a word to convey how ashamed I was.

                                                                         ----

As I walked down the same streets I had walked, or in fact, driven down in my Lamborghini multiple times, I was a completely different person.

He had left me anguished with his dignity and kindness. I felt heavy and light at the same time. Sinful, but pardoned. Trapped, but rescued. Evil, but redeemed.

I walked by many expensive shops, malls, and showrooms displaying all sorts of luxurious, attractive items.

The old me would have been infatuated with every other thing. But the new me hardly looked at them.

My mind was somewhere else. Somewhere it had never been before. It was a strange place and very uncomfortable. But my heart seemed to be enjoying it.

I never knew it before, but now that it was happening, I realized my heart had always been in this place, but my mind had always pulled against it.

This complete misalignment between my heart and mind, like a stretched rubber band, had materialized in my whole being, making me a stiff, almost abominable person.

But when my heart and mind came together in harmony, it was so unusually satisfying. Uncomfortable, but satisfying.

Slowly but surely, I began to understand what this new feeling was. It was EMPATHY. I was beginning to feel for those who weren’t as privileged as I was. Or those who couldn’t afford to live a “wealthy, carefree life” like me.

Instead of looking for extravagant things to buy, my eyes were searching for needy people.

I couldn’t help them today. I hadn’t reached that level of selflessness that the little boy had shown — to help others while I myself needed help.

But I was taking note of them. Of people who looked like they could do with some help, support, and empathy.

The hours passed by, and when my stomach grumbled for some lunch, the watch showed 4 p.m.

I walked up to a momo stall by the side of the road. The note hung on the side of the cart read:
“Half plate = ₹30, Full plate = ₹60”

I requested a half plate. As I sat on a nearby bench eating it, my eyes began watering. It was too spicy.

Luckily, a soan-papdi vendor was passing by just then, crying:
“2 for ₹10! 2 for ₹10”

I stopped him and bought one soan-padi for ₹5.

After finishing my momos, I got up and walked towards a local park. It was deserted. Who would come to a park on a scorching afternoon?

I sat down on a wooden bench under a huge banyan tree. This was the first time I was tasting ‘a tree shade on a sweltering summer afternoon’.

As someone who had spent all summer afternoons in rooms packed with multiple ACs, this new experience was pleasantly distinct.

The gentle breeze, the rustling of the leaves, the scattered chirping of sparrows on the tree, the distant sounds of vendors calling out their wares — all of it provided a cool that no AC could ever provide.

It was all so quiet and soothing that I dozed off.

                                                                      ----

When my eyes opened, the park was flooded with all sorts of people. Children playing, couples gossiping, elders walking. I immediately sat up, feeling embarrassed. But no one was paying attention to me. Everyone was busy having fun.

The weather had turned quite pleasant. The breeze had grown stronger and clouds were gathering in the sky. I looked at my watch. It was 6 o’clock.

I observed the children playing games. Cricket, badminton, pitto, kabaddi, and many more. I noticed Bunty among the children playing kabaddi. It was so fun to watch them.

Most of these children were poor, from the local slum areas. Rich children were shut inside AC rooms playing video games.

I walked up to where they were playing kabaddi and asked if I could join them. They were too engrossed to look at me or reply.

I thought I was not welcome. But just as I was about to turn around and go, a little girl cried out, “Catch him! Catch him! Don’t let him escape!”

I watched a little boy dart forward, tap one of his opponents’ shoulders, slip free from grasping hands, and bolt back towards his line.

I immediately took off my branded shoes for comfort’s sake and ran after the boy. Catching him by his sleeve just in time, I tried to drag him back.

In a second, I was swarmed by little children all tugging at the boy to keep him from reaching his line, while poor him exerted all his might and power, trying to wriggle out of our grip.

His comrades on the other side of the line were shouting and cheering.

“Come on! Just a little more effort!”
“You’re almost there!”
“Focus!”
“Kick at them!”
“Bite their fingers!”

Before I knew it, I was bitten hard.

“Ouch!” I yelped, and my grip loosened.

There were a few more ouches, and the boy finally escaped and landed in his line.

I was too distracted from the game to hear the groans and cheers that followed. My finger was bleeding, and it hurt.

A girl looked at my finger and gasped, “Bablu, look what you did!”

Immediately, all the kids surrounded me. Looking at my bleeding finger, they all rounded on him.

“Why did you bite Appi’s finger?”
“This is so stupid of you.”
“Say sorry right now.”
“You need good scolding.”
“Let’s make him out.”

“Oh! It’s okay, it’s okay,” I said, trying to calm them down.

But they were having none of it.

The boy looked crestfallen. Tears had collected in his eyes.

“I’m so sorry, Appi,” he said in a small voice. “I thought it was Bunty’s finger.”

“It’s okay, dear. I’m completely fine. Let’s continue with the game,” I said, surprised at why they were making such a fuss over my finger. He had bitten other children as well, and I could see their fingers were wounded too. I couldn’t understand why they were treating me differently. Maybe because I was older? Or was it because they had recognized me as the daughter of the wealthy business tycoon?

“Let me bandage it,” he said.

“Oh no, it’s not necessary — ”

But he tore off a piece from his vest, took my hand, and began tying it around my finger. I didn’t protest anymore.

When he was done, I smiled at him and ruffled his dust-coated hair.

In a playful tone, I said, “Now what about others? Won’t you bandage their fingers too?”

“Oh! No,” he said with an amused look in his eyes. “They are all used to it, and besides, they have bitten me too, multiple times. We keep getting even with each other. But you seem to be new here, and you’ve never bitten me. So I was wrong in hurting you. Please forgive me.”

I nodded, “It’s ok.”

I had been wrong once again. These children were not poor. They were the richest people I had ever met in my entire 20 years of life spent around the ‘elites’. These kids had a wealth that most of those ‘elites’ lacked, around whom I had always been. It was empathy.

Suddenly, a huge drop of water fell on my nose. I looked up. The sky was grey with huge clouds, and it was beginning to rain.

The elders quickly walked towards the gazebo in the centre of the park. The young couples also sought shelter there, while some others hurried out of the park towards their homes.

But the kids didn’t. For them, the sky was shelter and the rain was food.

They began running across the park, laughing and squealing, their arms spread open in anticipation.

Rain came pouring down heavily. They welcomed it with immense excitement, gulping in the fresh air flavoured with a refreshing earthy smell.

The old me would have hated the rain because it would spoil my expensive clothes.

The new me welcomed it just like the kids — arms spread open, the rain soaking my clothes, drops trickling down my neck, wetting every part of my body, as if washing away the sins… the leftover crumbs of my old self.

I found myself shrieking and squealing with laughter as I played with the kids, running about the park like crazy.

Unconcerned about my branded shoes and expensive clothes getting wet in the rain, and indifferent to the disapproving looks from the people standing in the shade.

Mum had been wrong about me living a “carefree” life. That was not carefree; this was.

All of a sudden, I had an idea. “Let’s party!” I yelled.

I had to shout multiple times before the children gathered around me eagerly.

“Let’s have a party!” I repeated when they had circled me.

“Where?” one of the kids piped up.

“Right here! Let’s get some delicious food and drinks, sit down in a circle on this wet ground, and gobble it up! What do you guys say?”

The kids burst out in excitement.

“Ohooo!”
“Yess!”
“What a brilliant idea!”
“Let’s do it!”
“We’ll have such fun!”

Suddenly, reality dawned on me. I only had a completely drenched 10-rupee note and a 5-rupee coin in my pocket. And there were at least 10 kids to feed.

Going red in the face with embarrassment, I racked my brain for a way out of this situation.

The kids were jumping, happy and enthusiastic.

“What shall we get?” said a girl, gleefully.
“A chocolate cake!” declared a boy.
“That’s too expensive, silly,” said another.
“And unhealthy,” Bablu put in.
“Think of something easily affordable,” suggested Bunty.
“We’ll have to, because I have only 10 rupees with me,” said a girl.
“Be grateful. I have only 5,” another boy said.
“And I have zero,” said a girl with an innocent laugh.
“Let’s take out all the money we’ve got and count it,” another girl suggested.
“Yes,” agreed Bunty, “and then we can see what can be bought in that amount.”

And with that, the kids had once again taught me a great lesson, without even realizing it.

Teamwork. When with friends, one didn’t feed another. They ate together.

Everyone produced all the money they had. I produced mine. When it was counted, the total came out to be just 50 rupees. But the kids delighted at this meagre amount like it was treasure.

Bunty collected all the money and said, “Now you all wait here. I’ll go and bring the yummiest thing I can find with this money.”

I was hesitant, but the kids agreed without a second thought. Bunty bounded across the park and was gone.

Minutes passed by, and I grew impatient. Doubts began flooding my petty mind. What if he has run away with the money? Has he stolen it? After all, he said he was out of rations. He’s a thief.

But the kids around me were too happy and excited to notice the delay. Or was it because they trusted him too much? They kept chatting, guessing what he would bring, where he would be by now, and how much fun they would have.

I looked at my watch. It was 7 p.m.

Another five minutes passed by. Just when I had decided to go after him, I caught a glimpse of him walking towards us, struggling as his little hands balanced a plate of food and a bottle of apple juice.

When the children saw him coming, they dashed up to him, showering him with greetings and approval at what he had brought. It was a plate of warm, delicious-looking poha.

I watched them from a distance, sitting on the wet ground. I watched as they took the plate from him, as he was relieved and rubbed his hands on the cold bottle, and my conscience began pricking at me again.

The reason Bunty was a little late was that he was carrying a plate too big and too hot for his little hands.

Soon, we were sitting in a circle with the plate of poha and the opened bottle of apple juice set in the centre. But I was hardly eating.

I was watching.

I watched as they gobbled up the simple meal, happily and gratefully, sharing the same plate, some sharing the same spoon, others eating with their hands, and drinking the juice from the same bottle.

I remembered how we ‘elites’ always had separate plates, separate spoons, separate forks, and no wonder, separate hearts.

Suddenly, I had discovered it! Discovered the reason why they had trusted Bunty with all the money they had, the reason why they hadn’t doubted him one bit when he was late; they hadn’t even realized he was getting late. And when I had been relieved to see him coming with the food, they had shown no surprise, no relief — only excitement, because nothing against their expectation had happened. And they had run up to greet him just like they had greeted the rain!

The secret was their united hearts. They were many, but they were one.

Oh God! How many lessons was I going to learn today?

The old me would have cringed at the thought of multiple people eating from the same plate sitting on wet, muddy ground.

The new me devoured every moment of it.

Soon the dinner was over. None of our stomachs was filled but we were content — a feeling I had had after a long, long time, or was it the first time?

It had grown dark by now, and mosquitoes were at their work. It was time to go. We got up, didn’t care to dust our clothes — they needed washing anyway, bid goodbye to each other, and went our ways.

I felt strangely alone. So many parties I had attended, so many gatherings I had taken part in, but none of their endings had ever made me so desolate, so abandoned.

Maybe it was because, for the first time in my life, I had made real friends with real people. There was no pretense, no vanity — only genuine affection and deep bond.
                                                                   ----

Carrying these thoughts with me, I reached the doorstep of my home and knocked. A little while later, Mum answered.

She was shocked at my state. Why wouldn’t she? My clothes, my shoes, my arms — everything was damp and mud-stained.

“Where have you been?!” she exclaimed. “Don’t tell me you got into a fight with someone again.”

I smiled but didn’t say anything. There was a lot to say and I didn’t know where to begin. I walked past her and made my way towards my room.

“Look at you,” Mum was saying behind me. “You look completely different.”

Well, because I was.

                                                                    ----

The next day, after breakfast and all the household chores that were meant for me, I took my car keys and went out.

I walked up to the auto gallery and got into my Lamborghini. Pulling out onto the driveway, I drove through the main gate and down the street.

In a few minutes, I was knocking on the door of a familiar hut. Bunty answered.

I immediately put my hands over his eyes.

“Oh!” he exclaimed, “Appi?”

“Just come with me,” I said, and led him out with my hands still over his eyes.

I stopped him in front of my car.

“Don’t open your eyes yet,” I said, removing my hands.

I took his hands, opened his palms, and placed the keys in them. He smiled.

“Open now,” I said.

He obeyed.
                                                          ----

That evening, as I walked back home without my car, I felt a strange feeling.

I didn’t know what it was and still don’t.

What I do know, though, is that the old me would have hated it. The new me was rejoicing in it.

Mum had successfully “un-spoiled” me, after all.

Title: कसे सांगू?
Content:
कसे सांगू?
कसे सांगू ते भाव मनी काय,
ना ते कळे कोणाला.
नाते हे जगावेगळे आपुले,
कसे सांगू कोणाला.
बोलनी खूप, बोलनही,
न बोललेले जाणे माझा कान्हा.
मनी उमलती सख्याचे भाव,
असा तो माझा पाठीीराखा.
कसे सांगू माझे भाव कोणाला?
ना कळे हे नाते.
जरी नसे तू जवळी माझ्या,
तरी वसे अंतरी माझ्या.
कशी सांगू तुझी ओढ मनी लागे,
जशी विठ्ठला लागे ओढ
आपुल्या लेकरांची.
तशी मला लागे ओढ
तुझ्या सख्यप्रितीची.
क्षणाक्षणाला वाढत जाई,
आस तुझ्या सहवासाची.
मनी अनंत भाव त्याचे,
मुखी मात्र हास्य सदा.
अंतरी भावनांचा अथांग सागर,
कसे सांगू कोणाला?
कधी सखा, कधी बंधू,
कधी पुत्र, कधी मायबाप.
असे हे जगावेगळे,
आपुले अनोखे नाते.
कसे सांगू हे भावनांचे नाते
आपल्या लोकांना?
ज्यांनी उमजला नाही कृष्ण,
ते काय जाणती या प्रेमाला?
कसे सांगू कोणाला,
हे आपुले अजब नाते.
शब्द हरवती वाटेवर,
प्रेमाची नाळ अंतरी अखंड नांदे.

Name: Ruma Chakraborty
Title: UNKINDEST CUT OF ALL
Content:
The butcher wiped his chopper at the edge of the wood block to rid it of the congealing, clotting blood of the slaughtered animal. With something akin to almost nurturing, he inspected the gleaming knife and went quietly back to the hacking of the goat carcass. Lovingly preparing choicest cuts of meat for the connoisseurs of mutton, a delicacy in this part of the country.

As dusk approached, he checked the shop once more with his sweeping glance to make sure it was spotlessly clean. Downing the shutters, he stepped into the darkening alley and turned the corner for the shortcut to his shanty. 

The knife was driven home with a brutality even he did not know. Twisted and pulled out with no thought of precision. Even as he lost consciousness and eventually his life, he grimaced at the disregard for clean cuts and noticed how the bloodied knife was dumped, uncleaned in the dumpster beside him, with his blood congealing in clumpy clots on the blade and hilt.
