हमारे देश की धरोहरें

 सुनो सहेलियों एक बात तुमको बताती हूँ,
 अपने देश की धरोहरों के बारे में कुछ बताती हूँ।

हम जब समझेंगे अपने सोने की चिड़िया के देश की
 सोने की धरोहरों के बारे में,
 तभी हम इसको बचा पाएँगे।

ना शोर मचाना है ना वक्त गँवाना है,
बस खुद से शुरू करके लहर पैदा कर पाएँगे।

 ताजमहल, शीश महल, लाल किला इनके
 बारे में तो सब बता पाएँगे।

 आज अपने अनोखे भारत से सबको मिलवाएँगे।

आज सबको दूसरे देशों में पढ़ने की होड़ है
 पर पता है भारत में विश्व की सबसे बड़ी
 विश्वविद्यालय आप गया   में पाएँगे।

कृष्ण, सुदामा, महाभारत तो सब जानते होंगे
 पर क्या आपको पता है राजा जयद्रथ की
मुक्ति गुरु गोबिंद सिंह जी के हाथों से नाहन में पाएँगे।

लाल किला और बड़े-बड़े किलों का तो
पता होगा,
 पर भारत का सबसे पहला किला
 आप  बठिंडा में पाएँगे |

ग्वालियर में गुर्जर तोमर वंश तो मिल जाएंगे पर ,
पता है तुम्हें ,ग्वालियर में 40 दिन सुखमनी साहिब के पाठ से शनि से मुक्ति पाएँगे।

यह तो छोटी सी पहल है अपनी धरोहरों के ज्ञान की,
इतिहास तो खोलो बहुत कुछ हम पाएँगे।
अपने बच्चों को सिखा तो दिया सब कुछ पर धरोहरों के बारे में कैसे बताएँगे।

नेह! कहती है इंसान जो अपनी धरोहरों से दूर हो रहा है, उसको पास लाने के लिए कुछ कर पाएँगे।

Name: Piya Poppy Rathbone
Title: A Dinner for My Dear Inspector
Content:
Author Biography
Piya Poppy Rathbone (pen name) is a multidisciplinary artist and writer from Kolkata, India, currently residing in Russia. Her creative work spans international fan art, poetry, photography, music, short-story writing, children's book editing, and animal rescue.
She is the recipient of several national and international honours, including the Global International Artist of the Year 2024, Jamini Roy Achievement Award, Vinci Honor Award, Tagore Award, Dream Pride Award, and other recognitions from institutions including 4T Success Academy, Manikarnika Art Gallery, Delhi Art International, and CAA Talent Hunt 2021.
Her creative works have appeared in four published anthologies worldwide, including publications by SGSH Publication and Inkfetish Publication. She also serves as President of Vladimir Putin's Society in Moscow and Administrator of the “We Stand with Mr. Vladimir Putin Society.”
🌹 Author's Note
“A Dinner for My Dear Inspector” is a short fictional love letter written entirely from the imagination.
The character of Inspector Mirov is an original fictional creation inspired by my admiration for the distinguished screen presence, dignity and mature artistic persona of the legendary Spanish actor Sir Julio Peña Muñoz.
Piya Poppy and Inspector Mirov's marriage, relationship, correspondence, conversations and circumstances described in this letter are entirely fictional and form part of my artistic imagination. They are not intended to represent the personal life or biography of Sir Julio Peña Muñoz.
This letter is a small imagined moment from the life of two fictional characters who have found love, companionship and tenderness in one another. Through it, I wished to explore the quieter side of love—the affection found in an ordinary dinner, a remembered promise, a little teasing between husband and wife, and the simple knowledge that someone is waiting for you to come home.
I would also like to make one important distinction clear:
This work is dedicated specifically to the legendary Spanish actor Sir Julio Peña Muñoz (1917–1972), the classical twentieth-century actor, and is entirely separate from and unrelated to the contemporary Spanish actor Julio Peña Fernández, despite the similarity of their names.
This letter is my humble artistic tribute to Sir Julio Peña Muñoz and to the timeless qualities I associate with his screen presence—maturity, dignity, grace, restraint and quiet strength.
With love, admiration, compassion and artistic imagination,
Piya Poppy Rathbone 🌹

🌹 A Dinner for My Dear Inspector
A Little Love Letter from Piya Poppy to Inspector Mirov
My Dear Mirov,
I am sending your dinner to the office tonight because, knowing you, you will probably become so absorbed in your work that you will forget that you have not eaten. 😌
Please do not argue with me.
Yes, I know you are an Inspector.
Yes, I know there are investigations that cannot wait.
But your dinner can wait for neither you nor your investigations. 😤
So I am sending it to you myself—along with this little letter.
And while I was packing your meal, I suddenly remembered something.
Do you remember the promise you once made to me?
You said that one day, when your duties finally allowed you a little time, you would take me to that beautiful lakeside park.
You made me wait rather patiently, Inspector.
But eventually…
you kept your promise. 🌹
There we were together beside the quiet lake.
No investigation.
No reports.
No telephone calls.
No hurried footsteps.
Just you and me.
There were birds above the water, butterflies among the flowers, and rose petals drifting through the air as though the whole afternoon had been arranged especially for us.
Then you looked at me with that wonderfully serious expression of yours and asked,
“I love you, Poppy. Do you love me?”
What did you expect me to say, my dear Inspector? 🤭
After making me wait all that time?
I looked at you and whispered,
“I love you too.” ❤️
And apparently, that was enough to make you so happy that you decided to bury your wife beneath an entire shower of roses. 🤣🌹🌹🌹
When you carried me in your arms beneath them, I must confess, I did not object.
Not even a little. 😝🤭
Perhaps that is what I love most about you.
You are so serious about everything—the law, your duties, your responsibilities, your work.
And yet, somewhere beneath that stern Inspector's exterior, there is a man who remembers a promise made to his wife and quietly keeps it.
So tonight, while you are sitting at your desk surrounded by papers, I hope you will stop for a few minutes.
Eat your dinner.
Drink something warm.
And remember that somewhere beyond your office, there is a woman waiting for you to come home.
Your work may belong to the world.
But you, my dear Inspector, are loved at home. ❤️
And next time you promise to take me somewhere beautiful…
please don't make me wait quite so long.
Your wife has very little patience when roses are involved. 😝🌹
With all my love,
Your Poppy ❤️

Name: Anjali Joshi
Theme: Modern Work Life Balance - Alpha Feminity
Title: The Quite Architect of Endurance
Content:
*THE QUIET ARCHITECTURE OF ENDURANCE*

At 5:17 AM, the alarm had not yet rung when Anjali was already awake.

It was a practiced wakefulness, the kind that comes after two decades of negotiating with time. Outside her beautiful villa in the serene cantonment lanes of Dehradun, the morning was still veiled in a thin, winter mist. The milk vendor's bicycle bell was still distant. Inside, she lay for exactly ninety seconds, staring at the white ceiling of a house that finally felt like her own, letting the two worlds she inhabited assemble themselves in her mind like desks in a classroom before the students arrive.

By 5:30, she was two people, no, four people at once.

One, a mother, plaiting her son Aadhya's school hair with oil-slick fingers — he was thirteen and insisted he didn't need oiling, but she did it anyway — packing tiffin boxes where the gravy never leaked, while answering the house help's endless queries about whether to buy the local palak or the hill palak.

The second, a daughter, whose day always began with two phone calls that were her real alarm clock.

The phone rang at 5:42 AM. 

“Anju",  her mother's voice, crisp, efficient, even at this hour. Her mother, had retired as a Superintendent in the State Government Secretariat, and thirty years of noting files had made her punctuality a religion. 

“Aayi, you are up so early?” Anjali whispered, tucking the phone between shoulder and ear while folding Aadhya's uniform. Anjali and Kanchana had always called her Aayi — not Amma, not Mummy — a word that held both respect and warmth.

“Up since 4:30. Your father has gone for his walk. He left his tablet on. Remind him to take his BP pill, he will forget. You know your father. Senior Banker even in retirement, still thinks the world runs on SWIFT codes.”

Anjali laughed. Her father, Mr. Joshi, had been a senior officer at Bank, a man who could read a balance sheet like poetry and who was ever stylish in his appearance. 

Her Aayi continued, “Your sister called. She was stuck at the branch till 9 PM yesterday. A party for her achievement of exceeding the target . Kanchana said she will call you after her morning huddle.”

Kanchana, was an ambitious funloving woman— a Senior Manager at a private sector bank in Pune, brilliant with numbers, exhausted by them. And Poorvi, niece, was the family's latest philosopher.

“I will call her, Aayi. And you — did you take your tablet?”

“Ask Kiran to worry about me, not you. How is he?”

That was the third presence of the morning, but in person. Kiran, her husband, was already in the kitchen, making his strong filter coffee. Kiran was an anomaly in their family of salaried, pension-seeking professionals. He ran two successful parallel businesses — a chain of educational stationery distribution across Uttarakhand, and a small but thriving logistics startup for hill areas. He understood risk in a way her banker father never would.

“Your dad called me yesterday,” Kiran said, 

Anjali smiled. That was the architecture of her life — a Government employee Aayi who believed in procedure, a Senior Banker father who believed in prudence, a Senior Banker sister who was winning her own corporate battles in Pune, a niece who sent her voice notes saying “Doddamma, when will you come?”, husband Kiran who was building enterprises from scratch, and a son who just wanted his mother to watch his cricket match & let him on his own terms  to play games on phone.

And in the middle of it all, Anjali herself.

She left for the University at 9:45 AM. Not on her old scooter anymore — Dehradun's slopes had forced an upgrade to a small second-hand car — but with the same purple saree tucked with precision, the same battered, overstuffed laptop bag hanging heavy on her shoulder. The bag contained multitudes: registers for her Ph.D scholars, a half-written research paper on Jhumpa Lahiri's cultural dissonance, a permission letter for a new international seminar, and a small, carefully folded handkerchief embroidered by her Aayi five years ago, before her eyesight weakened.

The University gate was a threshold. On one side, she was Anjali, who needed to remind her father to take his pill, remind her sister to eat, remind Kiran to not skip lunch, and remind Aadhya to drink water. On the other, she was Dr. Joshi, Associate Professor.

“Good morning, Madam!” The chorus of Masters students in flying colors and trending fashion was her daily coronation.

Her cabin was small, but its walls were lined with history. Not just her own — SOF Olympiad shields from her previous work life , a Principal Leadership trophy from Prodigy Brains, a framed certificate from the Indian Talent Olympiad that read _Best Principal 2026_. They were not vanity. They were evidence. Proof that a woman who had once been told that a woman's high ambition ends up making things impossible had proven that high ambition ends up making things possible for oneself as well as others. She had rewritten an institution's destiny in her work place, Now she was trying to do it in the hills.

At 10:15 AM, her father called on video. He was back from his walk, in his tracksuit, holding his large SBI-branded diary.

“Anju” he said, his voice carrying the authoritative gentleness of a man used to sanctioning crores. “Your Aayi told me you didn't sleep well. I told your Aayi — banking and academia are same. Both have NPAs. Non-Performing Attitudes. You have to manage them.”

Anjali propped her phone against the trophy. “Daddy, you are giving me banking gyaan for my English department?”

“I am giving you life gyaan. Listen. Your sister Kanchana — she called me last night, exclaiming. Her Regional Head said she is apt for leadership. I told her the same thing I told you in 2006 when you got IV Rank in Kuvempu University and everyone said, what will you do with English? I told her — a Senior Banker never shows the ledger to everyone. You show them the profit. Let them wonder how you balanced it.”

He paused and softened. “Your Aayi and I, we are proud of you & Kanchana both, We had fixed salaries. Fixed DA. But you — you and Kiran —Kanchana & Ramesh, you are creating something new...building businesses, That is riskier than any loan I ever approved.”

That was their conversation. Short, coded, full of love disguised as financial advice. Her Aayi, the Govt employee, would never say “I love you” directly. She would say, “Have you filed your Income Tax return?” Her father would never say “I am worried about you.” He would say, “What is your CIBIL score of health?”

Next morning, at 11 AM, she delivered a lecture on Deconstruction in the Dept of English to her MA Final Year students, many of whom were pursuing research.

“The word 'ephemeral' — what does it mean?” she asked.

A boy in the back row, in a faded Nirvana t-shirt, mumbled, “Short-lived, Madam.”

“Good. Now use it in a sentence about your mother's love.”

The class laughed. Then fell silent. Then understood. She was not teaching vocabulary. She was teaching them to feel the weight of words, to understand that theory lives in kitchens and tiffin boxes.

After the lecture, her phone buzzed. A video call from Kanchana. Her sister was in her bank cabin, still in her formal blazer, eyes tired.


Anjali closed her cabin door.

“Kanchi,” she said, receiving her call, “Remember Appa's rule? He taught us — in banking, you never mix personal and professional accounts. But for us women, he forgot to tell us — we ARE the bank where both accounts are held. We have to overdraft ourselves daily.”

Kanchana laughed, tears coming. “Appa today told me to be less emotional. Can you imagine? The same Appa who was blissful, when I got my first promotion?”

.He advises because he was a Senior Banker. He cannot help it. He thinks every problem can be solved by provisioning. Keep some emotional capital for yourself. Don't lend it all to the office. And did you talk to Aayi?”

“I did. At 6 AM. She said, 'Kanchi, have you drunk warm water? Have you submitted your audit report?' Same sentence, same breath. That's our Aayi. Government file and motherly love in one memo,” Kanchana said.

“And Poorvi?” Anjali asked.

“On call with her now,” Kanchana said and flipped the camera. A small, cherubic face with ponytail appeared.

“Doddamma! See my new drawing! It is you! With a purple saree and a big book!” Poorvi shouted.

That was the dividend. That was the interest on all the endurance.

Lunch was a hurried affair at 1:15 PM, eaten while signing files and listening to a podcast on Robert Greene's laws of power. Her phone was a switchboard for an entire universe — a WhatsApp group for Ph.D scholars, another for faculty, a message from Aadhya's cricket coach, and a message from Kiran: _First consignment cleared for Nainital. Second truck stuck at Rishikesh. Will be late. Don't wait for dinner._

Kiran's two businesses meant he was often late, often stressed, often on the phone speaking about inventory and diesel prices. But he never once asked her to quit.

 “Logistics I can handle anywhere in North India. Stationery I can distribute from anywhere. You go build your department near Aayi-Appa.”

The afternoon brought a meeting with the Dean. He spoke in acronyms and deadlines. He questioned her decision to implement an international-level seminar on Diaspora Literature for a small hill university.

She didn't argue. She simply opened her laptop and showed him the publications of her students who were research aspirants, the same students who had once been told they were not good enough for Delhi.

He left, quieter than he had arrived.

At 5:30 PM, the siren bell rang, and the students flooded out like released birds. Anjali stayed. This was her second shift — the invisible one. She drafted a proposal for a teachers' workshop on “Empowerment for Modern Classrooms.” She corrected twenty essays, prepared a PPT for her next day's presentation on Cultural Conflict in Lahiri, and finally left the campus as the Dehradun dusk turned violet.

She reached home at 7:10 PM. The bindi on her forehead was still intact, a small miracle of endurance. The house smelled of freshly chopped onions and coriander — her Aayi had come over and was making dinner, because that's what Govt employee Aayis do after retirement; they take over their daughter's kitchen to show efficiency.

Her father was on the sofa, reading an economic newspaper with a magnifier, arguing with the TV news anchor.

“See this Anju,” he said, “Repo rate increased. Kiran's logistics cost will increase.”

“Appa, you are retired. Stop increasing my BP,” her Aayi called from the kitchen, in a saree that was as crisp as her notings had once been. “Anju, go change. You look tired. Kiran called, he said he will be home by 8.”

Aadhya was at the dining table, struggling with a Keats poem.

“Amma used to teach me this,” he said. “But I don't understand, Amma, what does 'to cease upon the midnight with no pain' mean?”

Anjali slipped off her sandals, her feet aching in a deep, familiar way, and sat beside her son. For a moment, she was not Dr. Joshi, not Madam, not Akka, not a daughter. She was just a woman who loved poetry.

“It means,” she said softly, translating the sublime into the domestic, “that sometimes, the most profound things happen quietly, without drama. Like falling asleep after a long day of honest work.”

Her son looked at her, truly looked at her, and said, “You are tired, Amma. Did you eat properly?”

It was the rare time that day someone had seen her, not her role.

Evenings were much awaited by her, cozy with her Aayi-Appa in Dehradun, the two pillars who had given her both discipline and dreams. Kiran returned at 8:15, his face tired but lit up, carrying two boxes of pastries — one for Aadhya, one for her parents.

“Second truck cleared,” he said. “Your logistics husband did it. Stationery order for three schools also done. Today profit, tomorrow tension.”

Her father immediately engaged him: “Kiran, what is your working capital cycle?”

Kiran grinned, “Appa, again audit? Aayi, save me.”

Her Aayi emerged with sambar, “ leave the boy alone. He has already done two businesses.

The whole house burst into laughter. That was their dinner — economics, English, logistics, and love.

And then the final ritual — phone calls with her younger sister Kanchana and her niece Poorvi. Two senior bankers from two different generations talking about NPAs and nappies, about CASA ratios and crayons, but both daughters calling their mother the same thing.

At 10 PM, it was a conference call.

“Aayi, are you there?” Kanchana asked.

“I am here, ” Aayi answered, now back at her own house next lane.

“Aayi, I told Appa today that I am taking one week leave. Just for Poorvi,” Kanchana said on the phone.

“And what did Appa say?” Anjali asked.

“He said, 'Good. Even RBI gives a moratorium. You are my daughter, you deserve one too,'” Kanchana mimicked.

Aayi interrupted, “Kanchana, moratorium is fine, but have you kept your leave application in writing? Government and Bank — both need everything in writing.”

“Aayi! You and Appa — one Government, one Bank. I am stuck between two audit systems,” Kanchana laughed.

Anjali smiled listening to them. This was her matriarchy — a mother who filed everything, a father who calculated everything, a sister who balanced everything, a husband Kiran who risked everything, and a son who was watching and learning what a woman could be.

That night, after the dishes were washed and the next day's schedule was sorted, Anjali sat at her small study table in the corner of the villa. She opened her diary — not the official one with meetings and deadlines, but a private, battered notebook. In it, she wrote one sentence in her elegant, looping handwriting:

_Today, I did not shatter. I endured. And endurance is its own kind of excellence._

She thought of Virginia Woolf's demand for "a room of one's own." She had her space now. Not a large one. A corner in a beautiful villa in Dehradun, a small car, a siren bell, and a large, loud, loving family of a Govt employee Aayi, a Senior Banker father, a Senior Banker sister, a niece who draws her in purple, a husband Kiran who runs two worlds in parallel, and a son Aadhya who is learning Keats from his mother and courage from his Aayi.

And yet, from that corner, she had built a life that was entirely hers — intellectually autonomous, economically independent, emotionally resilient.

The modern working woman is not a superwoman. She does not fly. She walks, heavily laden, across a tightrope stretched between tradition and ambition, between duty and desire. Sometimes she wobbles. Sometimes she weeps in a place where no one can hear. But every morning, she ties her saree, adjusts her bindi, and walks again.

Because the rope, she has learned, does not exist to make her fall.

It exists so she can learn that she can balance.

She switched off the light at 11:04 PM. The alarm was set for 5:17 AM.

And she would be awake before it rang.

Name: Trisha Vallamkonda Prathap
Title: The Amusing Irony
Content:
Just thinking of you
Makes my day,
My love is so true
That it'll never sway.

When you look at me
Like the most precious gem,
I make a silent plea:
I want this in every realm.

My heart melts at your smile,
My lips curve in your presence.
I know our bond isn't fragile;
I can fight the world in your defense.

You invade my dreams,
Covering your face.
Oh, how cruel this seems;
You make my heart race.

By the time I wake up,
Your voice that echoed in my ears—
Like a beautiful mashup—
Amazingly just disappears.

How are you there without being there?
How do I see you without seeing you?
I am fantasizing, I swear,
Yet I know everything I imagine is you.

It's an amusing irony:
I know you without knowing you.
It's just that one day destiny
Will make me meet you.

Name: Abhishek Garg
Theme: Criticism of Romeo Juliet Clause in India
Title: Childhood in Danger!
Content:
Introduction
In January 2026, the honorable Supreme Court of India in its landmark judgement of State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anurudh & Anr. Proposed a suggestion to the legislature to consider making a “Romeo Juliet Clause” to decriminalize consensual sex between adolescents for the purpose of balancing POCSO Act with personal choice and consent of adolescents.
What's the Issue?
This poses a major threat to the childhood, education and career of the adolescents, and especially the girl. Because the couple may not be able to handle the stress and responsibilities that come in case of pregnancy and the boy my back off from taking responsibility but the girl has to carry the pregnancy and give birth and carry the child. Being a teen single mother may create a life-long taboo on the girl and limit her education and career perspectives at a very young age. Hence in my opinion, the minimum age to have consensual sex should either remain at 18, though it is still a very young age and most of the teens in India are either in college or final years of school at that age, it would be better if the age is extended to 21 or 23, since most of the youth in India have completed their college and are enrolled in job by that age and attained considerable real world understanding and mental and emotional maturity to take this big decision wisely, this minimizes the stress of pregnancy and risk of one of them refusing to take the responsibility. 
Foreign Examples
Countries like the US, Canada and Germany, where such clause is in practice, have special provisions like: 
1.	State welfare schemes to provide nutrition, shelter, etc. for single teen mothers. 
2.	Families and guardians of the teens are involved to prevent abandonment of responsibilities or child by any of the 2 parents. 
3.	Schools have special programs to support teen parents to balance studies with parental responsibilities. 
4.	The teen parents are sent for counseling to help them cope with pregnancy stress and anxiety. 
5.	Family law allows the girl to claim maintenance from the boy even if both are below 18 in case of pregnancy.  
6.	Some states provide for abortion with or without the consent of both the teen’s parents, depending upon the state specific laws.
Problem with Implementation in India
But these require strong societal and administrative support and social acceptance that are clearly visible in those countries in all aspects but are still not quiet available in India, up to that mark. Even abortion  in adult couples, is a taboo and administrative infrastructure is well debated to be up to the mark, we are still a developing country with most of the families coming under middle or lower middle class economic bracket and education and awareness still not evenly spread nationwide. Also courts are too stuck in backlogs that even minute cases take years. In such a condition, managing teen pregnancy will be a significant hassle and frustration for the teen couple and their families as well as the judicial and administrative system.  
Schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Startup India, and MGNREGA faltered due to diversion of funds, weak monitoring, corruption, lack of public support and acceptance, contrast with deeply rooted norms, beliefs and practices and bureaucratic delays—hardly reassuring precedents for new welfare promises. 
Considering the streak of failed government schemes, launching new schemes to provide shelter, nutrition, etc. to the abandoned teen mother is most likely to be just another addition to the streak of failed schemes at the hands of malpractices and corruption in the system, or a huge load on national budget and funds, also, sexual assault cases of women of all age groups are soaring beyond limits. If we make shelters for teenage girls, pregnant from premature relationship, we are basically creating an open ground for any criminal minded person in the management of such facility to take advantage of such girls, since women who have children cannot take risk of moving out or getting into the hassle of legal procedures, we will basically be dragging such girls into a hell that they can’t escape partly because they are too afraid for their personal safety and partly for the child’s safety. All this can be avoided by making appropriate law to improve the current system, rather than adopting a completely foreign system that has too many red flags, in its implementation in our country, to be trusted.
Conclusion
Romeo Juliet law has sustained in many countries but at huge financial, legal, mental costs to the parties and the State. Hence we, keeping in mind the condition and past track record of our country and the condition of other countries that have passed such law, should refrain from making such a law. If the minimum age of consensual sex needs a reform, it shouldn’t be by reducing it, instead, to avoid forced or influenced marriages or relationships, the minimum age of consensual sex should be raised to 21 or 23, so the couple is mentally and emotionally mature enough and financially independent and stable enough o take such big decisions and accept all responsibilities that come along with such decisions.

Name: Nithya S
Title: Paths That Cross
Content:
Some people enter without a sound,
Like shadows drifting, barely found,
A passing glance, a fleeting stay
Yet something in them chooses to stay.

They leave a mark we can’t explain,
A quiet echo, a tender pain,
No storm can wash, no time can bend
The fragile space they came to mend.

There must be more than chance at play,
In how our lives just slip their way,
Through unseen threads our paths align,
As if your story touches mine.

Some bring lessons wrapped in ache,
Truths that only hearts can wake,
Some hold mirrors to our soul,
And show the parts we can’t control.

So hold each bond, though it may fade,
For nothing shared is ever wasted,
Even love that cannot stay
Still changes who we are today.

For love that comes, yet won’t remain,
Still softens loss, still shapes the pain
And in its quiet, fleeting sound,
The deepest kind of love is found.

Name: Saikat Kumar Maji
Title: The Man Who Collected Sunrises
Content:
Nobody in the village knew exactly what Shankar did for a living.
Some said he was a fisherman.
Some said he had once worked on a ship.
The children believed he was a magician because he disappeared every morning before sunrise and returned only after the first light touched the temple bell.
Shankar never corrected anyone. He lived alone in a small house at the edge of the village, beside an abandoned lighthouse. Every morning, he carried an old metal box to the shore. And every morning, before the sun appeared, he opened it. The villagers thought he kept money inside. The truth was stranger. He kept photographs. Hundreds of them.
Sunrises.
Not beautiful tourist photographs.
Ordinary ones.
A sunrise behind a fishing boat.
A sunrise over a railway bridge.
A sunrise seen through a hospital window.
A sunrise behind a school building with broken walls.
A sunrise above a farmer's field.
A sunrise reflected in a puddle beside a crowded road.
Each photograph had a date written on the back. And beneath the date was a name. Shankar called them his “morning witnesses.” One winter morning, a twelve-year-old girl named Mira followed him.

She hid behind rocks until he reached the lighthouse.

When Shankar opened the metal box, she stepped out.

“What are you doing?”

Shankar nearly dropped the box.

“You walk very quietly.”

“You walk very suspiciously.”

He smiled.

“What do you want?”

“I want to know why you collect sunrises.”

Shankar looked toward the horizon.

“Because people forget.”

“Forget what?”

“How beautiful an ordinary day can be.”

Mira shook her head.

“That doesn't explain the names.”

Shankar looked at the photographs.

“No.”

“What do the names mean?”

He sat on a rock.

“Every sunrise belongs to someone.”

Mira laughed.

“That's nonsense.”

“Probably.”

Then Shankar handed her a photograph.

It showed a railway station at dawn.

On the back was written:

**17 July — Ramesh, pointsman.**

“Who is Ramesh?”

“A railway worker.”

“And why did you photograph his sunrise?”

“Because that morning he stood on the tracks and stopped a train from entering a flooded section.”

Mira looked at him.

“Did he die?”

“No.”

“Was he famous?”

“No.”

“Did anyone give him a medal?”

Shankar smiled.

“I don't know.”

He took another photograph.

A woman standing outside a hospital.

**3 October — Dr. Leela.**

Another.

A young boy carrying a sack of rice.

**29 November — Arif.**

Another.

An old farmer sleeping beside a field.

**8 January — Haran.**

Mira looked confused.

“These people did great things?”

“Sometimes.”

“And sometimes?”

“Sometimes they simply survived a difficult day.”

Mira stared at the photographs.

“Why are you keeping all this?”

Shankar closed the box.

“Because one day someone may ask whether ordinary people mattered.”

“And you want proof?”

“Exactly.”

Years earlier, Shankar had worked in a government archive.

His job had been to preserve records of historical events.

He had discovered something that disturbed him.

History remembered battles.

Governments.

Leaders.

Disasters.

Victories.

But it rarely remembered the people who quietly held everything together.

The nurse who stayed after her shift.

The farmer who shared seeds with a neighbour.

The bus driver who waited for an old passenger.

The stranger who carried a child out of a flood.

The teacher who bought a student's books.

People disappeared.

Their names disappeared.

Their small acts disappeared.

Shankar decided to collect them.

Not for a museum.

Not for fame.

For the future.

One morning, many years later, Shankar did not return home.

Mira, now sixteen, went looking for him.

She found the metal box beside the lighthouse.

The photographs were gone.

Only one envelope remained.

Her name was written on it.

Inside was a letter.

**Mira,**

**You once asked why I collected sunrises.**

**The truth is, I was never collecting photographs.**

**I was collecting evidence.**

**Evidence that this country was built by people whose names were never printed in history books.**

**One day, you will leave this village. You will see cities, airports, factories, towers and highways. You will think those things are the country.**

**They are not.**

**The country is the invisible work done by millions of people every morning before anyone notices.**

**Don't forget them.**

Mira looked toward the sea.

The sun was rising.

For the first time, she understood why Shankar had photographed ordinary mornings.

They were never ordinary.

Not really.

She returned home and opened an old wooden cupboard.

Inside were thousands of blank photographs.

She took one.

Then another.

The next morning, she walked to the railway station.

A woman was sweeping the platform.

Mira took a photograph.

On the back, she wrote:

**15 September — Kamala.**

Then she walked to the fishing harbour.

An old man was repairing a torn net.

Another photograph.

**15 September — Joseph.**

At the government school, a teacher was unlocking the classroom before everyone else arrived.

Another photograph.

**15 September — Meera.**

Day after day, she continued.

Years passed.

Mira became a journalist.

Then a historian.

Then the founder of an unusual archive.

She called it:

**The Sunrise Archive.**

People began sending photographs from every corner of the country.

A sanitation worker beginning his shift before dawn.

A soldier writing a letter home.

A farmer opening his fields.

A baker lighting his oven.

A nurse leaving a night shift.

A student studying under a streetlight.

A mechanic opening his workshop.

A mother preparing breakfast for her children before going to work.

Each photograph carried a name.

No titles.

No awards.

No politics.

Just names.

And underneath every name, the same sentence:

**“One of the people who kept the country awake.”**

Decades later, an old woman stood in front of the archive's final wall.

She was Mira.

Her hands trembled as she placed one last photograph inside the frame.

It showed a lighthouse at sunrise.

Beside it stood an old man holding a metal box.

Shankar.

On the back of the photograph, Mira had written:

**“The man who taught me that a country is not remembered by how loudly it speaks, but by how quietly its people keep it alive.”**

She stepped back.

Outside, dawn was breaking.

For a moment, the entire city seemed to pause.

Then thousands of lights switched off.

Shops opened.

Buses moved.

Factories started.

Fishermen pushed their boats into the water.

Children ran toward schools.

Hospitals woke into another busy day.

The country began another morning.

And somewhere inside that enormous, restless morning was the life of a man who had spent his entire life proving one simple thing:

**Every sunrise has a witness.**

And every country has people worth remembering.

Name: Aruna Chaturvedi
Title: मन के हारे हार है,मन के जीते जीत
Content:
मन के हारे हार है, मन के जीते जीत।
संकल्प अटल हो तो मिलती हर मंज़िल निश्चित।
हार अगर मन में हो तो मंज़िल दूर नज़र आती है।
मन में यदि विश्वास हो, किस्मत भी राह बनाती है।

आईआईटी की हार ने अभिजय का साहस न तोड़ा,
गूगल तक पहुँचने का उसने अपना सपना न छोड़ा।
असफलताओं ने राह रोकी, पर हौसले कभी झुके नहीं,
मन ने जीत का दीप जलाया, इसलिए कदम कभी रुके नहीं।

टाइम्स स्क्वायर पर माँ का गौरव जब मुस्काया,
दुनिया की हर ऊँचाई ने चरणों में शीश झुकाया।
जीवन कहता है— हिम्मत कभी मत हार,
दृढ़ संकल्प से ही मिलता विजयी उपहार।

जो अपने संकल्पों पर हर पल अडिग खड़ा रहता है,
समय भी उसके साहस का सम्मान सदा करता है।
विश्वास की लौ कभी न बुझने देना, यही जीवन की रीत,
सच है, मन के हारे हार है, मन के जीते जीत।

Name: Yonick Sequeira
Title: Feeling
Content:
The strangest thing, this truly is. 
The feeling that comes and goes as waves on the shore.
The raging of a storm, in cloudy bliss, 
the drops of rain crashing down in rhythmic motif.
A strike of the flint, a spray of sparks, 
the flame that arrives like swift beats on a broken bar.
Allowed a while, stayed too long, 
did light a burn that seemed to sing and atone.
As Cupid’s being, his ancestry did beget, 
a powerful kiss his arrows do portray,
With Venus and War, together entwined, 
this being of chaos, a damning fate will invite.
As subtle a thing, as first snow of winter on rosy cheek, 
ever so soft, sweet, gentle, a living to see.
A violent kind, this sweet thing, can possess, 
the nature of it, a burning blaze, a tormenting ache.
Purest of all, known to be, this mysterious mystery, 
radiating light around all engulfed by darkness.
This, but a small fraction, of a marvelous draft, 
this emotion is amiss, plainly tough.

As Dante did, with Virgil write, his traversal through Inferno in all its might
All to save lovely Beatrice’s fate, captivated by The Prince, in darkness plight.
With vim and zest, he did slay, fiends and demons, all who crossed his way
Etching in time, the power of It, harnessed, able to withstand hellish fright.

“These violent delights have violent ends.” Very true these words, Romeo did hear,
Waiting for Juliet, at weddings gate, with friar and all, eager to bear,
The burden that awaited, the odyssey imminent, an impulse out of control, oust logic
Transforms into a dreary date, with sorrow and misery, a fate, ever so tragic.

Just as The Sun and The Moon, struck by the same emotion of doom
Separated by time, the ghastly force, keeping them apart, in cruel tune.
This power of the sense, so high in potent, invoked the divine, to split the sane,
An eclipse, He did create, for these stellar beasts, in union, together, to be, keeping torment abate, 
even if, only for an hour.

This mystery of mysteries, the feeling so sweet, the potential to burn, the ability to save
A needy soul, on stranger tide. This emotion of chaos, of beauty bright, vibrant lit in a dying light,
The sense to fight beyond all fear, for something of such allure, a mind always will cave.
To Live is to Love, or so they say. True is all, worth the horrendous fight.
“Never fall off, never do stray. Love is a feeling, that always must stay,
Trial or tribulation, in path will appear, nothing this sense cannot handle, 
unto ends it will wage, unbeknownst time, now and forever.”

Name: Sugitha
Title: Love I had once
Content:
The most joyful chapters of my life unfolded with my beloved babies.
Their delicate paws, their spirited energy, their comforting presence, their unconditional affection… I didn't realize I was treasuring moments that I would later desperately wish to relive.

Today, I carry these precious memories within a heart that has never fully mended.
I long for them with such profound ache that even the thought of their joy brings tears to my eyes.

I simply want my babies back.
Just one more day. One more gentle touch. One more loving call.

Until that time comes, I'll nurture the belief that somewhere in the beyond, they're holding space for me… and someday, I'll be reunited with all my babies, cradled safely in my arms once more.

Name: Naramon Baneh Uriah
Title: The Thief Who Stole My Peace
Content:
Once, I shed my tears for a love I surrendered,
A love that was never meant to be remembered.
A single mother, with a heart burnt and bruised,
I had forgotten the love I once refused.

Then someone came quietly, like a thief in the night,
Stole my wounded heart and made the darkness light.
He awakened the songs I had buried away,
And taught my tired soul to dream once again.

For a little while, love sounded sweet,
Like an old forgotten song with a beautiful beat.
I smiled at the feelings I thought I had lost,
Not knowing that loving again would carry a cost.

Then time flew by, and sleep wouldn't come,
My restless heart asking, “Where have you gone?”
I searched through the silence, I questioned the night,
Trying to understand what had once felt so right.

And then I learned the truth, painful and clear—
The thief who stole my heart had stolen my peace too, my dear.
He came like a dream, then vanished like rain,
Leaving me holding the echoes of love and pain.

Perhaps some thieves don't come to stay;
They only come to steal a piece of you away.
And perhaps some loves are lessons in disguise—
They break your heart, yet open your eyes.

So I gather my pieces, though tender they may be,
And return my stolen heart back to me.
No more sleepless nights, no more chasing the past—
Some thieves steal your peace, but you still rise at last.
